In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu al-Darda', that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever memorises ten verses from the beginning of Surat al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjal." In another narration: "from the end of al-Kahf." Also in Muslim, from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an: "Whoever among you meets him (i.e., the Dajjal), let him recite over him the opening verses of Surat al-Kahf." This was also mentioned by al-Tha'labi. He said: Samurah ibn Jundub said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ten verses of Surat al-Kahf by heart, the trial of the Dajjal will not harm him." And whoever recites the whole surah enters Paradise.

"All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book, and has not made in it any crookedness. [He made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever." (1–3)

His Exalted saying: "All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book and has not made in it any crookedness, [but has made it] straight." Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the rabbis of the Jews, and said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad, describe his attributes to them and inform them of what he says, for they are the People of the First Book, and they possess knowledge that we do not have, [being] the knowledge of the prophets." So the two set out until they reached Medina, and they asked the rabbis of the Jews about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), described his affair to them, and informed them of some of his words. They said to them: "You are the People of the Torah, and we have come to you so that you may tell us about this companion of ours." The rabbis of the Jews said to them: "Ask him about three things which we instruct you [to ask], for if he informs you of them, then he is a sent prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator, so decide about him as you see fit. Ask him about youths who went forth in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about a wandering man who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, what his account was. And ask him about the Spirit, what it is. If he informs you of that, then follow him, for he is a prophet; and if he does not, then he is a fabricating man, so do with his affair what seems best to you."

Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt came back and reached Mecca to the Quraysh, and they said: "O assembly of Quraysh! We have come to you with the decisive matter between you and Muhammad (ﷺ). The rabbis of the Jews instructed us to ask him about things they told us [to ask]. If he informs you of them, then he is a prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator, so decide about him as you see fit." They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, inform us about youths who went forth in the earliest age, for they had a wondrous story; and about a man who was a wanderer who reached the easts and wests of the earth; and inform us about the Spirit, what is it?" He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "I will inform you of what you asked about tomorrow," and he did not make an exception [by saying "if Allah wills"]. So they departed from him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained, as they claimed, fifteen nights, while Allah did not send down any revelation to him concerning that and Jibril did not come to him, until the people of Mecca spread rumours and said: "Muhammad promised us tomorrow, and today it is fifteen nights, and we have awoken [each morning] without him informing us of anything of what we asked him about." The delay of revelation grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) greatly, and what the people of Mecca were saying distressed him. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with the surah of the People of the Cave, in which is His reproach to him for his grief over them, and the account of what they had asked him about: the affair of the youths, the wandering man, and the Spirit.

Ibn Ishaq said: It was reported to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "You have delayed from me, O Jibril, until I have thought ill [of you]." Jibril said to him: "And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that, and your Lord is never forgetful." Then He opened the surah, blessed and exalted is He, with His praise and with mention of the prophethood of His Messenger (ﷺ), when they denied it on his account. He said: "All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book," meaning Muhammad, "that you are a messenger from Me," i.e., a confirmation of what they asked about of your prophethood. "And has not made in it any crookedness, [but has made it] straight," i.e., upright, without any contradiction in it. "To warn of severe punishment from Him," i.e., the swift punishment in this world, and a painful torment in the Hereafter, i.e., from the presence of your Lord who sent you as a messenger. "And to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds, that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever," i.e., the abode of eternity in which they will not die: those who believed you in what you brought, which others denied, and who acted upon the deeds you commanded them.

"And to warn those who say, 'Allah has taken a son.'" He means the Quraysh in their saying: "We worship the angels, and they are the daughters of Allah." "They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers," who greatly disliked his separation [from them] and the disparagement of their religion. "Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths," i.e., their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. "They say nothing but a lie." "Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this discourse," [grieving] over them when he missed what he had hoped from them; i.e., do not do it. Ibn Hisham said: "Bakhi'un nafsaka" means destroying yourself, as related to me by Abu 'Ubayda. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Ah, is this one who destroys himself with grief,
by a thing the decrees have plucked from his hands?

Its plural is bakhi'un and bakha'a. This verse is from a qasida of his [whose opening is: "The traces of Lamiyya at Hazwa, the remains, the rains and the streams have effaced them after us"]. And the Arabs' saying: "I have exhausted my counsel and myself for him," meaning I exerted myself for him.

"Indeed, We have made what is upon the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed." Ibn Ishaq said: i.e., which of them follows My command most and acts most in obedience to Me. "And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren, dust-dry ground." i.e., the earth; and what is upon it is perishing and will pass away, and the return is to Me, and I will recompense each for his deed. So do not despair, and let not what you see and hear in it grieve you. Ibn Hisham said: al-sa'id is the surface of the earth, its plural is su'ud. Dhu al-Rummah, describing a young gazelle, said:

As if, in the forenoon, it throws over the surface [of the earth] a wine-brewing dabbaba with the pure wine of a head...

This verse is from a qasida of his [whose opening is: "Does the longing for the trace of Kharqa's dwelling, the water of love, flow from your eyes?"]. Al-sa'id also means the road, and it has come in a hadith: "Beware of sitting on the sa'udat," meaning the roads. Al-juruz is land that produces nothing; its plural is ajraz. It is said: "a juruz year and ajraz years," which is the one without rain, in which there is dryness, aridity and hardship. Dhu al-Rummah, describing camels, said:

The wasting and the barren years have consumed what was in their bellies, so only the thick ribs remain.

Ibn Ishaq said: Then he proceeded to the account of what they had asked about concerning the youths, saying: "Or do you think that the People of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?" i.e., there were among My signs in them what I placed upon the servants of My proof that is more wondrous than that. Ibn Hisham said: al-Raqim is the writing in which their account was inscribed; its plural is ruqum. Al-Ajjaj said:

And the place of rest of the inscribed Mushaf.

This verse is from an urjuza of his [whose opening is: "O abode of Salma, be at peace, then be at peace, at Sasam or to the right of Samsam"]. Ibn Ishaq said: Then He said: "When the youths retreated to the cave and said, 'Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us from our affair right guidance.' So We struck over their ears in the cave for a number of years. Then We awakened them that We might know which of the two parties was most accurate in computing the time they had remained." Then He said: "We relate to you their account in truth," i.e., with the truth of the report: "Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance. And We fortified their hearts when they stood up and said, 'Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; never will we invoke other than Him a deity. We would have certainly spoken, then, an excessive transgression.'" i.e., they did not associate with Me as you associated with Me that of which you have no knowledge. Ibn Hisham said: al-shatat is extremism and going beyond the truth. Aʿsha of Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba said:

Will you desist, while no one restrains those of excess, as a spear-thrust in which the oil and the wick go?

This verse is from a qasida of his [whose opening is: "Bid farewell to Hurayra, for the caravan is departing, and can you bear a farewell, O man?"]. Ibn Ishaq said: "These our people have taken other deities besides Him; why do they not bring for them a clear authority?" Ibn Ishaq said: i.e., with a conclusive proof. "Who is more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah a lie? And when you have withdrawn from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you from your affair ease." "And you would see the sun when it rises inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets passing them on the left, while they are in a spacious place from it." Ibn Hisham said: tazawaru means inclines, and it is from al-zawr. Abu al-Zahf al-Kulaybi said, describing a land:

Beyond Layla is a land of samhadar... [its wide, far, misleading expanse; the pasture; the crooked road...] the barren pasture far from our desire, where the camels are worn out by the Khums [watering of the camels] and the harsh...

These two verses are from an urjuza of his. "Taqridhum dhat al-shimal" means it passes them and leaves them on its left. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Toward caravans which pass the high sand-hills of Mushrif on the left, and on their right the Fawaris...

This verse is from a qasida of his [whose opening is: "Did you not ask today of the deserted traces at Hazwa, and does the desolate wilderness know?"]. Al-fajwa is the spaciousness; its plural is al-fija'. The poet said:

You clothed your people in shame and disgrace, until they were laid bare and took up residence in the wide space of the house.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 1–3 (part 2 of 2):

﴿That is among the signs of Allah.﴾ That is, it is a proof against those among the People of the Book who knew these matters about them, those whom these people were directed to question you about, to test the truth of your prophethood through the report about them.

﴿Whom Allah guides, he is the one guided; but whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for him a protector to guide him.﴾ And you think them awake, while they are asleep. And We turn them to the right and to the left, and their dog stretches forth its forelegs at the threshold (al-wasid).﴾ Ibn Hisham said: al-Wasid is the door. Al-Absi, whose name is ʿAbd ibn Wahb (in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "ʿUbayd ibn Wahb"), said:

In a desert wasteland whose gate does not close against me,
and my acquaintance there is not disliked.

This line is among several verses of his. Al-Wasid also means the courtyard (al-finaʾ), and its plural is waṣāʾid, wuṣud, and wuṣdān.

﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾ up to His saying ﴿those who prevailed over their affair﴾, meaning the people of authority and kingship among them.

﴿We will surely take over them a place of worship.﴾ ﴿They will say: "[They were] three, the fourth of them their dog"; and they will say: "[They were] five, the sixth of them their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say: "[They were] seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Say: "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument, and do not seek a ruling from any of them about them."﴾ That is, do not dispute with them, for they have no knowledge of them.

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [when adding], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance."﴾ That is: do not say about anything they ask you of, as you said in this case, "I will inform you tomorrow," but add "If Allah wills," and remember your Lord when you forget, and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the report of what you asked me about, to right guidance," for you do not know what I will do in that matter.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and exceeded by nine.﴾ That is, they will say that.

﴿Say: "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears! They have no protector other than Him, and He does not share His command with anyone."﴾ That is, nothing that they asked you about was hidden from Him.

I say: This is what occurred in the Sirah concerning the report of the People of the Cave, which we have mentioned in its order.[[See Sirah Ibn Hisham, p. 192, Europe edition, and vol. 1, p. 321, Matbaʿat al-Halabi edition.]] The report of Dhu al-Qarnayn will come later, then we return to the beginning of the surah and say: the meaning of "al-hamdu lillah" has already been explained.

Al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Abu ʿUbayd, and the majority of the exegetes claimed that in the beginning of this surah there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and that the meaning is: "Praise belongs to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book, upright (qayyiman), and did not make in it any crookedness." "Qayyiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Qatada said: the statement is in its natural order without any inversion or postponement, and its meaning is: "He did not make for it any crookedness, but We made it upright (qayyim)." The saying of al-Dahhak regarding it is good, namely that the meaning of "qayyiman" is "straight" (mustaqim), that is, straight in wisdom, with no error, no corruption, and no contradiction. It was also said: "qayyiman" means guardian over the earlier books, confirming them. It was also said: "qayyiman" means always establishing proofs.

"ʿIwajan" is the object (maf'ul bihi). The word ʿiwaj, with the ʿayn vowelled with a kasra, is used for crookedness in religion, opinion, affairs, and paths; and with the ʿayn vowelled with a fatha, it is used for physical objects, such as wood or a wall. This has already been explained.

There is no crookedness in the Qur'an, that is, no defect; that is, it is not self-contradictory or inconsistent, as the Exalted said: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much inconsistency.﴾[[See vol. 5, p. 288.]] It was also said: that is, He did not make it created, as is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the Exalted's saying: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness﴾.[[See vol. 15, p. 5 (252). This is the second half of a line by Ghaylan ibn Huraith. Its complete form, as in Lisan al-ʿArab:

"yastawiʿu al-bawʿayni min jarīrati"

"al-manhur" (with the letter ḥāʾ and a ḍamma on the mīm) is a dialectal form of "al-nahr," meaning the chest. This word appears in the originals, in al-Jawhari's Sihah, and in Lisan al-ʿArab under the root "nakhara," and "ladun" (with the letter khāʾ, which is the nose). Ibn Barri added a correction, saying: the correct recitation is as Sibawayh recited it: "ila manhurihi" with ḥāʾ. The poet described a camel or a horse with a long neck, so that its neck fills, from its halter with which it is tied, a measure of two bāʿ (outstretched arms) between its jaws and its chest. "Al-jarir" is the rope.]] He said: "uncreated."

Muqatil said: "ʿiwajan" means disagreement. The poet said:

I continue my love for the true friend out of generosity,
and there is no good in one who is crooked in love.

﴿To warn of a severe punishment﴾, that is, that Muhammad or the Qur'an may warn. There is an implied object here, namely: to warn the disbelievers of the punishment of Allah. This severe punishment may be in this world and may be in the Hereafter.

﴿From Him﴾, that is, from His presence. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "min ladunhu" with the dal silent and with the ḍamma indicated, and the kasra on the nun, and the hāʾ is joined to a yāʾ. The rest read "ladunhu," with a ḍamma on the dal, the nun silent, and a ḍamma on the hāʾ.

Al-Jawhari said: there are three dialectal forms of "ladun": ladun, ladā, and ladu. He said:

"min ladu liḥyayhi ila manḥurihi"

Al-manḥur is a dialectal form of al-manḥar.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾, that is, "that they will have" (bi-anna lahum).

(A good reward) is Paradise.

(Remaining therein) means abiding forever.

(Forever) means without any end. If you take "tabshir" to mean "bayan" (clarification), then the preposition "bi" in "bi-anna" is not needed. "Al-ajr al-hasan" is the great reward that leads to Paradise.

Toward caravans which pass the high sand-hills of Mushrif on the left, and on their right the Fawaris...

You clothed your people in shame and disgrace, until they were laid bare and took up residence in the wide space of the house.

And We turn them to the right and to the left, and their dog stretches forth its forelegs at the threshold (al-wasid).﴾ Ibn Hisham said: al-Wasid is the door. Al-Absi, whose name is ʿAbd ibn Wahb (in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "ʿUbayd ibn Wahb"), said:

In a desert wasteland whose gate does not close against me,
and my acquaintance there is not disliked.

﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾ up to His saying ﴿those who prevailed over their affair﴾, meaning the people of authority and kingship among them.

Say: "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument, and do not seek a ruling from any of them about them."﴾ That is, do not dispute with them, for they have no knowledge of them.

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [when adding], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance."﴾ That is: do not say about anything they ask you of, as you said in this case, "I will inform you tomorrow," but add "If Allah wills," and remember your Lord when you forget, and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the report of what you asked me about, to right guidance," for you do not know what I will do in that matter.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and exceeded by nine.﴾ That is, they will say that.

﴿Say: "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears! They have no protector other than Him, and He does not share His command with anyone."﴾ That is, nothing that they asked you about was hidden from Him.

I say: This is what occurred in the Sirah concerning the report of the People of the Cave, which we have mentioned in its order.[[See Sirah Ibn Hisham, p. 192, Europe edition, and vol. 1, p. 321, Matbaʿat al-Halabi edition.]] The report of Dhu al-Qarnayn will come later, then we return to the beginning of the surah and say: the meaning of "al-hamdu lillah" has already been explained.

Al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Abu ʿUbayd, and the majority of the exegetes claimed that in the beginning of this surah there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and that the meaning is: "Praise belongs to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book, upright (qayyiman), and did not make in it any crookedness." "Qayyiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Qatada said: the statement is in its natural order without any inversion or postponement, and its meaning is: "He did not make for it any crookedness, but We made it upright (qayyim)." The saying of al-Dahhak regarding it is good, namely that the meaning of "qayyiman" is "straight" (mustaqim), that is, straight in wisdom, with no error, no corruption, and no contradiction. It was also said: "qayyiman" means guardian over the earlier books, confirming them. It was also said: "qayyiman" means always establishing proofs.

"ʿIwajan" is the object (maf'ul bihi). The word ʿiwaj, with the ʿayn vowelled with a kasra, is used for crookedness in religion, opinion, affairs, and paths; and with the ʿayn vowelled with a fatha, it is used for physical objects, such as wood or a wall. This has already been explained.

"yastawiʿu al-bawʿayni min jarīrati"

"al-manhur" (with the letter ḥāʾ and a ḍamma on the mīm) is a dialectal form of "al-nahr," meaning the chest. This word appears in the originals, in al-Jawhari's Sihah, and in Lisan al-ʿArab under the root "nakhara," and "ladun" (with the letter khāʾ, which is the nose). Ibn Barri added a correction, saying: the correct recitation is as Sibawayh recited it: "ila manhurihi" with ḥāʾ. The poet described a camel or a horse with a long neck, so that its neck fills, from its halter with which it is tied, a measure of two bāʿ (outstretched arms) between its jaws and its chest. "Al-jarir" is the rope.]] He said: "uncreated."

Muqatil said: "ʿiwajan" means disagreement. The poet said:

I continue my love for the true friend out of generosity,
and there is no good in one who is crooked in love.

﴿To warn of a severe punishment﴾, that is, that Muhammad or the Qur'an may warn. There is an implied object here, namely: to warn the disbelievers of the punishment of Allah. This severe punishment may be in this world and may be in the Hereafter.

﴿From Him﴾, that is, from His presence. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "min ladunhu" with the dal silent and with the ḍamma indicated, and the kasra on the nun, and the hāʾ is joined to a yāʾ. The rest read "ladunhu," with a ḍamma on the dal, the nun silent, and a ḍamma on the hāʾ.

Al-Jawhari said: there are three dialectal forms of "ladun": ladun, ladā, and ladu. He said:

"min ladu liḥyayhi ila manḥurihi"

Al-manḥur is a dialectal form of al-manḥar.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾, that is, "that they will have" (bi-anna lahum).

(A good reward) is Paradise.

(Remaining therein) means abiding forever.

(Forever) means without any end. If you take "tabshir" to mean "bayan" (clarification), then the preposition "bi" in "bi-anna" is not needed. "Al-ajr al-hasan" is the great reward that leads to Paradise.

They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "The surah of the People of the Cave. Whoever recites it on Friday, he is forgiven for the following Friday and three additional days, and he is given a light that reaches the heaven, and he is protected from the trial of the Dajjal." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, and al-Mahdawi also mentioned it with the same meaning. In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, he said: Whoever recites Surat al-Kahf on the night of Friday, light will shine for him from what is between him and the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-'Atiq). In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu al-Darda', that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever memorises ten verses from the beginning of Surat al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjal." In another narration: "from the end of al-Kahf." Also in Muslim, from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an: "Whoever among you meets him (i.e., the Dajjal), let him recite over him the opening verses of Surat al-Kahf." This was also mentioned by al-Tha'labi. He said: Samurah ibn Jundub said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ten verses of Surat al-Kahf by heart, the trial of the Dajjal will not harm him." And whoever recites the whole surah enters Paradise.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

"All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book, and has not made in it any crookedness. [He made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever." Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the rabbis of the Jews, and said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad, describe his attributes to them and inform them of what he says, for they are the People of the First Book, and they possess knowledge that we do not have, [being] the knowledge of the prophets." So the two set out until they reached Medina, and they asked the rabbis of the Jews about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), described his affair to them, and informed them of some of his words. They said to them: "You are the People of the Torah, and we have come to you so that you may tell us about this companion of ours." The rabbis of the Jews said to them: "Ask him about three things which we instruct you [to ask], for if he informs you of them, then he is a sent prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator, so decide about him as you see fit. Ask him about youths who went forth in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about a wandering man who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, what his account was. And ask him about the Spirit, what it is. If he informs you of that, then follow him, for he is a prophet; and if he does not, then he is a fabricating man, so do with his affair what seems best to you."

Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt came back and reached Mecca to the Quraysh, and they said: "O assembly of Quraysh! We have come to you with the decisive matter between you and Muhammad (ﷺ). The rabbis of the Jews instructed us to ask him about things they told us [to ask]. If he informs you of them, then he is a prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator, so decide about him as you see fit." They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, inform us about youths who went forth in the earliest age, for they had a wondrous story; and about a man who was a wanderer who reached the easts and wests of the earth; and inform us about the Spirit, what is it?" He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "I will inform you of what you asked about tomorrow," and he did not make an exception [by saying "if Allah wills"]. So they departed from him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained, as they claimed, fifteen nights, while Allah did not send down any revelation to him concerning that and Jibril did not come to him, until the people of Mecca spread rumours and said: "Muhammad promised us tomorrow, and today it is fifteen nights, and we have awoken [each morning] without him informing us of anything of what we asked him about." The delay of revelation grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) greatly, and what the people of Mecca were saying distressed him. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with the surah of the People of the Cave, in which is His reproach to him for his grief over them, and the account of what they had asked him about: the affair of the youths, the wandering man, and the Spirit.

Ibn Ishaq said: It was reported to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "You have delayed from me, O Jibril, until I have thought ill [of you]." Jibril said to him: "And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord; to Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that, and your Lord is never forgetful." Then He opened the surah, blessed and exalted is He, with His praise and with mention of the prophethood of His Messenger (ﷺ), when they denied it on his account. He said: "All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book," meaning Muhammad, "that you are a messenger from Me," i.e., a confirmation of what they asked about of your prophethood. "And has not made in it any crookedness, [but has made it] straight," i.e., upright, without any contradiction in it. "To warn of severe punishment from Him," i.e., the swift punishment in this world, and a painful torment in the Hereafter, i.e., from the presence of your Lord who sent you as a messenger. "And to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds, that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever," i.e., the abode of eternity in which they will not die: those who believed you in what you brought, which others denied, and who acted upon the deeds you commanded them.

"And to warn those who say, 'Allah has taken a son.'" He means the Quraysh in their saying: "We worship the angels, and they are the daughters of Allah." "They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers," who greatly disliked his separation [from them] and the disparagement of their religion. "Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths," i.e., their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. "They say nothing but a lie." "Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this discourse," [grieving] over them when he missed what he had hoped from them; i.e., do not do it. Ibn Hisham said: "Bakhi'un nafsaka" means destroying yourself, as related to me by Abu 'Ubayda. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Ah, is this one who destroys himself with grief,
by a thing the decrees have plucked from his hands?

Its plural is bakhi'un and bakha'a. This verse is from a qasida of his [whose opening is: "The traces of Lamiyya at Hazwa, the remains, the rains and the streams have effaced them after us"]. And the Arabs' saying: "I have exhausted my counsel and myself for him," meaning I exerted myself for him.

This word appears in the originals, in al-Jawhari's Sihah, and in Lisan al-ʿArab under the root "nakhara," and "ladun" (with the letter khāʾ, which is the nose). Ibn Barri added a correction, saying: the correct recitation is as Sibawayh recited it: "ila manhurihi" with ḥāʾ. The poet described a camel or a horse with a long neck, so that its neck fills, from its halter with which it is tied, a measure of two bāʿ (outstretched arms) between its jaws and its chest. "Al-jarir" is the rope.]] He said: "uncreated."

Muqatil said: "ʿiwajan" means disagreement. The poet said:

I continue my love for the true friend out of generosity,
and there is no good in one who is crooked in love.

﴿To warn of a severe punishment﴾, that is, that Muhammad or the Qur'an may warn. There is an implied object here, namely: to warn the disbelievers of the punishment of Allah. This severe punishment may be in this world and may be in the Hereafter.

﴿From Him﴾, that is, from His presence. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "min ladunhu" with the dal silent and with the ḍamma indicated, and the kasra on the nun, and the hāʾ is joined to a yāʾ. The rest read "ladunhu," with a ḍamma on the dal, the nun silent, and a ḍamma on the hāʾ.

Al-Jawhari said: there are three dialectal forms of "ladun": ladun, ladā, and ladu. He said:

"min ladu liḥyayhi ila manḥurihi"

Al-manḥur is a dialectal form of al-manḥar.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾, that is, "that they will have" (bi-anna lahum).

(A good reward) is Paradise.

(Remaining therein) means abiding forever.

(Forever) means without any end. If you take "tabshir" to mean "bayan" (clarification), then the preposition "bi" in "bi-anna" is not needed. "Al-ajr al-hasan" is the great reward that leads to Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 4–5:

Allah's saying: ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ They are the Jews, who said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians, who said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the Quraysh, who said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So the warning at the beginning of the surah is general, and this one is specific to those who say that Allah has a son.

(﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾) "Min" (min) is extra (silah), meaning: they have no knowledge of that statement, because they are imitators (muqallidah) who said it without evidence.

(﴿Nor do their fathers﴾) meaning their forefathers (aslaf).

(﴿How dreadful is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾) "Kalimatan" (kalimatan) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), meaning: how dreadful is that word as a word. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "kalimatun" (kalimatun) in the nominative, meaning: a word has become great, namely their saying "Allah has taken a son." According to this reading there is no need for an implied element. It is said: "kabura al-shay'" (kabura al-shay') means the thing became great, and "kabura al-rajul" (kabura al-rajul) means the man became old.

(﴿Comes out of their mouths﴾) This is in the position of a qualifier (sifah).

(﴿They speak only lies﴾) meaning: they say nothing but falsehood.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps﴾. "Bakhi'un" means destroying and killing, and it has already been discussed. "Atharihim" is the plural of "athar," and it is also said "ithr." The meaning is: after their turning away and their aversion from you.

(If they do not believe in this discourse) that is, the Qur'an.

(Asafan) that is, sorrow and anger over their disbelief. It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 7:

The Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: the Exalted's words, "Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it." "Ma" (whatever) and "zinatan" (an adornment) are two objects. The adornment (zinah) is everything that is on the surface of the earth, and so it is general, because it indicates its Creator. Ibn Jubayr said, relating from Ibn Abbas, that by "adornment" he meant the men; Mujahid said the same. Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas that the adornment is the caliphs and the rulers. Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, concerning the Exalted's words, "Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it," that he said: "The scholars are the adornment of the earth." A group said: He meant the blessings, the garments, the fruits, the greenery, the waters, and what is similar to these, of which there is adornment; and the solid mountains and everything that has no adornment in it, such as snakes and scorpions, are not included. The view that it is general is more preferable, and that everything on the earth has adornment in terms of its creation, its making, and its perfection.

The verse is an extensive consolation, meaning: Do not be concerned, O Muhammad, about the world and its people, for We have only made that a trial and a test for its people. Among them are those who reflect and believe, and among them are those who disbelieve. Then on the Day of Resurrection they will be before Us, so let their disbelief not grieve you greatly, for We will recompense them.

The second: The meaning of this verse is to be understood in light of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, the world is green and sweet, and Allah is making you successors in it, and He will see how you act." And his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed, what I fear most for you is what Allah brings forth for you from the splendour of the world." He was asked: "And what is the splendour of the world?" He said: "The blessings of the earth." Muslim and others narrated both from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The meaning: the world is pleasant in its taste and pleasing in its appearance, like sweet, attractive fruit to the eye. Allah tests His servants with it, to see which of them is best in deed, that is, who is most detached from it and most abandons it. There is no way for the servants to hate what Allah has adorned except that He helps them in that. For this reason, Umar used to say, as al-Bukhari recorded: "O Allah, we cannot but rejoice in what You have adorned for us. O Allah, I ask You to let me spend it in its right place." So he asked Allah to help him spend it rightly. This is the meaning of his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever takes it with a contented soul, blessing will be placed in it for him, and whoever takes it with a greedy soul is like one who eats and is never satisfied."

Likewise is the one who accumulates from the world; he is not content with what he obtains from it, but his aspiration is to gather it, and that is due to a lack of understanding of Allah and His Messenger. For trial is present with it, and safety from harm is rare. Indeed, whoever submits, is given sufficient provision, and Allah makes him content with what He has given him, has succeeded.

Ibn Atiyyah said: My father, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say concerning the Exalted's words, "best in deed": The best deed is taking by right, spending in right, along with faith, performing the obligatory duties, avoiding the prohibitions, and increasing in the recommended acts. I say: This is a fine statement, concise in its wording and eloquent in its meaning, and the Prophet (ﷺ) gathered it into a single phrase when Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me in Islam a saying about which I will not ask anyone after you" (in one narration: "other than you"). He said: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then be upright." Muslim recorded it.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "best in deed" means most detached from it. Likewise Abu Isam al-Asqalani said: "best in deed" means most abandoning of it.

The expressions of the scholars have differed regarding asceticism (zuhd). One group said: it is shortness of hope, and it is not eating coarse food or wearing a cloak; this was said by Sufyan al-Thawri. Our scholars said: He spoke truly, may Allah be pleased with him, because whoever has short hope does not become elaborate in food, nor does he become refined in clothing; he takes from the world what is easy and suffices himself with what is enough.

Another group said: it is disliking praise and loving commendation. This is the view of al-Awza'i and whoever holds his opinion.

Another group said: abandoning the world entirely is asceticism, whether one loves leaving it or dislikes it. This is the view of Fudayl.

It is related from Bishr ibn al-Harith that he said: Love of the world is love of meeting people, and asceticism regarding the world is asceticism regarding meeting people. Also from Fudayl: The sign of asceticism regarding the world is asceticism regarding people.

Another group said: The ascetic does not become an ascetic until leaving the world is more beloved to him than taking it; this was said by Ibrahim ibn Adham.

Another group said: Asceticism is that you be ascetic regarding the world in your heart; this was said by Ibn al-Mubarak.

Another group said: Asceticism is love of death.

The first statement encompasses these statements in meaning, so it is the more preferable.

Previously explained (see p. 348 of this volume). Abu Sahl said: "Dust with no plant growing in it, as if its plants have been cut off." Al-Juruz (the barren land) means cut off, and from it comes the expression sanah jaraz (a year of drought) [in another manuscript: sayf jarraz, a sword that cuts (per Lisan al-Arab: a sharp sword)]. The poet said:

قَدْ جَرَفَتْهُنَّ السِّنُونُ الاجراز

"Years of drought have swept them away."

Al-Juruz (the barren land) is the land in which there is no plant, nor any sign of cultivation or anything else, as if it has been cut off and removed. This refers to the Day of Resurrection, when the earth will be level with no place to hide in it.

Al-Nahhas said: In the language, al-juruz is the land in which there is no plant. Al-Kisa'i said: It is said jarizat al-ard tajraz (the land became barren), and jarazahā al-qawm yajruzunahā (the people grazed it bare) when they eat everything that comes from it of plants and crops, so it is majrūza (grazed bare) and jurz. In the word there are four dialects: jarz, jurz, jarz, jurz.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 9:

The view of Sibawayh is that "am" (أم), when it comes without an interrogative alif preceding it, means "bal" (بل, "rather") together with an interrogative alif, and it is then the disjunctive ("munqati'ah") use. It has also been said that "am" is a conjunction ('atf) on the meaning of the interrogative in "fala'allaka" (﴿فَلَعَلَّكَ﴾, "then perhaps you"), or that it has the meaning of the interrogative alif in a denial (inkar).

Al-Tabari said: This is a reproach to the Prophet ﷺ regarding his reckoning that the People of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of denying that to him, i.e. that this should not be magnified in the way the disbelieving questioners magnified it for you, for all of God's signs are greater than their story and more widespread. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, because the polytheists asked him about youths who had disappeared, about Dhu'l-Qarnayn and about the Spirit, and the revelation was delayed, as was mentioned earlier. When it came down, God Most High said to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "Did you suppose, O Muhammad, that the People of the Cave and the Inscription were a wonder among Our signs?" That is, they are not a wonder among Our signs; rather, among Our signs there is what is more wondrous than their account.

Al-Kalbi: the creation of the heavens and the earth is more wondrous than their account.
Al-Dahhak: what We made you aware of of the unseen is more wondrous.
Al-Junayd: your matter in the Isra' is more wondrous.
Al-Mawardi: the meaning of the speech is negation, i.e. you would not have supposed it had We not informed you.
Abu Sahl: it is an interrogative of affirmation (taqrir), i.e. did you suppose that, when they are a wonder?

Al-kahf (الكهف) is a wide opening in a mountain; what is not wide is a ghar (غار, cave). Al-Naqqash related from Anas ibn Malik that he said: al-kahf is the mountain, but this is not well known in the language.

The people differed concerning al-raqim (الرقيم). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Everything in the Qur'an I know, except four: ghislin, hanan, al-awwah and al-raqim." Once he was asked about al-raqim and said: "Ka'b claims it is a village from which they went out." Mujahid said: al-raqim is a valley. Al-Suddi said: al-raqim is the rock that was over the cave. Ibn Zayd said: al-raqim is a book whose matter God concealed from us, and He did not explain its story to us. A group said: al-raqim is a writing on a tablet of copper. Ibn 'Abbas said: on a tablet of lead, in which the disbelieving people, from whom the youths fled, wrote their story and made it a record for themselves, noting the time of their disappearance, how many they were, and who they were. Likewise said the reciters; he said: al-raqim is a lead tablet on which their names, lineages, religion and of whom they fled were written.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It appears from these reports that they were a people who recorded events as historians, and that is a sign of the nobility of the kingdom, and it is a useful matter. These sayings are derived from raqm (الرقم, "inscribing"), and from it comes "kitab marqum" (﴿كِتَابٌ مَرْقُومٌ﴾, "an inscribed book"). [See vol. 19, p. 254.] From it also comes al-aqram (الأرقم, the spotted one), for its markings, and raqmat al-wadi (رقمة الوادي), i.e. the place where water flows and bends.

What is related from Ibn 'Abbas is not contradictory, because the first saying he heard from Ka'b, and the second he may have come to know of al-raqim afterwards. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from him, saying: Ibn 'Abbas mentioned the People of the Cave and said: The youths disappeared, and their families searched for them and did not find them, so the matter was raised to the king, who said: "There must be news of them." He brought a lead tablet and wrote their names on it and placed it in his treasury; that tablet is the raqim. It has also been said: two believers were in the king's house, and they wrote the affair of the youths and their names and lineages on a lead tablet, then put it in a copper chest and placed it in the building. God knows best.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: al-raqim is a written book which they had, containing the law to which they adhered from the religion of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Al-Naqqash related from Qatadah: al-raqim is their dirhams. Anas ibn Malik and al-Sha'bi said: al-raqim is their dog. 'Ikrimah said: al-raqim is the inkwell. It has also been said: al-raqim is a gold tablet beneath the wall which al-Khidr built. It has also been said: al-raqim are the people of the cave into which the rock sealed, each of whom mentioned the best of his deeds.

I say: In this there is a well-known hadith which the two Sahihs reported, and al-Bukhari adhered to it. A group said: God informed us about the People of the Cave, and did not inform us about the People of the Raqim with anything. Al-Dahhak said: al-raqim is a town in the Byzantine lands, in which there is a cave containing twenty-one souls, who appear to be asleep in the form of the People of the Cave; according to this they are other youths to whom what happened to the People of the Cave happened. And God knows best.

It has also been said: al-raqim is a valley below Filastin in which there is a cave, derived from raqmat al-wadi, which is the place of water; it is said: "Upon you is al-raqmah, and leave the rest," mentioned by al-Ghaznawi.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In al-Sham, as I have heard from many people, there is a cave (kahf) containing dead bodies, whose neighbours claim that they are the People of the Cave; over them is a mosque and a building called al-Raqim, and with them is a dog, a decayed carcass. In al-Andalus, in the direction of Gharnata, near a village called Lawshah, there is a cave containing dead bodies, and with them a dog, a decayed carcass; most of them have had their flesh stripped away, and some remain intact. Many centuries have passed, and we have not found from knowledge of their affair any remnant (athara, "remainder"). Some people claim that they are the People of the Cave; I entered upon them in the year 504 while they were in this condition, and over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim, like a decayed palace of which some walls remain, in a wasteland of the earth. And on the upper part of Gharnata, on the side of the qiblah, are traces of an ancient Roman city called the city of Daqyus; in its traces we found wonders of graves and the like.

I say: What was mentioned of his seeing them in al-Andalus, they are others, because God Most High says concerning the People of the Cave: ﴿لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِرَاراً وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْباً﴾ ("Had you looked upon them, you would surely have turned from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them"). Ibn 'Abbas said to Mu'awiyah when he wanted to see them: "God has prevented one better than you from that," and it will come at the end of the story.

Mujahid, regarding the words ﴿كانُوا مِنْ آياتِنا عَجَباً﴾ ("were a wonder among Our signs"), said: "They are a wonder." Thus Ibn Juraij related from him, going to the view that this is a denial addressed to the Prophet ﷺ that he should consider them a wonder. Ibn Najih related from him, saying: it means "not the most wondrous of Our signs."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 10:

There are three issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾. It is narrated that they were a group of the sons of the nobles of the city of Daqyus (Daqlus is also said), the disbelieving king. It is also said Daqnyus. It is narrated that they were adorned with gold torques and bracelets (until their heads), with locks of hair, and that they were from the Romans and followed the religion of Jesus. It is also said that they were before Jesus, and Allah knows best.

Ibn Abbas said: A king among the kings, called Diqyanus, prevailed over a city of the cities of the Romans called Afsus. It is also said it was Tarsus, and he was after the time of Jesus, peace be upon him. He commanded the worship of idols and called its people to worship idols. There were in it seven youths who worshipped in secret. Their news reached the king, and they feared him, so they fled at night. They passed by a shepherd with a dog, and it followed them, and they took refuge in the cave. The king followed them to the mouth of the cave, and found the traces of their entering but did not find the traces of their leaving. They entered, and Allah blinded their sight so they saw nothing. The king said: "Block the entrance of the cave upon them, so that they die in it of hunger and thirst."

Mujahid also related from Ibn Abbas that these youths were in the religion of a king who worshipped idols, sacrificed to them, and disbelieved in Allah, and the people of the city followed him in that. Knowledge came to the youths from some of the disciples (hawariyyun) (as al-Naqqash mentioned), or from the believers of the nations before them. They believed in Allah and saw with their insight the ugliness of the people's deeds, so they bound themselves to adhering to the religion and worshipping Allah. Their matter was reported to the king, and it was said to him: "They have abandoned your religion, mocked your gods, and disbelieved in them." The king summoned them to his assembly and ordered them to follow his religion and sacrifice to his gods, and he threatened them with death if they abandoned that. They said to him, as it is related: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth..." up to His saying: "and when you withdraw from them." It is also related that they said something similar to this speech, but not exactly. The king said to them: "You are young men, inexperienced and without reason, but I will not hasten against you; rather I will give you time. So go to your homes, consider your opinion, and return to my command." He set for them a term in this matter. Then during the term, the youths consulted about fleeing with their religion. One of them said: "I know a cave in the mountain of such-and-such, into which my father used to bring his sheep. Let us go and hide in it until Allah opens (a way) for us." So they went out, as it is related, playing with the polo stick and the ball, rolling the ball toward their route so that people would not notice them. It is also related that they were cultivated (mutaqqifun), and when a festival came they went out to it and rode among the people, then they began playing with the polo stick until they got away by that.

Wahb ibn Munabbih related that the beginning of their matter was that a disciple of Jesus son of Mary came to the city of the People of the Cave wishing to enter it, so he hired himself out to the owner of the bathhouse and worked in it. The owner of the bathhouse saw great blessing in his work, so he entrusted him with all his affairs. Some youths of the city came to know this man, and Allah made them know him, so they believed in him and followed his religion. Their association with him became well known. One day the son of the king came to that bathhouse with a woman whom he wanted to be alone with (to enter with her), and the disciple forbade him, so he desisted. Then he came a second time, and he forbade him again, so he insulted him and carried out his intention of entering the bathhouse with the prostitute. He entered, and they both died in it together. The disciple and his companions were accused of killing them, so they all fled until they entered the cave. Other accounts of their departure are also mentioned.

As for the dog, it is narrated that it was a hunting dog belonging to them. It is also narrated that on their way they found a shepherd who had a dog, so the shepherd followed them in their opinion, and the dog went with them. Ibn Abbas said: The dog's name was Humran, and it is said Qitmir.

As for the names of the People of the Cave, they are non-Arabic, and the chain of transmission for knowing them is weak. What al-Tabari mentioned is these: Maksalmina, who was the eldest of them and their spokesman; Mahsimilina and Yamlikha, who is the one who went with the silver to the city when they were raised from their sleep; Marṭus, Kashtutush, Daynamus, Yatunus, and Biranus. Muqatil said: The dog belonged to Maksalmina, who was the oldest of them and the owner of sheep.

The second issue: This verse is explicit about fleeing with one's religion and emigrating from family, children, relatives, friends, homelands, and wealth, out of fear of trial and of the affliction a person encounters. The Prophet ﷺ went out fleeing with his religion, as did his companions, and he sat in the cave as has been mentioned previously in Surah "al-Nahl" (see what we have already set down, p. 159 of this part). Allah, exalted is He, has also stated this explicitly in "Bara'ah" and it has been mentioned earlier (see vol. 8, p. 143 and following). They abandoned their homelands, left their land, dwellings, households, children, relatives, and brothers, hoping for safety of religion and deliverance from the trial of the disbelievers. Thus, dwelling in the mountains, entering caves, withdrawal from people, solitude with the Creator, and the permissibility of fleeing from the oppressor are the sunnah of the prophets, may Allah's blessings be upon them, and of the saints. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ preferred seclusion, and a group of scholars also preferred it, especially when trials appear and people become corrupt. Allah, exalted is He, has stated it explicitly in His Book, saying: "Then take refuge in the cave."

The scholars said: Withdrawal from people happens sometimes in the mountains and ravines, sometimes on the shores and in the frontier posts (ribat), and sometimes in houses. It has come in a report: "When trial occurs, hide your place and restrain your tongue." It did not specify one place over another. A group of scholars made seclusion to mean withdrawing from evil and its people in your heart and your deeds, even if you are among them. Ibn al-Mubarak, explaining seclusion, said: Be with the people, so that when they plunge into the remembrance of Allah, you plunge with them, and when they plunge into other than that, be silent. Al-Baghawi related from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The believer who mixes with people and endures their harm is better than the believer who does not mix with them and does not endure their harm." It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The houses of the believers are excellent monasteries," from the mursal reports of al-Hasan and others. Uqbah ibn Amir said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "What is salvation, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "O Uqbah, keep your tongue to yourself, let your house suffice you, and weep over your sin." He ﷺ also said: "A time will come upon the people when the best property of a Muslim man will be sheep, which he herds to the peaks of mountains and the places where rain falls, fleeing with his religion from trials." Al-Bukhari transmitted it. Ali ibn Sa'd mentioned from al-Hasan ibn Waqid, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When the year one hundred and eighty comes, celibacy, seclusion, and monasticism on the tops of mountains have become permissible for my community." Ali ibn Sa'd also mentioned from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from Mubarak ibn Fadalah, from al-Hasan, raising it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "A time will come upon the people when no one of religion will keep his religion safe except one who flees with his religion from peak to peak or from stone (hajar, meaning a place; everything you wall off from a wall is a jahr) to stone. When that happens, livelihood will not be obtained except by disobedience to Allah. When that happens, celibacy becomes permissible." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can celibacy be permissible when you command us to marry?" He said: "When that happens, a man's ruin will come at the hands of his parents; if he has no parents, his destruction will come at the hands of his wife; if he has no wife, his destruction will come at the hands of his children; if he has no children, his destruction will come at the hands of relatives and neighbors." They said: "How is that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "They will reproach him for narrowness of livelihood and burden him with what he cannot bear, and then he will throw himself into the places of ruin in which he perishes."

I say: The conditions of people in this matter differ. A man may have the strength to dwell in caves and ravines in the mountains, and this is the highest state, because it is the state Allah chose for His Prophet ﷺ at the beginning of his affair, and He stated it in His Book, reporting about the youths, saying: "And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah, then take refuge in the cave." (See p. 367 of this part.) And a man for whom seclusion in his house is lighter and easier. Men of Badr withdrew and stayed in their houses after the killing of Uthman, and they did not go out except to their graves. And a man who is between these two, who has the strength to endure mixing with people and their harm, is with them outwardly and opposed to them inwardly.

Ibn al-Mubarak related: Wuhayb ibn al-Ward told us: A man came to Wahb ibn Munabbih and said: "People have fallen into what they have fallen into, and I have resolved to myself not to mix with them." He said: "Do not do that. You cannot do without people, and they cannot do without you. You have needs from them and they have needs from you. But be among them deaf to what is harmful, hearing what is good, blind to what is unlawful, seeing what is right, silent in harm, and speaking in truth."

It has been said: Every place that is far from people falls within the meaning of mountains and ravines, like i'tikaf in mosques, staying on the shores for frontier posts and remembrance, and remaining in houses to flee from the evils of people. The hadiths mention ravines, mountains, and following sheep—Allah knows best—because that is most common in the places where one withdraws. So every place far from people falls within its meaning, as we have mentioned, and Allah is the Granter of success, and in Him is protection.

Uqbah ibn Amir related: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Your Lord is amazed at a shepherd on the top of a rocky peak of a mountain who calls to prayer and prays, and Allah, mighty and majestic, says: 'Look at My servant, who calls to prayer and establishes prayer, fearing Me. I have forgiven My servant and admitted him to Paradise.'" Al-Nasa'i transmitted it.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And provide for us from our affair a right course﴾. When they fled from those who sought them, they turned to supplication and sought refuge with Allah, exalted is He, saying: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself," that is, forgiveness and provision.

(And provide for us from our affair a right course) guidance to rectitude. Ibn Abbas said: a way out of the cave in safety. It is also said: correctness. In this same sense, when a matter distressed him, he (peace be upon him) would turn to prayer.

This is an expression for God, exalted be He, casting sleep upon them. This is one of the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an, which the Arabs acknowledged they could not match. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, We prevented them from hearing, because a sleeper who hears is awakened. Ibn 'Abbas said: "We struck upon their ears with sleep," that is, We sealed their ears against the sounds reaching them. It was also said: the meaning of "So We struck upon their ears" is that We answered their supplication, averted from them the evil of their people, and made them sleep. The meanings are all close to one another. Qutrub said: This is like the saying of the Arabs, "The ruler struck upon the hand of his subjects," when he prevented them from corruption, and "The master struck upon the hand of his slave who was licensed to trade," when he prevented him from disposing of property. Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, who was blind, said:

"Of the calamities, may you have no father, the earth was struck upon me with blindnesses." [[The word is asdad, singular sadd, which means loss of sight. He says: I was blocked on the road, that is, I became blind to my ways.]]

As for the singling out of the ears for mention, it is because they are the organ through which sleep's disruption is greatest. A sleeper is rarely roused except through his ear, and sleep is not made deep except by the deadening of hearing. Among the mention of the ear in relation to sleep is his saying (ﷺ): "That is a man whom Satan has urinated into his ear," related in the Sahih. He (ﷺ) pointed to a man who slept too long and did not rise for the night prayer.

"'Adadan" is an adjective for "years," meaning "counted," and the purpose of it is to express abundance, because a small number does not need counting, since it is already known. "Al-'add" is the verbal noun, and "al-'adad" is the name of the counted thing, like "al-naqd" and "al-khabt." Abu 'Ubayda said: "'Adadan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun. Then some said: God, exalted be He, later specified the number of those years when He said: "And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 12:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then We awakened them﴾, meaning: after their sleep. It is said of one who is revived or raised up from his sleep: "mab'uth" (sent forth/raised), because he had been prevented from rising and moving about.

The words of Allah the Exalted: (﴿That We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing﴾) "Li-na'lam" (that We might know) is an expression for that thing coming into existence and being witnessed, and this is in the manner of the speech of the Arabs; that is, that We might know it as existing. Otherwise, Allah the Exalted had already known which of the two parties computed the term best. al-Zuhri read "li-ya'lam" with the yaa'. "Al-hizbayn" means the two groups. The apparent meaning of the verse is that one party is the youths, when they thought their stay was short. The second party is the people of the city among whom the youths were raised up, at the time when they had the record of the affair of the youths. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. A group said: they are two parties of the disbelievers, who disagreed about the duration of the People of the Cave. It was also said: they are two parties of the believers. And other things were said that are not connected to the wording of the verse.

"Ahsa" is a past-tense verb. "Amadan" is in the accusative as the object (maf'ul bihi), as said by Abu 'Ali. al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), meaning: which of the two parties computed best their stay in the term, and "al-amad" is the limit (ghayah). Mujahid said: "amadan" in the accusative, its meaning is "adadan" (a number); this is an interpretation by meaning, in an approximate sense. al-Tabari said: "amadan" is in the accusative governed by "labithu" (they remained). Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is not sound. As for one who says it is accusative by way of specification (tafsir), it incurs the flaw that af'ala does not come from a quadriliteral verb except in rare cases, and "ahsa" is a quadriliteral verb. It may be argued in its favour that af'ala in quadriliteral verbs has become common, as in your saying: "ma a'taahu lil-mal" (how generous he is with wealth) and "atahu lil-khayr" (how he gives to good). And he said, describing his Basin (ﷺ): "Its water is whiter than milk." And 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "He is, for whatever else, more wasteful."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾. When His saying, exalted is He, "that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the time they had stayed" (Q. 18:12) implied a disagreement that arose concerning the duration of the youths' stay, He followed it with news that He, mighty and majestic, knows their affair in accordance with the truth that occurred.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they were youths﴾, meaning young men and adolescents, whom He judged to possess (al-futuwwa, youthful nobility and chivalry) when they believed, without any intermediary. Likewise the people of the language (ahl al-lisan, the scholars of Arabic) said: the foundation of futuwwa is faith. Al-Junayd said: futuwwa is the giving of generosity, the restraint of harm, and the abandonment of complaint. It was also said: futuwwa is avoiding what is forbidden and hastening to noble deeds. Other things have been said besides this. This statement is very good, because in meaning it encompasses everything that has been said about futuwwa.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾, meaning We made it easy for them to perform righteous deeds, such as devoting themselves to God, keeping away from people, and renouncing the world. This is an increase beyond faith. Al-Suddi said: He increased them in guidance through the shepherd's dog, when they drove it away and stoned it, fearing that it would bark at them and alert others to them. The dog raised itself toward the sky like one who supplicates, so God made it speak, and it said: "O people! Why do you drive me away? Why do you stone me? Why do you strike me? By God, I knew God forty years before you knew Him." Thus God increased them in guidance by this.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾. This is an expression for intense resolve and firmness of patience, which Allah bestowed upon them, so that they said before the disbelievers: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke any god besides Him. Otherwise we would have uttered an enormous falsehood." Since fear and the weakening of the soul resemble, by correspondence, loosening (inhilal), it is fitting that intense resolve and strength of determination be likened to tying (rabt). From this one says: "So-and-so is rabit al-jash (firm of heart)," when his soul does not quail at fear, war, or other things. From this is the "tying of the heart of the mother of Musa" (Musa's mother). And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that He may strengthen your hearts and make your feet firm thereby﴾. This has already been discussed [[See vol. 7, p. 371.]].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they stood up and said﴾. In this there are two issues. The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they stood up and said﴾ may bear three meanings. One of them: that this describes their standing before the disbelieving king, as previously mentioned, a standing that requires the tying of the heart, since they opposed his religion and, for the sake of Allah, set aside his awe. The second meaning, as it is said: they were the sons of the great men of that city, who went out and gathered outside the city without prior appointment. The eldest of them said: "I find in myself that my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." They said: "We too find this within ourselves." Then they all stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke any god besides Him. Otherwise we would have uttered an enormous falsehood." That is: if we invoked any god other than Him, we would then have uttered injustice and absurdity. The third meaning: that "standing" is an expression for their rising, with resolve, to flee to Allah, Exalted is He, and to separate themselves from the people, as you say: "So-and-so stood up to such-and-such a matter," when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness. The second issue: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The Sufis have clung to the standing and the saying: ﴿When they stood up and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth.﴾" I say: this clinging is not valid. These men stood up, remembered Allah for His guidance, and gave thanks for His blessings and favours; then they went off on their faces, cut off toward their Lord, fearing their people. This is the way of Allah with the messengers, the prophets, and the excellent friends of Allah. How far is this from striking the earth with the feet and dancing with the sleeves, especially in these times, upon hearing the beautiful voices of beardless youths and women! Far indeed, by Allah, is the distance between them, as far as between earth and heaven. Moreover, this is forbidden according to the majority of scholars, as will be explained in Surah Luqman, if Allah wills [[See vol. 14, p. 69 onward.]]. What has been said in Surah al-Isra' at His saying: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ [[See p. 260 of this part.]] suffices. And Imam Abu Bakr al-Tartushi, when asked about the doctrine of the Sufis, said: As for dancing and ecstatic swaying, the first to introduce it were the companions of al-Samiri, when he made for them a calf of a body that had a lowing sound; they stood dancing around it and swaying in ecstasy. So it is the religion of the disbelievers and the worshippers of the calf, as will be explained.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These our people have taken gods besides Him﴾. That is, some of them said to others: "These are our people," meaning the people of our era and our land, who worshipped idols by blind imitation (taqlid) without any proof.

(Law-la) means "why did they not" (halla).

(﴿They should bring for them a clear authority﴾), that is, a proof for their worship of the idol. It has also been said that "for them" refers back to the gods, meaning: why did they not establish clear evidence that the idols are gods? Their saying "law-la" is then a rebuke (tahdid) in the sense of challenge (ta'jiz), and when they cannot do that, their claim should not be given any attention.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you withdraw from them﴾. It was said: this is from the words of God to them, meaning: "And when you withdraw from them, they took refuge in the cave." It was also said: it is from the words of their leader, Yamlikha, as mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Ghaznawi said: their leader was Maksalmina, who said to them that, meaning: "When you withdraw from them and withdraw from what they worship." Then he made an exception and said: ﴿except God﴾, meaning: you have not abandoned His worship. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati').

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is on the assumption that those from whom the People of the Cave fled did not know God and had no knowledge of Him, and only believed in the idols as divinities. But if we suppose that they knew God, as the Arabs used to do, yet associated their idols with Him in worship, then the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), because the withdrawal occurred from everything the disbelievers worship except in the direction of God.

In the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "and what they worship besides God." Qatada said: this is its explanation.

I say: What supports this is what Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz related from 'Ata al-Khurasani concerning the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except God﴾. He said: There was a group of young men from a people who worshipped God and also worshipped other gods alongside Him. The young men withdrew from the worship of those gods, but did not withdraw from the worship of God.

Ibn 'Atiyya: According to what Qatada said, "illa" (except) carries the meaning of "ghayr" (other than), and "ma" in the phrase ﴿and what they worship except God﴾ is in the accusative position, in coordination with the pronoun in the phrase "i'tazaltumuhum" (you withdrew from them). The implication of this verse is that some of them said to others: "If we part from the disbelievers and are alone with God, exalted is He, let us make the cave a refuge and rely upon God; He will spread His mercy over us and extend it to us, and will prepare for us a way out of our affair (mirfaqan)." All of this is supplication concerning worldly matters, and they were, with regard to the matter of their Hereafter, certain of God.

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with him, said: The People of the Cave were sword-polishers (sayaqila) [[sayaqila: those who sharpen swords]], and the name of the cave was Hayyum.

(Mirfaqan) is read with a kasra and with a fatha on the mim. It means that by which one benefits or is supported, and likewise the mirfaq (elbow) of a person and his marfiq. Some read "al-marfaq" with a fatha on the mim, and with a kasra on the fa' as an imperative, and al-marfaq for a person's elbow; and it has been said: al-marfaq with a fatha on the mim refers to a place, like al-masjid (mosque); and these are two dialects.

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾. That is, O listener, you would see the sun at its rising veering away from their cave. The meaning is: if you had seen them, you would have seen them thus, not that the addressee actually saw them in reality. "Tatazawaru" means "to turn aside and incline," from al-izwirar. Al-zawr is inclination. In the eye, al-azwar is one whose gaze is inclined toward a side, and the word is used of other than the eye, as Ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

*"And my side, out of fear of the people, is turned aside [azwar]"* [[The full verse as in his Diwan:
"And he lowered my voice, when he came walking softly, / and my person, out of fear of the tribe, turned aside [azwar]."
Al-Habab (with a damma): the snake. It is also said this is a verse:
"When I lost the voice from them and the lamps were put out, / lamps that were lit at nightfall and shone, / and the moon set, whose setting I used to love, / and the shepherds came back and the night-watchers slept."]]

From the same root is the saying of 'Antarah:

*"Turned aside [azwar] from the impact of the spears upon his chest"* [[Its completion:
"And he complained to me with a tear, and neighed [tahammuh]."
Al-liban (with a fatha): the chest. Al-tahammum: a broken sound that is not a neigh.]]

In the hadith of the expedition of Mu'tah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in the bier of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah a turning aside [izwiraran] from the biers of Ja'far and Zayd ibn Harithah.

The people of the two Holy Harams (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu 'Amr read *"tazzawaru"* with the assimilation of the *ta'* into the *zay*, the original being *"tatazawaru."* 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *"tatazawaru"* with the *zay* lightened.

Ibn 'Amir read *"tazwarru,"* like *tahmarru*. Al-Farra' related *"tazwaarru,"* like *tahmaarru*. All of these have one meaning.

﴿And when it sets, it passes them by on the left﴾: The majority read it with the *ta'* [taqriduhum], meaning "leaves them," as Mujahid said. Qatadah said: "it leaves them." Al-Nahhas said: This is well known in the language; the Basrans related that one says *qaradahu yaqridhu* when one leaves him. The meaning is that they were not struck by the sun at all, as an honour for them, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. That is, when the sun rises it inclines away from their cave to the right, meaning the right side of the cave, and when it sets it passes them on the left, meaning the left side of the cave. So it does not reach them at the beginning of the day or at its end. Their cave faced the Bear (Banat Na'sh) in the land of the Romans, so the sun would incline away from them while rising, setting and moving, not reaching them to harm them with its heat, change their colours or wear out their clothing. It has also been said that the cave had a screen on the south side and a screen on the north-west side, and they were in its corner. Al-Zajjaj held that the action of the sun was a sign from Allah, rather than the cave's opening being in a direction that necessitated this.

A group read *"yaqridhuhum"* with the *ya'* from *al-qardh*, which is cutting: that is, the cave cuts them off with its shadow from the light of the sun. It was also said: "and when it sets, it touches them [taqriduhum]", that is, a little of it reaches them, taken from *qaridat al-dhahab wa'l-fiddah* (the gold and silver shavings), meaning the sun gives them a little of its rays. They said: its touching them in the evening was a benefit for their bodies.

In sum, the verse on this point means that Allah sheltered them in a cave with this description, not in another cave where they would be harmed by the sun spreading over them for most of the day. On this basis it is possible that the sun was turned away from them by a cloud shading them, or by another cause. The purpose is to show their preservation from the reaching of harm, from changes of bodies and colours, and from being hurt by heat or cold.

﴿While they were in a spacious place within it﴾: That is, within the cave. Al-fajwah is the wide space; its plurals are *fajawat* and *fija'*, like *rakwah*, *rika'*, *rakawat*. The poet said:

*"We filled every valley and open space [fajwah] / with men and horses, not cowardly [mayl] nor unarmed ['uzl]."* [[Mayl: plural of amyal, and it is the coward. It has other meanings.]]

That is, they were in a position where the breeze of the air reached them.

﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾: a kindness toward them. This strengthens the view of al-Zajjaj. The people of tafsir said: their eyes were open while they slept, so the one who saw them would think they were awake. It was also said: "you would think them awake" [tahsabuhum ayqaza] on account of their frequent turning, like one who wakes in his bed. *Ayqaz* is the plural of *yaqiz* and *yaqzan*, which means alert.

﴿And they were sleeping﴾: like their saying, "they are a people who bow, prostrate and sit," so the plural is described with a verbal noun.
