﴿And We turned them to the right and to the left﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: so that the earth would not consume their flesh. Abu Hurayrah said: they had two turnings each year. It was also said: once every year. Mujahid said: once every seven years. A group said: they were only turned in the last nine years, and not in the three hundred. The apparent sense of the words of the mufassirun is that the turning was the action of Allah, though it may be by an angel by the command of Allah, and so it is ascribed to Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And their dog was stretching out its two forelegs at the threshold﴾: On this there are four issues.

**First:** Allah's words "and their dog." 'Amr ibn Dinar said: among what was taken as a covenant from the scorpion is that it should not sting anyone in his night or his day, [and] he said: "Peace be upon Nuh" [in Hayat al-Hayawan: "Allah bless Nuh"]. Among what was taken as a covenant from the dog is that it should not harm anyone who invokes against it [if he says]: "and their dog was stretching out its two forelegs at the threshold."

The majority of the mufassirun hold that it was a dog in reality, and it was kept for the hunting of one of them, or for his crops or his flock, as Muqatil said. Its colour has been disputed in many ways, as al-Tha'labi mentioned. In summary, whatever colour you mention, you are right, to the point that it was said the colour of stone, and it was said the colour of the sky. Its name has also been disputed. From 'Ali: Rayyan. From Ibn 'Abbas: Qitmir. Al-Awza'i: Musheer [in another copy: Tabr]. 'Abdullah ibn Salam: Basit. Ka'b: Sahya. Wahb: Naqya. It was also said: Qatfir [from another copy], as al-Tha'labi mentioned. Keeping a dog was permissible in their time, as it is permissible in our Shari'ah today.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they fled by night, and they were seven. They passed by a shepherd who had a dog, and it followed them in their religion. Ka'b said: they passed by a dog which barked at them, and they drove it away, but it returned, and they drove it away several times. Then the dog stood on its hind legs and raised its forelegs to the sky, in the manner of one who supplicates, and it spoke, saying: "Do not fear me, I love the friends of Allah, the Exalted. So sleep, and I will guard you."

**Second:** It is recorded in the Sahih, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever keeps a dog, except a dog for hunting or for livestock, loses two qirats of his reward every day." The Sahih also narrates from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever keeps a dog, except a dog for livestock, hunting or crops, loses one qirat of his reward every day." Al-Zuhri said: Abu Hurayrah's saying was mentioned to Ibn 'Umar, and he said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu Hurayrah, he was a man of crops."

So the established Sunnah shows the permissibility of keeping a dog for hunting, crops and livestock. The loss of reward for the one who keeps it for other than these benefits is either because the dog frightens the Muslims and disturbs them with its barking, or because it prevents the angels from entering the house, or because of its impurity, according to what al-Shafi'i holds, or because of the prohibition against keeping what has no benefit, and Allah knows best.

In one of the two narrations it says "two qirats," and in the other "one qirat." This may be because there are two types of dogs, one of which is more harmful than the other, like the black dog which the Prophet (peace be upon him) ordered to be killed, and which he did not include in the exception when he forbade killing dogs, as is stated in the hadith of Jabir, recorded in the Sahih. He said: "Upon you is the entirely black dog with two spots, for it is a devil." It may also be that this is due to differences of places, so that one who keeps it in Madinah or Makkah, for example, loses two qirats, and elsewhere one qirat. As for the permissible keeping of it, such as a horse or a cat, it does not diminish reward. And Allah knows best.

**Third:** According to Malik, the dog of livestock whose keeping is permitted is the one that goes out with them to pasture, not the one that guards them in the house from thieves. The dog of crops is the one that guards them from wild animals by night or by day, not from thieves. Other than Malik has permitted keeping it for guarding livestock and crops from thieves. Something sufficient about the rulings on dogs has already been mentioned in *al-Ma'idah* [see vol. 6, p. 65], and all praise is due to Allah.

**Fourth:** Ibn 'Atiyyah said: my father, may Allah be pleased with him, told me, saying: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari in the Jami' of Egypt say from the pulpit of his preaching, in the year four hundred and sixty-nine: "Whoever loves the people of goodness attains a share of their blessing. A dog loved the people of virtue and accompanied them, so Allah mentioned it in His revealed Book."

I say: since some dogs attained this high rank through their companionship and their association with the righteous and the friends of Allah, so that Allah, exalted is He, informed of that in His Book, then what do you think of the believing, monotheist associates who love the friends and the righteous? Indeed, in this is consolation and comfort for the believers who fall short of the ranks of perfection, who love the Prophet (ﷺ) and his family, the best of families.

The Sahih narrates from Anas ibn Malik who said: "While I and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were going out of the mosque, a man met us at the step of the mosque and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when is the Hour?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What have you prepared for it?' The man seemed humbled, then said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have not prepared for it much prayer, nor fasting, nor charity, but I love Allah and His Messenger.' He said: 'You will be with the one you love.'" In another narration, Anas ibn Malik said: "We never rejoiced after Islam with a joy greater than the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'You will be with the one you love.'" Anas said: "I love Allah and His Messenger, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar, so I hope to be with them, even if I do not act by their deeds."

I say: this which Anas held to includes every soul among the Muslims. Likewise our hopes are attached to it, though we fall short, and we hope for the mercy of the Most Merciful, though we are not deserving. If a dog loved a people and Allah mentioned it along with them, then how about us, when we have the bond of faith, the word of Islam, and the love of the Prophet (ﷺ)? *"And We have honoured the children of Adam, and carried them on land and sea, and provided them with good things, and preferred them above many of those whom We created with a marked preference"* [[See p. 293 of this part.]].

Another group said: it was not a dog in reality, but rather one of them. He had sat at the door of the cave as a sentry for them, so he was named with the name of the animal that is attached to that place among people, just as the star that follows al-Jawza' (Orion) was named "dog," because it is from it as the dog is from the man, and it is called "the dog of al-Jabbar" [al-Jabbar: the name of al-Jawza']. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: so he was named with the name of the animal that is attached to that place. However, this view is weakened by the mention of the stretching of the two forelegs, for in common usage that is a description of the dog in reality. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you stretch out his forelegs in the manner of a dog stretching out." Abu 'Umar al-Mutarriz has related in the book *al-Yawaqit*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 17–18 (part 2 of 2):

It was read: "وَكَالِبُهُمْ بَاسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ بِالْوَصِيدِ" (wa-kalbuhum basitun dhira'ayhi bil-wasid). It may be that by "kalib" here he means a man, according to what has been narrated, since spreading the two forelegs and pressing to the ground while raising the head to look out is the posture of one who is wary and hides himself. It may also be that by "al-kalib" he means the dog. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq read "kalibuhum," meaning the owner of the dog.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ﴾ (spreading his two forelegs). The active participle is used here though it carries the sense of the past, because this is a narration of a state, and the intention was not to report an action of the dog. The "dhira'" (forearm) is from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. Then it was said: he spread his forelegs for the length of the time. It was also said: the dog slept, and that was one of the signs. And it was said: he slept with his eyes open. Al-wasid: the threshold (al-fina'), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, i.e., the courtyard of the cave. Its plural is "wasa'id" and "wusud." It was also said: the door. Ibn 'Abbas also said this, and he recited:

"In a wide land whose wasid is not closed against me, and my good standing in it is not unknown."

This has already been mentioned. 'Ata' said: the threshold of the door. The "bab mu'sad" is the closed door; one says "awsadtu al-bab" and "asadtuhu," meaning I closed it. Al-wasid also means plants with closely joined roots, so the word is shared (mushtarak). And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (If you had looked upon them). The majority read it with a kasra on the waw. Al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on it.

(لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِراراً) (you would have turned away from them in flight), i.e., if you had come upon them you would have fled from them.

(وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْباً) (and you would have been filled with terror of them), i.e., because of the awe God, exalted is He, had enveloped them with and the dread that surrounded them. It was also said: because of the desolation of their place, for God had sheltered them in this place, which was apparently desolate [[makan wahsh: khali.]], so that people would keep away from them. It was also said: people were screened from them by terror, so that none of them dared to approach them. It was also said: the flight was from them because of the length of their hair and nails. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, al-Nahhas, al-Zajjaj and al-Qushayri. But this is far-fetched, because when they awoke, some of them said to others: "We have remained a day or part of a day." This indicates that their hair and nails were in their original state, unless it is said that they said this before looking at their nails and hair. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The correct view concerning their situation is that God, mighty and majestic, preserved for them the state in which they had slept, so that it would be a sign for them and for others concerning them. Thus no garment of theirs was worn out and no attribute was changed, and the one who rose up to go to the city found nothing unfamiliar except the landmarks of the land and the buildings; and if there had been in himself a state that he found strange, it would have been more important to him.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas and the people of Makkah and Madinah read "لَمُلِّئْتَ مِنْهُمْ" (lamullittа minhum) with a shadda on the lam, for the intensive doubling, i.e., you were filled and then filled again. The rest read "لَمُلِئْتَ" (lamuli'ta) with lightness, and the lightened form is more common in the language. The doubled form has also come in the verse of al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di:

"And when al-Nu'man slew the people in violation of what was sacred, the chains of Ka'b ibn 'Awf were filled from them."

The majority read "رُعْباً" (ru'ban) with a sukun on the 'ain. Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on it. Abu Hatim said: both are dialects. "Firaran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and "ru'ban" is a second object or a specification (tamyiz).

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾. That is, O listener, you would see the sun at its rising veering away from their cave. The meaning is: if you had seen them, you would have seen them thus, not that the addressee actually saw them in reality. "Tatazawaru" means "to turn aside and incline," from al-izwirar. Al-zawr is inclination. In the eye, al-azwar is one whose gaze is inclined toward a side, and the word is used of other than the eye, as Ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

*"And my side, out of fear of the people, is turned aside [azwar]"* [[The full verse as in his Diwan:
"And he lowered my voice, when he came walking softly, / and my person, out of fear of the tribe, turned aside [azwar]."
Al-Habab (with a damma): the snake. It is also said this is a verse:
"When I lost the voice from them and the lamps were put out, / lamps that were lit at nightfall and shone, / and the moon set, whose setting I used to love, / and the shepherds came back and the night-watchers slept."]]

From the same root is the saying of 'Antarah:

*"Turned aside [azwar] from the impact of the spears upon his chest"* [[Its completion:
"And he complained to me with a tear, and neighed [tahammuh]."
Al-liban (with a fatha): the chest. Al-tahammum: a broken sound that is not a neigh.]]

In the hadith of the expedition of Mu'tah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in the bier of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah a turning aside [izwiraran] from the biers of Ja'far and Zayd ibn Harithah.

The people of the two Holy Harams (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu 'Amr read *"tazzawaru"* with the assimilation of the *ta'* into the *zay*, the original being *"tatazawaru."* 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *"tatazawaru"* with the *zay* lightened.

Ibn 'Amir read *"tazwarru,"* like *tahmarru*. Al-Farra' related *"tazwaarru,"* like *tahmaarru*. All of these have one meaning.

﴿And when it sets, it passes them by on the left﴾: The majority read it with the *ta'* [taqriduhum], meaning "leaves them," as Mujahid said. Qatadah said: "it leaves them." Al-Nahhas said: This is well known in the language; the Basrans related that one says *qaradahu yaqridhu* when one leaves him. The meaning is that they were not struck by the sun at all, as an honour for them, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. That is, when the sun rises it inclines away from their cave to the right, meaning the right side of the cave, and when it sets it passes them on the left, meaning the left side of the cave. So it does not reach them at the beginning of the day or at its end. Their cave faced the Bear (Banat Na'sh) in the land of the Romans, so the sun would incline away from them while rising, setting and moving, not reaching them to harm them with its heat, change their colours or wear out their clothing. It has also been said that the cave had a screen on the south side and a screen on the north-west side, and they were in its corner. Al-Zajjaj held that the action of the sun was a sign from Allah, rather than the cave's opening being in a direction that necessitated this.

A group read *"yaqridhuhum"* with the *ya'* from *al-qardh*, which is cutting: that is, the cave cuts them off with its shadow from the light of the sun. It was also said: "and when it sets, it touches them [taqriduhum]", that is, a little of it reaches them, taken from *qaridat al-dhahab wa'l-fiddah* (the gold and silver shavings), meaning the sun gives them a little of its rays. They said: its touching them in the evening was a benefit for their bodies.

In sum, the verse on this point means that Allah sheltered them in a cave with this description, not in another cave where they would be harmed by the sun spreading over them for most of the day. On this basis it is possible that the sun was turned away from them by a cloud shading them, or by another cause. The purpose is to show their preservation from the reaching of harm, from changes of bodies and colours, and from being hurt by heat or cold.

﴿While they were in a spacious place within it﴾: That is, within the cave. Al-fajwah is the wide space; its plurals are *fajawat* and *fija'*, like *rakwah*, *rika'*, *rakawat*. The poet said:

*"We filled every valley and open space [fajwah] / with men and horses, not cowardly [mayl] nor unarmed ['uzl]."* [[Mayl: plural of amyal, and it is the coward. It has other meanings.]]

That is, they were in a position where the breeze of the air reached them.

﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾: a kindness toward them. This strengthens the view of al-Zajjaj. The people of tafsir said: their eyes were open while they slept, so the one who saw them would think they were awake. It was also said: "you would think them awake" [tahsabuhum ayqaza] on account of their frequent turning, like one who wakes in his bed. *Ayqaz* is the plural of *yaqiz* and *yaqzan*, which means alert.

﴿And they were sleeping﴾: like their saying, "they are a people who bow, prostrate and sit," so the plural is described with a verbal noun.

﴿And We turned them to the right and to the left﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: so that the earth would not consume their flesh. Abu Hurayrah said: they had two turnings each year. It was also said: once every year. Mujahid said: once every seven years. A group said: they were only turned in the last nine years, and not in the three hundred. The apparent sense of the words of the mufassirun is that the turning was the action of Allah, though it may be by an angel by the command of Allah, and so it is ascribed to Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And their dog was stretching out its two forelegs at the threshold﴾: On this there are four issues.

**First:** Allah's words "and their dog." 'Amr ibn Dinar said: among what was taken as a covenant from the scorpion is that it should not sting anyone in his night or his day, [and] he said: "Peace be upon Nuh" [in Hayat al-Hayawan: "Allah bless Nuh"]. Among what was taken as a covenant from the dog is that it should not harm anyone who invokes against it [if he says]: "and their dog was stretching out its two forelegs at the threshold."

The majority of the mufassirun hold that it was a dog in reality, and it was kept for the hunting of one of them, or for his crops or his flock, as Muqatil said. Its colour has been disputed in many ways, as al-Tha'labi mentioned. In summary, whatever colour you mention, you are right, to the point that it was said the colour of stone, and it was said the colour of the sky. Its name has also been disputed. From 'Ali: Rayyan. From Ibn 'Abbas: Qitmir. Al-Awza'i: Musheer [in another copy: Tabr]. 'Abdullah ibn Salam: Basit. Ka'b: Sahya. Wahb: Naqya. It was also said: Qatfir [from another copy], as al-Tha'labi mentioned. Keeping a dog was permissible in their time, as it is permissible in our Shari'ah today.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they fled by night, and they were seven. They passed by a shepherd who had a dog, and it followed them in their religion. Ka'b said: they passed by a dog which barked at them, and they drove it away, but it returned, and they drove it away several times. Then the dog stood on its hind legs and raised its forelegs to the sky, in the manner of one who supplicates, and it spoke, saying: "Do not fear me, I love the friends of Allah, the Exalted. So sleep, and I will guard you."

**Second:** It is recorded in the Sahih, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever keeps a dog, except a dog for hunting or for livestock, loses two qirats of his reward every day." The Sahih also narrates from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever keeps a dog, except a dog for livestock, hunting or crops, loses one qirat of his reward every day." Al-Zuhri said: Abu Hurayrah's saying was mentioned to Ibn 'Umar, and he said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu Hurayrah, he was a man of crops."

So the established Sunnah shows the permissibility of keeping a dog for hunting, crops and livestock. The loss of reward for the one who keeps it for other than these benefits is either because the dog frightens the Muslims and disturbs them with its barking, or because it prevents the angels from entering the house, or because of its impurity, according to what al-Shafi'i holds, or because of the prohibition against keeping what has no benefit, and Allah knows best.

In one of the two narrations it says "two qirats," and in the other "one qirat." This may be because there are two types of dogs, one of which is more harmful than the other, like the black dog which the Prophet (peace be upon him) ordered to be killed, and which he did not include in the exception when he forbade killing dogs, as is stated in the hadith of Jabir, recorded in the Sahih. He said: "Upon you is the entirely black dog with two spots, for it is a devil." It may also be that this is due to differences of places, so that one who keeps it in Madinah or Makkah, for example, loses two qirats, and elsewhere one qirat. As for the permissible keeping of it, such as a horse or a cat, it does not diminish reward. And Allah knows best.

**Third:** According to Malik, the dog of livestock whose keeping is permitted is the one that goes out with them to pasture, not the one that guards them in the house from thieves. The dog of crops is the one that guards them from wild animals by night or by day, not from thieves. Other than Malik has permitted keeping it for guarding livestock and crops from thieves. Something sufficient about the rulings on dogs has already been mentioned in *al-Ma'idah* [see vol. 6, p. 65], and all praise is due to Allah.

**Fourth:** Ibn 'Atiyyah said: my father, may Allah be pleased with him, told me, saying: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari in the Jami' of Egypt say from the pulpit of his preaching, in the year four hundred and sixty-nine: "Whoever loves the people of goodness attains a share of their blessing. A dog loved the people of virtue and accompanied them, so Allah mentioned it in His revealed Book."

I say: since some dogs attained this high rank through their companionship and their association with the righteous and the friends of Allah, so that Allah, exalted is He, informed of that in His Book, then what do you think of the believing, monotheist associates who love the friends and the righteous? Indeed, in this is consolation and comfort for the believers who fall short of the ranks of perfection, who love the Prophet (ﷺ) and his family, the best of families.

The Sahih narrates from Anas ibn Malik who said: "While I and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were going out of the mosque, a man met us at the step of the mosque and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, when is the Hour?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What have you prepared for it?' The man seemed humbled, then said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have not prepared for it much prayer, nor fasting, nor charity, but I love Allah and His Messenger.' He said: 'You will be with the one you love.'" In another narration, Anas ibn Malik said: "We never rejoiced after Islam with a joy greater than the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'You will be with the one you love.'" Anas said: "I love Allah and His Messenger, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar, so I hope to be with them, even if I do not act by their deeds."

I say: this which Anas held to includes every soul among the Muslims. Likewise our hopes are attached to it, though we fall short, and we hope for the mercy of the Most Merciful, though we are not deserving. If a dog loved a people and Allah mentioned it along with them, then how about us, when we have the bond of faith, the word of Islam, and the love of the Prophet (ﷺ)? *"And We have honoured the children of Adam, and carried them on land and sea, and provided them with good things, and preferred them above many of those whom We created with a marked preference"* [[See p. 293 of this part.]].

Another group said: it was not a dog in reality, but rather one of them. He had sat at the door of the cave as a sentry for them, so he was named with the name of the animal that is attached to that place among people, just as the star that follows al-Jawza' (Orion) was named "dog," because it is from it as the dog is from the man, and it is called "the dog of al-Jabbar" [al-Jabbar: the name of al-Jawza']. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: so he was named with the name of the animal that is attached to that place. However, this view is weakened by the mention of the stretching of the two forelegs, for in common usage that is a description of the dog in reality. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you stretch out his forelegs in the manner of a dog stretching out." Abu 'Umar al-Mutarriz has related in the book *al-Yawaqit*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 17–18 (part 2 of 2):

It was read: "وَكَالِبُهُمْ بَاسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ بِالْوَصِيدِ" (wa-kalbuhum basitun dhira'ayhi bil-wasid). It may be that by "kalib" here he means a man, according to what has been narrated, since spreading the two forelegs and pressing to the ground while raising the head to look out is the posture of one who is wary and hides himself. It may also be that by "al-kalib" he means the dog. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq read "kalibuhum," meaning the owner of the dog.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ﴾ (spreading his two forelegs). The active participle is used here though it carries the sense of the past, because this is a narration of a state, and the intention was not to report an action of the dog. The "dhira'" (forearm) is from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. Then it was said: he spread his forelegs for the length of the time. It was also said: the dog slept, and that was one of the signs. And it was said: he slept with his eyes open. Al-wasid: the threshold (al-fina'), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, i.e., the courtyard of the cave. Its plural is "wasa'id" and "wusud." It was also said: the door. Ibn 'Abbas also said this, and he recited:

"In a wide land whose wasid is not closed against me, and my good standing in it is not unknown."

This has already been mentioned. 'Ata' said: the threshold of the door. The "bab mu'sad" is the closed door; one says "awsadtu al-bab" and "asadtuhu," meaning I closed it. Al-wasid also means plants with closely joined roots, so the word is shared (mushtarak). And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿لَوِ اطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (If you had looked upon them). The majority read it with a kasra on the waw. Al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on it.

(لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِراراً) (you would have turned away from them in flight), i.e., if you had come upon them you would have fled from them.

(وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْباً) (and you would have been filled with terror of them), i.e., because of the awe God, exalted is He, had enveloped them with and the dread that surrounded them. It was also said: because of the desolation of their place, for God had sheltered them in this place, which was apparently desolate [[makan wahsh: khali.]], so that people would keep away from them. It was also said: people were screened from them by terror, so that none of them dared to approach them. It was also said: the flight was from them because of the length of their hair and nails. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, al-Nahhas, al-Zajjaj and al-Qushayri. But this is far-fetched, because when they awoke, some of them said to others: "We have remained a day or part of a day." This indicates that their hair and nails were in their original state, unless it is said that they said this before looking at their nails and hair. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The correct view concerning their situation is that God, mighty and majestic, preserved for them the state in which they had slept, so that it would be a sign for them and for others concerning them. Thus no garment of theirs was worn out and no attribute was changed, and the one who rose up to go to the city found nothing unfamiliar except the landmarks of the land and the buildings; and if there had been in himself a state that he found strange, it would have been more important to him.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas and the people of Makkah and Madinah read "لَمُلِّئْتَ مِنْهُمْ" (lamullittа minhum) with a shadda on the lam, for the intensive doubling, i.e., you were filled and then filled again. The rest read "لَمُلِئْتَ" (lamuli'ta) with lightness, and the lightened form is more common in the language. The doubled form has also come in the verse of al-Mukhabbal al-Sa'di:

"And when al-Nu'man slew the people in violation of what was sacred, the chains of Ka'b ibn 'Awf were filled from them."

The majority read "رُعْباً" (ru'ban) with a sukun on the 'ain. Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on it. Abu Hatim said: both are dialects. "Firaran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and "ru'ban" is a second object or a specification (tamyiz).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: (And thus We roused them that they might question one another). Al-ba'th (raising up) is moving something from stillness. The meaning: just as We set a seal upon their ears, increased them in guidance, and turned them over, so also We roused them, that is, We woke them from their sleep, in the state they were in with respect to their garments and conditions. The poet said:

"And young men of truth, whom I roused at the pre-dawn hour, and they all stood up between staggering and drunken." [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. Al-suhrah (with a damma) means the pre-dawn hour; it is said it is the highest part of the night. It is also said it is the last third of the night until the break of dawn.]]

That is, I woke them. The lam in His saying "li-yatasa'alu" (that they might question) is the lam of becoming (lam al-sayrurah), which is the lam of consequence, as in His saying "that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow" (al-Qasas 28:8). So their being roused was not for the sake of their questioning.

His saying, Exalted is He: (They said: We have tarried a day or part of a day). That is because they had entered (the cave) in the morning, and God roused them at the end of the day. Their leader, Yamlikha, or Maksilmina, said: God knows best the duration.

His saying, Exalted is He: (So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city). On this there are seven issues.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: their silver was like the young camels' hooves (al-rabi', i.e., the foal born in spring), reported by al-Nahhas. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read "bi-wariqikum" with a kasra on the ra'. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "bi-warqikum" with a sukun on the ra', dropping the kasra because of its heaviness; both are dialects. al-Zajjaj read "bi-wiriqikum" with a kasra on the waw and a sukun on the ra'. It is reported that they awoke hungry, and that the one sent was Yamlikha, who was the youngest of them, as recorded by al-Ghaznawi. The city: Afsus; it is said it is Tarsus, and its name in the pre-Islamic period was Afsus, and when Islam came they named it Tarsus. Ibn 'Abbas said: they had dirhams on which was the image of the king who was in their time.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: (Then let him look which is the purer in food). Ibn 'Abbas said: the most lawful slaughter, because the people of their town used to slaughter in the name of the idol, and among them were people who concealed their faith. Ibn 'Abbas also said: most of them were Magians. It is said: "azka ta'aman" means more blessed. It is said that they ordered him to buy what he thinks is the food of two or three persons, so that he would not be noticed; then when it was cooked it sufficed a group. For this reason it is said: that food was rice. It is said: it was raisins. It is said: dates, and God knows best. It is said: "azka" means best. It is said: cheapest.

(Then let him bring you a provision from it), that is, sustenance.

(And let him be discreet), that is, in entering the city and buying food.

(And let him not make anyone aware of you), that is, let him not inform anyone. It is said: if he is discovered, let him not expose his brethren to what has befallen them.

(For if they come to know of you, they will stone you), said al-Zajjaj: it means with stones, and it is the most wretched form of killing. It is said: they will revile you with abuse and insult. The first is more correct, because he was determined to kill them, as has been mentioned earlier in their narrative. Stoning in the past was, as was mentioned before it, a punishment for opposing the religion of the people, since it is the most effective for the whole body of that religion's adherents in that they all take part in it.

The third: In this sending with silver there is evidence for agency (wakalah) and its validity. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib appointed his brother 'Aqil as agent before 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and there is no disagreement about it in general. Agency was known in the pre-Islamic period and in Islam. Do you not see how 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf appointed Umayyah ibn Khalaf as agent over his family and dependents in Makkah, that is, to protect them, while Umayyah was a polytheist; and 'Abd al-Rahman undertook for Umayyah the same protection of his dependents in Madinah, as a recompense for his conduct. al-Bukhari related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf who said: I made a written agreement with Umayyah ibn Khalaf that he would protect me regarding my dependents in Makkah, and I would protect him regarding his dependents in Madinah. When I mentioned "al-Rahman," he said: I do not know al-Rahman; write to me with your name that you had in the pre-Islamic period. So I wrote to him "Abd 'Amr" ... and he mentioned the hadith. Al-Asma'i said: the saghiyah (dependents) of a man are those who incline towards him and come to him; it is derived from saghā yasghū and yasghā, when one inclines; and everyone who inclines to a thing or is with it has saghā towards it and asghā, from the Book of Verbs.

The fourth: Agency is a contract of representation, which Allah, glory be to Him, permitted because of the need for it and the realization of benefit in it, since not everyone is able to handle his affairs except with the help of another, or he may be at ease and appoint someone to relieve him. Our scholars have cited verses of the Book as evidence for its validity, among them this verse, and His saying, Exalted is He: (and those employed to collect it) [[See vol. 8, p. 177.]], and His saying: (Go with this shirt of mine) [[See vol. 9, p. 258.]]. As for the Sunnah, there are many hadiths, among them the hadith of 'Urwah al-Bariqi, which has been mentioned at the end of al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 156.]]. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah related: I wished to set out for Khaybar, so I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said to him: I wish to set out for Khaybar. He said: "When you come to my agent, take from him fifteen wasq, and if he seeks a sign from you, place your hand on his collarbone" [[al-tarquwah: the bone between the base of the throat and the shoulder.]]. Abu Dawud recorded it. The hadiths on this meaning are many, and the consensus of the community on its permissibility is sufficient.

The fifth: Agency is permissible in every right in which representation is permitted. So if one appoints a usurper as agent, it is not permitted, and he would be the agent, because every act that is forbidden to do, representation in it is not permitted.

The sixth: In this verse there is a wonderful point, namely that the agency was only with caution, for fear that anyone should become aware, because of the fear they had for themselves. The permissibility of appointing one with a valid excuse is agreed upon. As for one who has no excuse, the majority hold it is permissible. Abu Hanifah and Sahnun said: it is not permissible. Ibn al-'Arabi said: It seems Sahnun took it from Asad ibn al-Furat and ruled by it during his judgeship, and perhaps he did this with people of oppression and tyranny, as a means of obtaining justice from them and humiliating them, and this is the truth, for agency is an aid and is not for the people of falsehood. I say: this is good. As for people of religion and virtue, they may appoint an agent even if they are present and healthy. The proof of the validity of appointing an agent for a healthy present person is what the two Sahihs and others recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: a man had a claim against the Prophet ﷺ for a she-camel of a certain age, and he came demanding it. He said: "Give him," and they sought a camel of that age for him but found only one older than it. He said: "Give him." The man said: You have paid me in full, may Allah pay you in full. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The best of you are those who are best in repaying." This is the wording of al-Bukhari. This hadith, with its authenticity, shows the permissibility of appointing an agent for a present person in sound body, for the Prophet ﷺ ordered his companions to give on his behalf the camel that was owed, and that was a confirmation from him to them of this; and the Prophet ﷺ was neither sick nor travelling. This refutes the view of Abu Hanifah and Sahnun in their saying that it is not permissible to appoint an agent for a present person in sound body unless his opponent consents; this hadith contradicts their view.

The seventh: Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: this verse includes the permissibility of partnership, because the silver belonged to all of them; it includes the permissibility of agency, because they sent the one whom they had appointed to buy; and it includes the permissibility of companions eating together and mixing their food together, even if some of them eat more than others. Similar to it is His saying: (And if you mix with them, they are your brethren) [[See vol. 3, p. 62, where its explanation was given earlier in al-Baqarah.]]. For this reason our companions said regarding a poor man who is given charity and mixes it with the food of a rich man and then eats with him: this is permissible. They also said regarding a mudarib (investment partner) who mixes his food with the food of another and then eats with him: this is permissible. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed one who bought a sacrificial animal for him. Ibn al-'Arabi said: there is no evidence in the verse for this, because it is possible that each of them had given him money individually, so there is no partnership in it. In this issue there is no reliance except on two hadiths: the first, that Ibn 'Umar passed by people eating dates and said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade combining (in eating) except that a man seeks permission from his brother. The second: the hadith of Abu 'Ubaydah concerning the army of al-Khabt [[They were called the army of al-Khabt because they set out on an expedition to the land of Juhaynah and were struck by hunger, so they ate al-khabt, which is the leaves of the acacia and similar trees, knocked down with a stick.]]. This is weaker than the first in clarity, because it is possible that Abu 'Ubaydah gave them only enough of that food to sustain them, and did not pool it for them. I say: what indicates the opposite of this from the Book is His saying: (And if you mix with them, they are your brethren), and His saying: (There is no blame on you that you eat together or separately) [[See vol. 12, p. 317.]], as will come, God willing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: (And thus We roused them that they might question one another). Al-ba'th (raising up) is moving something from stillness. The meaning: just as We set a seal upon their ears, increased them in guidance, and turned them over, so also We roused them, that is, We woke them from their sleep, in the state they were in with respect to their garments and conditions. The poet said:

"And young men of truth, whom I roused at the pre-dawn hour, and they all stood up between staggering and drunken." [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays. Al-suhrah (with a damma) means the pre-dawn hour; it is said it is the highest part of the night. It is also said it is the last third of the night until the break of dawn.]]

That is, I woke them. The lam in His saying "li-yatasa'alu" (that they might question) is the lam of becoming (lam al-sayrurah), which is the lam of consequence, as in His saying "that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow" (al-Qasas 28:8). So their being roused was not for the sake of their questioning.

His saying, Exalted is He: (They said: We have tarried a day or part of a day). That is because they had entered (the cave) in the morning, and God roused them at the end of the day. Their leader, Yamlikha, or Maksilmina, said: God knows best the duration.

His saying, Exalted is He: (So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city). On this there are seven issues.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: their silver was like the young camels' hooves (al-rabi', i.e., the foal born in spring), reported by al-Nahhas. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read "bi-wariqikum" with a kasra on the ra'. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "bi-warqikum" with a sukun on the ra', dropping the kasra because of its heaviness; both are dialects. al-Zajjaj read "bi-wiriqikum" with a kasra on the waw and a sukun on the ra'. It is reported that they awoke hungry, and that the one sent was Yamlikha, who was the youngest of them, as recorded by al-Ghaznawi. The city: Afsus; it is said it is Tarsus, and its name in the pre-Islamic period was Afsus, and when Islam came they named it Tarsus. Ibn 'Abbas said: they had dirhams on which was the image of the king who was in their time.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: (Then let him look which is the purer in food). Ibn 'Abbas said: the most lawful slaughter, because the people of their town used to slaughter in the name of the idol, and among them were people who concealed their faith. Ibn 'Abbas also said: most of them were Magians. It is said: "azka ta'aman" means more blessed. It is said that they ordered him to buy what he thinks is the food of two or three persons, so that he would not be noticed; then when it was cooked it sufficed a group. For this reason it is said: that food was rice. It is said: it was raisins. It is said: dates, and God knows best. It is said: "azka" means best. It is said: cheapest.

(Then let him bring you a provision from it), that is, sustenance.

(And let him be discreet), that is, in entering the city and buying food.

(And let him not make anyone aware of you), that is, let him not inform anyone. It is said: if he is discovered, let him not expose his brethren to what has befallen them.

(For if they come to know of you, they will stone you), said al-Zajjaj: it means with stones, and it is the most wretched form of killing. It is said: they will revile you with abuse and insult. The first is more correct, because he was determined to kill them, as has been mentioned earlier in their narrative. Stoning in the past was, as was mentioned before it, a punishment for opposing the religion of the people, since it is the most effective for the whole body of that religion's adherents in that they all take part in it.

The third: In this sending with silver there is evidence for agency (wakalah) and its validity. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib appointed his brother 'Aqil as agent before 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and there is no disagreement about it in general. Agency was known in the pre-Islamic period and in Islam. Do you not see how 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf appointed Umayyah ibn Khalaf as agent over his family and dependents in Makkah, that is, to protect them, while Umayyah was a polytheist; and 'Abd al-Rahman undertook for Umayyah the same protection of his dependents in Madinah, as a recompense for his conduct. al-Bukhari related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf who said: I made a written agreement with Umayyah ibn Khalaf that he would protect me regarding my dependents in Makkah, and I would protect him regarding his dependents in Madinah. When I mentioned "al-Rahman," he said: I do not know al-Rahman; write to me with your name that you had in the pre-Islamic period. So I wrote to him "Abd 'Amr" ... and he mentioned the hadith. Al-Asma'i said: the saghiyah (dependents) of a man are those who incline towards him and come to him; it is derived from saghā yasghū and yasghā, when one inclines; and everyone who inclines to a thing or is with it has saghā towards it and asghā, from the Book of Verbs.

And thus We caused them to be discovered: meaning, We let them be known and made them manifest. *Atharа* is the causative form of *athara* (to stumble), and the root sense of *al-ithar* is stumbling in the foot.

﴿That they might know that the promise of Allah is true﴾: this refers to the Muslim community of the era in which the People of the Cave were raised up. The reason was that Decius died, many centuries passed, and a righteous man ruled the people of that land. The people of his city disagreed about the Gathering (*al-hashr*) and the resurrection of bodies from the graves. Some doubted it and considered it far-fetched, saying: "Only the souls will be gathered, and the body will be eaten by the earth." Others said: "Both the soul and the body will be raised together." This troubled the king, who remained perplexed, not knowing how to make the matter clear to them. He put on sackcloth, sat on ashes, and humbly prayed to Allah, the Exalted, for a proof and a clear sign. Then Allah caused the People of the Cave to be discovered. It is said that when they sent one of their number to the city with their silver coins to bring them food from it, his appearance seemed strange and his coins seemed strange, because of the long time that had passed. [[In manuscript J: "waraqah" (a single coin).]] He was brought to the king, who was righteous and whose followers had believed. When the king looked at him, he said: "Perhaps this is one of the youths who went out in the time of King Decius. I have been asking Allah to show them to me." He asked the young man, who informed him. The king rejoiced at this and said: "Perhaps Allah has sent you a sign. Let us go to the Cave with him." So the people of the city rode out to them. When they drew near to the Cave, the man said, as a stratagem (*tamlihan*): "I will enter upon them first, so that they do not become frightened." He entered upon them and informed them of the matter, and that the nation was now a nation of Islam. It is reported that they rejoiced at this, went out to the king, honored him, and he honored them. Then they returned to their cave. Most of the narrations hold that they died when Tamlikha informed them, a true death, as will be mentioned. Those who had doubted the resurrection of bodies returned to certainty. This is the meaning of "We caused them to be discovered, that they might know that the promise of Allah is true": that is, that the king and his subjects might know that the Hour is true and the resurrection is true.

﴿When they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾: they took only that single man as evidence for their news, and they were reluctant to enter upon them. The king said: "Build over them a structure." Those who were of the religion of the youths said: "Take over them a place of worship (*masjid*)." It is also reported that a disbelieving group said: "Let us build a church (*bi'ah*) or a shelter (*madafan*)." [[In J and in the margin of al-Jamal citing al-Qurtubi: "mas'adan" (a place).]] The Muslims opposed them and said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship." It is also reported that some of the people wanted to seal the cave over them and leave them concealed within it. It is reported from Abdullah [[In J: "from Ubayd ibn Umayr."]] ibn Umar that Allah, the Exalted, blinded the people at that time to their traces and kept them hidden from them. Therefore the king was prompted to build a structure so that it would be a marker for them. It is also said that the king wanted to bury them in a golden coffin, but one of them came to him in a dream and said: "You wanted to place us in a golden coffin, so do not do it. We were created from dust and to dust we shall return, so leave us."

Here issues arise that are forbidden and others that are permitted. Taking places of worship over graves, praying in them, and building upon them, along with other matters the Sunnah has prohibited, are forbidden and not lawful. This is because Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed women who visit graves, those who take places of worship over them, and those who use lamps upon them." Al-Tirmidhi said: "On this subject there are also narrations from Abu Hurayrah and Aisha, and the hadith of Ibn Abbas is a fair (*hasan*) hadith." The two Sahih collections [al-Bukhari and Muslim] relate from Aisha that Umm Habibah and Umm Salamah mentioned a church they had seen in Abyssinia, which had images of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Those people, when a righteous man among them died, they built a place of worship over his grave and made those images in it. Those are the worst of creation in the sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection." This is the wording of Muslim. Our scholars said: "This makes it unlawful for Muslims to take the graves of prophets and scholars as places of worship." The imams also related from Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Do not pray toward graves, and do not sit upon them.'" This is the wording of Muslim. That is, do not take them as a qiblah so that you pray upon them or toward them, as the Jews and Christians did, which leads to the worship of those buried in them, as was the cause of idol worship. So the Prophet (ﷺ) warned against such things and blocked the means that lead to them, saying: "The anger of Allah has intensified against a people who took the graves of their prophets and their righteous ones as places of worship."

The two Sahih collections relate from Aisha and Abdullah ibn Abbas that they said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was near death, he began to throw a cloak over his face, and when he felt suffocated, he uncovered it from his face. In that state he said: 'May the curse of Allah be upon the Jews and Christians, who took the graves of their prophets as places of worship,' warning against what they had done." [Meaning: he warned his community against doing to his grave what the Jews did to the graves of their prophets.]

Muslim related from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that graves be plastered, that people sit upon them, and that structures be built over them." Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi also related from Jabir: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that graves be plastered, that they be written upon, that structures be built over them, and that they be trodden upon." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a fair sound (*hasan sahih*) hadith." The Sahih relates from Abu al-Hayyaj al-Asadi, who said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib said to me: 'Shall I send you on the same mission the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me on? Do not leave any statue without obliterating it, nor any raised grave without leveling it.'" [In another narration: "nor any image without obliterating it."] Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi also related it. Our scholars said: "Its apparent meaning prohibits raising graves, elevating them, and making them flat." Some scholars held this view. The majority, however, held that the elevation that must be removed is what exceeds the *tasnim* (a slight hump), and that a grave may retain what marks it and honors it. This is the description of the grave of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and of his two companions, may Allah be pleased with them, as Malik mentioned in the Muwatta', and the grave of our father Adam (ﷺ), as related by al-Daraqutni from the hadith of Ibn Abbas. As for building much on the grave, in the manner the Jahiliyyah did, glorifying and magnifying it, that is to be demolished and removed, for it involves using the adornments of this world at the first stage of the Hereafter, and imitating those who magnified graves and worshipped them. Based on these meanings and the apparent prohibition, it should be said that it is unlawful.

The *tasnim* of a grave is raising it about a span, taken from the hump of a camel. It is sprinkled with water so that it will not be scattered by the wind. Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no harm in plastering the grave with clay." Abu Hanifah said: "The grave should not be plastered, nor clay applied to it, nor a structure raised upon it lest it collapse." There is no harm in placing stones to serve as a marker, based on what Abu Bakr al-Athram related, who said: "Musaddad related to us, Nuh ibn Darraj related to us, from Aban ibn Taghlib, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, who said: 'Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), used to visit the grave of Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib every Friday, and she marked it with a stone.'" Abu Umar mentioned this.

As for what is permitted: burial in a coffin (*tabut*) is permitted, especially in soft ground. It is related that Daniel, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, was in a stone coffin, and that Joseph, peace be upon him, instructed that a glass coffin be made for him and placed in a well, out of fear that he would be worshipped. He remained so until the time of Moses, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all, when an old woman guided them to him. He lifted it and placed it in the enclosure of Isaac, peace be upon him.

In the Sahih it is related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that during the illness from which he died, he said: "Make for me a lahd (a niche-grave) and set up unbaked bricks over me, as was done for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The *lahd* is that a recess is dug into the earth, and another grave is dug in the side of the pit toward the qiblah, if the ground is firm. The deceased is placed in it and sealed off with bricks. This is more excellent in our view than the *shaq* (a simple trench), because it is what Allah, the Exalted, chose for His Messenger (ﷺ). Abu Hanifah held the same view and said: "The Sunnah is the *lahd*." Al-Shafi'i said: "The *shaq*." Using fired brick (*ajurr*) in the *lahd* is disliked. Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no harm in it, since it is a type of stone." Abu Hanifah and his companions disliked it, because fired brick is used for strengthening structures, whereas the grave and what is in it are subject to decay, so strengthening is not fitting for it. On this basis, stone and fired brick are treated alike. It was also said: fired brick is a mark of fire, so it is disliked as an omen. On this basis, stone and fired brick are distinguished.

They said: unbaked brick (*labin*) and reeds (*qasab*) are recommended, because it is related that a bundle of reeds was placed on the grave of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is related from the Shaykh, the Imam Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Hanafi, may Allah have mercy on him, that he permitted the use of a coffin in their lands because the ground there is soft. He said: "If a coffin of iron were used, there would be no harm in it. However, dust should be spread in it, the upper layer that is next to the deceased should be plastered with clay, and light unbaked bricks should be placed on the right and left of the deceased, so that it is in the position of a *lahd*."

I say: On this same principle is the placing of a rug (*qatifah*) in the grave of the Prophet (ﷺ), for Madinah is salty land (*sabkhah*). [Salty land: land with salt and brackish moisture.] Shuqran said: "By Allah, I myself placed the rug beneath the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the grave." Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi said: "The hadith of Shuqran is a fair, sound (*hasan sahih*) and gharib (singular, isolated in chain) hadith."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 22:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth being their dog."﴾ The pronoun in "they will say" refers to the People of the Torah and the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is because they differed about the number of the People of the Cave in this manner that is recorded. It is also said that it refers to the Christians, for a group of them came to the Prophet (ﷺ) from Najran, and the mention of the Companions of the Cave came up. The Ya'qubiyya said: "They were three, the fourth being their dog." The Nestorians said: "They were five, the sixth being their dog." The Muslims said: "They were seven, the eighth being their dog." It is also said that it is a report about the Jews, who instructed the polytheists to question the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Companions of the Cave.

As for the wāw in the statement "and the eighth being their dog," the grammarians (al-nahwiyyun, the grammarians) hold that it is a wāw of conjunction (wāw al-'atf) that entered at the end of a report about their number, in order to separate their matter and to indicate that this is the final (ghāya, limit) of what was said. Had it been dropped, the sentence would still be correct. A group, among them Ibn Khalawayh, said: it is the wāw of the eight (wāw al-thamaniya, the wāw that marks the number eight). Al-Tha'labi reported from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that the Quraysh used to say in counting: "six, seven, and eight," adding the wāw to the eight. Al-Qaffal reported something similar, saying: some people said that among the Arabs counting ends at seven, so when more is needed beyond it, a new statement is begun with the insertion of the wāw, as in His saying: "the penitent, the worshipers..." — then he said — "...and those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who guard the limits of Allah." What points to this is that when He mentioned the gates of Hell, He said: ﴿until, when they come to it, its gates are opened﴾ without a wāw, and when He mentioned Paradise, He said: ﴿and its gates are opened﴾ with a wāw. And He said: ﴿better than you, submitting, believing... and virgins﴾. So seven is, in their usage, the final number, just as ten is now the final number for us.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: such speech is arbitrary (tahakkum). From where is seven a final number for them? Moreover, it is refuted by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Holy, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Majestic﴾, where He did not mention the eighth name with a wāw.

Some of those who held that their number was seven said: He mentioned the wāw in His saying "seven and the eighth being their dog" only to draw attention to the fact that this number is the truth, and that it is distinct from the other numbers which the People of the Book stated. For this reason He, may He be exalted, said regarding the two preceding statements: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, and He did not mention it in the third statement, and He did not criticize it in any way. It is as if He said to His Prophet: "They are seven, and the eighth is their dog."

And ar-rajm (guessing) means speaking by conjecture. It is said of anything that is estimated: "rujima fihi" (he guessed about it), "marjum" and "murajjam," as the poet said:

*"War is nothing but what you have known and tasted,
and it is not a matter related by guesswork."* [This is from the Mu'allaqa of Zuhayr.]

I (al-Qurtubi) say: Al-Mawardi and al-Ghaznawi have mentioned that Ibn Jurayj and Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: they were eight, and they understood His saying, may He be exalted, "and the eighth being their dog" to mean: the owner of their dog. This strengthens the path of the grammarians regarding the wāw, and that it is as they said. Al-Qushayri said: He did not mention the wāw in His saying "the fourth, the sixth," and had it been reversed it would have been permissible. Thus, seeking wisdom and a reason in such a wāw is a remote affectation, like His saying in another place: ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree﴾, and in another place: ﴿except that there were warners for it, as a reminder﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number."﴾ In this verse Allah commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to refer the knowledge of their number to Him, mighty and majestic. Then He informed that those among mankind who know this are few. What is meant by them is a group of the People of the Book, according to the saying of 'Ata'. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "I am among that few; they were seven, and the eighth was their dog." Then he mentioned the seven by their names. The dog's name was Qitmir, a black dog (kalb anmar), above the qalati and below the kurdi. (The qalati, in the form of ka'rabi, is the short one among people, cats, and dogs; al-Damiri said: "al-qalati is a Chinese dog.") Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it was a Chinese dog. The correct view is that it was a Zubayri (a dog of the Zubayr kind). And he said: "No narrator remained in Nishapur who did not write this hadith from me, except one for whom it was not decreed." He said: Abu 'Amr al-Hiri wrote it from me.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument﴾, meaning: do not dispute about the Companions of the Cave except with what We have revealed to you, and that is the referral of the knowledge of their number to Allah, may He be exalted. It is also said: the meaning of "outward argument" is that you say: "It is not as you say," and similar things, and that you do not argue on a matter that is established about it. In this there is evidence that Allah, may He be exalted, did not make their number clear to anyone; for this reason He said: ﴿except an outward argument﴾, meaning: a superficial one, as the poet said:

*"And that complaint, its shame has passed away from you..."* [This is half a line of Abu Dhu'ayb. Its first half is: "The slanderers reproached me that I love her."]

He did not permit him in this verse to argue, but His saying "except an argument" is a metaphor, in that the People of the Book argue with him; his responding to them was called "mira'" (argument), then it was qualified as "outward" so that it differs from the true, blameworthy argument. The pronoun in His saying "concerning them" refers to the People of the Cave, and the pronoun in His saying "from them" refers to the opposing People of the Book. His saying "so do not argue concerning them" means concerning their number, and the word "number" has been omitted because the apparent sense of the statement indicates it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not consult any of them concerning them.﴾ It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, asked the Christians of Najran about them, and he was forbidden from asking. In this there is evidence for prohibiting Muslims from referring to the People of the Book in any matter of knowledge.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 18, verses 23–24:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ On this verse there are two issues.

The first: The scholars said: Allah the Exalted rebuked His Prophet, peace be upon him, for his saying to the disbelievers, when they asked him about the Spirit, the young men of the Cave, and Dhu al-Qarnayn: "Tomorrow I will inform you of the answers to your questions," and he did not add an exception (istithna', the phrase "if Allah wills") to that. So the revelation was withheld from him for fifteen days, until this weighed heavily on him and the disbelievers spread rumors against him. Then this surah was revealed to him, bringing relief. In this verse he was commanded not to say, concerning any matter, "I will do such-and-such tomorrow," unless he attaches it to the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that the statement does not become a firm assertion of the outcome. For if he says, "I will certainly do that," and does not do it, he has been a liar; but if he says, "I will certainly do that, if Allah wills," he has gone outside being a firm assertion of what he reports. The "lam" in His saying "for anything" (li-shay') is in the sense of "fi" (in), or it is as if He said "for the sake of something."

The second issue: Ibn 'Atiyya said: People have spoken about this verse concerning the exception in oaths (al-istithna' fi al-yamin, the exception made in an oath), but the verse is not about oaths; rather, it concerns the practice of making an exception in statements other than oaths. His saying, "unless Allah wills," involves an ellipsis required by the apparent sense and made elegant by brevity. Its estimated meaning is: "unless you say, 'unless Allah wills'," or "unless you say, 'if Allah wills'." So the meaning is: unless he mentions the will of Allah. Therefore "unless Allah wills" is not part of the speech that was forbidden.

I say: What Ibn 'Atiyya chose and approved is the view of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. The Basrans said: The meaning is "unless by the will of Allah." So when a person says, "I will do this, if Allah wills," its meaning is "by the will of Allah."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: A group said that "unless Allah wills" is an exception from His saying "and never say." He said: This is a view transmitted by al-Tabari, who refuted it, and it is so corrupt that it should not have been related at all.

The discussion of the exception in oaths and its ruling has already been given in (Surat) al-Ma'idah [[see vol. 6, p. 264]].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾. On this there is one issue: the command to remember (Allah) after forgetting. Scholars differed about what remembrance is meant. It was said: It is His saying, ﴿And say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer to right conduct than this"﴾. Muhammad al-Kufi, the exegete, said: These words, by their wording, are among what everyone who did not make an exception was commanded to say, and they serve as an expiation (kaffarah) for forgetting the exception. Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: It is a supplication commanded, without this specific restriction.

It was also said: It is His saying, ﴿if Allah wills﴾ [al-Saffat: 102], which he had forgotten at the time of his oath. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that if a person forgets to make the exception and then remembers, even after a year, he does not break his oath, provided he was swearing. This is also the view of Mujahid. Isma'il ibn Ishaq related this from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying, ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: he said, "He should make the exception when he remembers it." Al-Hasan said: "As long as he is in the gathering of remembrance." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Two years." This was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi, who said: It is to be understood as seeking to attain the blessing of the exception in order to be freed from sin.

As for an exception that has a legal effect, it is not valid except when it is connected (to the statement).

Al-Suddi said: That is, every prayer that you forgot, when you remember it, pray it. It was also said: Make the exception by naming Him, lest you forget. It was said: Remember Him whenever you forget. It was said: When you forget something, remember it, and it will remind you of it. It was said: Remember Him when you forget something else, or when you yourself are forgotten; that is the true meaning of remembrance.

This verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and according to the most correct view it is the opening of a speech. It has nothing to do with the exception in oaths. Moreover, it encompasses his entire community, because it is a ruling that recurs among people due to how often it occurs.

And Allah is the Granter of success.
