And Allah is the Granter of success.

This is a report from God, Exalted is He, about the length of their stay. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it reads, "And they said: they remained." Al-Tabari said: The Children of Israel disagreed, in the past, about the length of time that had elapsed for them after they were discovered until the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Some of them said: they remained three hundred and nine years. So God, Exalted is He, informed His Prophet that this period was the time of their sleeping, and that what came after it is unknown to mankind. God then commanded that the knowledge of this be referred back to Him.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: According to this view, the first "remained" (labithu) refers to their stay in the sleep of the Cave, and the second "remained" refers to the period after they were discovered until the time of Muhammad ﷺ, or until the time of their being wiped out by calamity. Mujahid said: until the time the Qur'an was revealed. Al-Dahhak said: until they died.

Some said: when He said, "and they add nine," people did not know whether these were hours, days, weeks, months, or years. The Children of Israel differed accordingly, so God commanded that the knowledge of the nine be referred back to Him. On this view, the nine is vague. The apparent meaning of Arabic speech, as understood from it, is that they are years. The apparent sense of their situation is that they got up and entered the Cave shortly after 'Isa (Jesus), when some of the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun) still remained.

Others said other things, as will come. Al-Qushayri said: From "nine" one does not understand nine nights and nine hours, because the years were mentioned earlier, as you would say: "I have a hundred dirhams and five," and what is understood is five dirhams. Abu 'Ali said: "and they add nine" means "they added a stay of nine," and it was elided. Al-Dahhak said: When "and they remained in their Cave three hundred" was revealed, they said: "years or months or weeks or days?" So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed "years."

Al-Naqqash related a report whose meaning is that they remained three hundred solar years, calculated by days, so when the address here was to the Arab Prophet, the nine was mentioned, since the reckoning familiar to him is of lunar years, and this addition is the difference between the two calculations. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned something similar, namely the difference between solar and lunar years, because it accumulates one year every thirty-three and a third years, so in three hundred there are nine years.

The majority read "thalatha mi'atin sinin" with tanwin on mi'ah and a fatha on sinin, by inversion of the order, meaning sinina thalathami'atin, so the adjective is placed before the noun it qualifies; "sinin" in this case is then either a substitute (badal) or an appositive ( 'atf bayan). It has also been said: it is an explanation (tafsir) and a specification (tamyiz). And "sinin" is in the position of "sanah" (a year).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the mi'ah annexed to sinin (idafah), without tanwin, as though they treated sinin as equivalent to sanah, since the meaning of both is one. Abu 'Ali said: these numbers which in the common usage are annexed to singulars, such as "thalathumi'at rajul" (three hundred men) and "thawb" (garment), may also be annexed to plurals.

In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "thalathumi'at sanah" (three hundred year). Al-Dahhak read "thalathumi'at sunun" with a waw.

Abu 'Amr, in one of the two transmitted readings, read "tis'an" with a fatha on the ta', while the majority read it with a kasra.

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: the estimated sense is: "and they remained in their Cave, sinin thalathumi'at" (three hundred years).

"Say: Allah knows best how long they remained." It was said: after their death until the revelation of the Qur'an concerning them, according to the view of Mujahid; or until the time they died, according to the view of al-Dahhak; or until the time their bodies changed through decay, according to what has preceded. It was also said: "how long they remained" refers to their stay in the cave, which is the period that Allah mentioned regarding the Jews, even though they mentioned excess and deficiency; that is, none knows this knowledge except Allah or whoever He taught it. ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾

"How clearly He sees, and how clearly He hears." That is, how far His sight and hearing extend. Qatadah said: there is no one who sees more than Allah or hears more. These are expressions about perception. It is also possible that the meaning is: "See by it," i.e., by His revelation and His guidance, your guidance, your proofs and the truth of matters, and "hear by it" the world; so the two would be commands, not in the sense of wonder. It was also said: the meaning is, "Make them see and make them hear what Allah has said about them."

﴿They have no protector besides Him.﴾ That is, the People of the Cave had no guardian other than Allah who would take charge of protecting them. It is also possible that the pronoun in "for them" refers to the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ among the disbelievers. The meaning would be: these people who differ about the length of their stay have no protector besides Allah who manages their affairs, so how could they be more knowledgeable than Him, or how could they learn without His informing them?

"And He does not share His rule with anyone." It was read with the yā' and a raised kāf (وَلا يُشْرِكُ), in the sense of a report about Allah the Exalted. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah and al-Jahdari read "wa-lā tushrik" with the tā' at the beginning and a sukūn on the kāf, addressing the Prophet ﷺ, and then "wa-lā yushriku" would be coordinated with "abṣir bihi wa-asmi'" (the preceding imperative). Mujahid read "yushriku" with the yā' at the beginning and jazm. Ya'qub said: I do not know its basis.

Issue: It has been disputed whether the People of the Cave died and perished, or whether they are asleep while their bodies are preserved. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he passed through al-Sham on one of his campaigns with some people by the site of the cave and its mountain, and the people walked with him to it. They found bones, and they said: "These are the bones of the People of the Cave." Ibn 'Abbas said to them: "Those were a people who perished and were annihilated a long time ago." A monk heard him and said: "I did not think that any of the Arabs knew this." It was said to him: "This is the cousin of our Prophet ﷺ." A group also narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Jesus son of Mary will surely perform Hajj, and with him will be the companions of the cave, for they have not performed Hajj..." (the text is as transmitted). Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned it. I say: It is written in the Torah and the Gospel that Jesus son of Mary is the servant of Allah and His messenger, and that he will pass by al-Rawha' as a pilgrim or a visitor, or Allah will gather that for him, and Allah will make his disciples the companions of the cave and al-Raqim, and they will pass by as pilgrims, for they have not performed Hajj and have not died. We have mentioned this report in full in the book "al-Tadhkirah." Accordingly, they are asleep and have not died until the Day of Resurrection; rather, they will die shortly before the Hour.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 27:**

His words, may He be exalted: "And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words." It was said: this is part of the completion of the story of the People of the Cave, meaning: follow the Qur'an, for there is no one who can alter the words of God, and there is no contradiction in what He has reported of the story of the People of the Cave. Al-Tabari said: there is no one who can change what He has promised, in His words, to the people of disobedience and to those who oppose His Book.

"And you will not find," [O Prophet], "besides Him," [if you do not follow the Qur'an and oppose it], "any refuge" (مُلْتَحَداً). That is, any shelter. It was also said: any place to turn to. Its root meaning is inclination, since whoever seeks refuge in something has inclined towards it.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim said: this is the end of the story of the People of the Cave. When Mu'awiya (may God be pleased with him) campaigned in the expedition of al-Madiq towards the Byzantines, Ibn 'Abbas was with him. They reached the cave in which the People of the Cave were. Mu'awiya said: "If only it were uncovered for us, so that we could look at them." Ibn 'Abbas said: "God has prevented one better than you from that." [Mu'awiya] said: "If you had looked at them, you would have turned away from them in flight" (لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِراراً). [Mu'awiya] said: "I will not stop until I know their condition," and he sent a group for that purpose. When they entered the cave, God sent a wind upon them which brought them out. This was also reported by al-Tha'labi.

It is also mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked God to show him them, and He said: "You will not see them in the life of this world, but send to them four of your best companions to convey your message to them and call them to faith." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jibril (peace be upon him): "How shall I send them?" He said: "Spread your cloak and sit on one of its edges, Abu Bakr on one edge, 'Umar on the other edge, 'Uthman on the third, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib on the fourth. Then call the gentle wind subjected to Sulayman, for God commands it to obey you." He did so, and the wind carried them to the entrance of the cave. They took a stone from it, and the dog came at them. When it saw them, it shook its head, wagged its tail, and gestured to them with its head to enter. They entered the cave and said: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings." God returned their spirits to the youths, and they all stood up and said: "And upon you be peace, and the mercy of God and His blessings." They said to them: "O company of youths, the Prophet Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah (ﷺ) sends you his greetings." They said: "And upon Muhammad, Messenger of God, be peace for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and upon you for what you have conveyed." They accepted his religion and embraced Islam. Then they said: "Convey to Muhammad, Messenger of God, our greetings from us." They lay down on their resting places and returned to their sleep until the end of time, at the emergence of the Mahdi. It is said that the Mahdi will greet them, God will bring them back to life, and then they will return to their sleep and will not rise until the Hour comes.

Jibril informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of what had happened to them. Then the wind brought them back, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How did you find them?" They told him the news. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not separate me from my companions and my in-laws, forgive whoever is far from me, and love the people of my household, my close ones, and my companions."

It was also said: the People of the Cave entered the cave before the Messiah, and God informed the Messiah of their news, and then they were raised up in the interval between 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: they were before Musa (Moses) (peace be upon him), and that Musa mentioned them in the Torah, and for this reason the Jews asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was also said: they entered the cave after the Messiah. God knows best which of these was the case.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾. This is similar to His saying: "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening" (al-An'am). [See vol. 6, p. 432.] "The discussion of it has already passed. Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and al-Aqra' ibn Habis came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you were to sit at the head of the gathering and push these people away from us, and (the stench of) their woolen cloaks—they meant Salman, Abu Dharr and the poor Muslims, and they had nothing but woolen cloaks—we would sit with you, converse with you and take from you." So Allah revealed: "And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will not find any refuge besides Him. And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face," up to "Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure will surround them." (The verse) threatens them with the Fire.' Then the Prophet ﷺ went out seeking them, and when he found them at the back of the mosque remembering Allah, he said: "Praise be to Allah who has not taken me until He commanded me to keep myself patient with men from my community; your living and your dying are with you." "Seeking His face" means seeking His obedience.

Nasr ibn 'Asim, Malik ibn Dinar and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read: "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning (bil-ghadah)" [This is as it stands in the originals; he meant that these readers recited it here as al-ghadah, and in al-An'am as al-ghadwah.] "and evening (al-'ashiyy)." Their argument is that it is written with a waw in the Imam (codex). Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "This is not necessary, since they write al-hayah and al-salah with a waw as well, and the Arabs hardly say al-ghadwah since it is well known."

It is related from al-Hasan: ﴿and let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, i.e. do not let your eyes go past them to others among the people of this world, seeking its adornment. This was related by al-Yazidi. It was also said: "Let not your eyes despise them," as one says, "So-and-so is shunned by the eye," meaning, held in contempt.

(﴿You desire the adornment of the worldly life﴾): i.e., the adornment through sitting with those leaders who proposed removing the poor from your assembly. The Prophet ﷺ did not intend to do that, but Allah forbade him from doing it. This is no more severe than His saying: "If you associate partners (with Allah), your deeds will surely be nullified" [see vol. 15, p. 276], though Allah had protected him from shirk. "You desire" is a present-tense verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: do not let your eyes pass beyond them while desiring, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"I said to her: Do not let your eye weep, for we only seek a kingdom or die, and be excused."

Some claimed that the proper construction of the sentence is: "Do not let your eyes pass beyond them," since ta'du is transitive by itself. It was replied to him: the recitation that came with the raising of "al-'aynan" amounts in meaning to the accusative, if "la ta'du 'aynaka 'anhum" is like "la tanssarif 'aynaka 'anhum," and the meaning of "la tanṣarif 'aynaka 'anhum" is "la tasrif 'aynayka 'anhum." The verb is then ascribed to the eyes, but in reality it is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, as He, exalted is He, said: "So let not their wealth impress you" [see vol. 8, p. 164], where He ascribed the impressing to the wealth, while the meaning is: "Let not their wealth impress you, O Muhammad." What makes this clearer is al-Zajjaj's saying: the meaning is "do not turn your gaze away from them toward others among those of rank and adornment."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾. Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance," that he said: it was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, because he invited the Prophet ﷺ to a matter he disliked, namely the removal of the poor from him and drawing near the chiefs of Makkah. So Allah revealed: "And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance," meaning, one whose heart We have sealed against monotheism.

(﴿and follows his desire﴾): meaning, polytheism.

(﴿and whose affair is excess﴾): it was said: it is from tafrit, which is negligence and the preceding of incapacity by abandoning faith. It was also said: it is from ifrat, exceeding the limit, as if the people said: "We are the nobles of Mudar; if we embrace Islam, the people will embrace it," and this was from arrogance and excess in speech. It was also said: "furuta" means "forward in evil," from their saying: "a matter preceded (faratha) from him," i.e., went ahead. It was also said: the meaning of "We have made his heart heedless" is: We found him heedless, as you say: "I met so-and-so and found him praiseworthy (ahmadtuhu)," i.e., I found him praiseworthy. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said to the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b: "By Allah, we asked you and did not find you miserly; we fought you and did not find you cowardly; we exchanged satire with you and did not find you tongue-tied," meaning, we did not find you miserly, nor cowardly, nor tongue-tied. It was also said: this verse, "And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance," was revealed concerning 'Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari; 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned it, and al-Nahhas related it from Sufyan al-Thawri. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 29:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve."﴾ "الْحَقُّ" (al-haqq) is in the nominative case as the predicate (khabar) of an implied subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), meaning: say, "It is the truth." It was also said: it is nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in His saying "from your Lord." The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to those whose hearts We have made heedless of Our remembrance: O people! The truth is from your Lord. To Him belong success and abandonment, and in His hand are guidance and misguidance. He guides whom He wills, so he believes, and He leads astray whom He wills, so he disbelieves. None of that is up to me. Allah gives the truth to whom He wills, even if he is weak, and withholds it from whom He wills, even if he is strong and wealthy. I will not drive away the believers to satisfy your desires. So if you wish, believe, and if you wish, disbelieve. This is not a grant of permission or a choice between faith and disbelief; rather, it is a threat and a warning, meaning: if you disbelieve, then the Fire has been prepared for you, and if you believe, then Paradise is yours.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾, meaning: We have prepared.

﴿for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: for the disbelievers who deny.

﴿a Fire whose enclosure encompasses them﴾. Al-Jawhari said: al-suradiq (سُرَادِقٌ, "enclosure, tent-wall") is the singular of al-surādiqāt, the awnings stretched above the courtyard of a house. Every tent made of cotton [[al-kurfus: cotton]] is a surādiq. Ru'ba said [[As it stands in the original and in Lisan al-Arab; Lisan noted that the verse is by al-Kadhib al-Harmazi, and Sibawayh and al-A'lam al-Shantamari followed this. The rajaz poet praises one of the Banu al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud al-Abdi, and this ruler was one of the governors of Basra for Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. His grandfather was named al-Jarud because he raided a people and swept away their wealth, so he was likened to a flood that strips whatever passes over it.]]:

O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud,
the enclosure of glory is stretched over you.

It is said: "a bayt musardaq" (a tent with an enclosure). Salama ibn Jandal said, describing Abarwiz [[with the waw vowelled either fatha or kasra; a king of the Persian kings]] and his killing of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir under the feet of elephants:

He is the one who brought al-Nu'man into a house whose roof
was the chests of elephants, after a musardaq house.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "surādiquhā" (its enclosure) means its wall. It is related from Ibn Abbas: a wall of fire. Al-Kalbi said: a neck that emerges from the Fire and surrounds the disbelievers like a fence. Al-Qutabi said: al-surādiq is the screen that surrounds the tent-pole. Ibn Uzayz [[said]]. It was also said: it is a smoke that encompasses the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, and this is what Allah mentioned in the surah "Al-Mursalat," where He says: ﴿Proceed to a shadow of three branches﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 160.]] and His saying: ﴿and a shadow of black smoke﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 212.]]. This was said by Qatada. It was also said: it is the sea that encompasses the world. Ya'la ibn Umayya narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The sea is Jahannam," then he recited: ﴿a Fire whose enclosure encompasses them﴾, then he said: "By Allah, I will never enter it as long as I live, and not a drop of it will touch me." Al-Mawardi mentioned this. Ibn al-Mubarak related from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "The enclosure of the Fire has four thick walls, each wall the distance of forty years." Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi also related it and said about it: "It is a hasan sahih gharib hadith." I say: this indicates that the surādiq is what rises above the disbelievers of smoke or fire, and its walls are what has been described.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal, which scalds the faces﴾. Ibn Abbas said: al-muhl (الْمُهْلُ, "molten metal, dregs") is a thick water like the sediment of olive oil. Mujahid said: it is pus and blood. Al-Dahhak said: it is black water, for Jahannam is black, its water is black, its trees are black, and its people are black. Abu Ubayda said: it is anything melted from the substances of the earth, such as iron, lead, copper, and tin, which then seethes and boils; that is al-muhl. A similar view is related from Ibn Mas'ud. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is that whose heat has reached its extreme. He also said: al-muhl is a kind of tar; it is said: "mahaltu al-ba'īr, fa huwa mamhūl" (I smeared the camel with tar, so it is smeared). It was also said: it is poison. The meaning of these views is close. In al-Tirmidhi, from the Prophet ﷺ regarding His saying "like al-muhl," he said: "Like the dregs of oil; when he brings it near his face, the skin of his face falls off." Abu Isa said: this is a hadith we only know through the narration of Rishdin ibn Sa'd, and Rishdin has been criticized regarding his memory. He also related from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding His saying: ﴿and he is given to drink of pus-water, which he gulps﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 353.]], that he said: "It is brought close to his mouth, and he dislikes it. When it is brought near him, it scorches his face, and his scalp falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out of his anus. Allah says: ﴿and they are given boiling water, which cuts up their intestines﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 236.]], and He says: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.﴾" He said: this is a gharib hadith. I say: this indicates the soundness of those views, that they are all intended, and Allah knows best. Likewise, the lexicographers stated them. In al-Sihah: "al-muhl" is molten copper. Ibn al-A'rabi: al-muhl is molten lead. Abu Amr said: al-muhl is the dregs of oil. Al-muhl is also pus and discharge. And in the hadith of Abu Bakr: "Bury me in these two garments of mine, for they are for al-muhl and the dust."

(**مُرْتَفَقاً** *murtafaqan*, "resting place") Mujahid said: its meaning is "gathered together," as if he took the meaning of "companionship" (al-murafaqah). Ibn Abbas: a dwelling. Ata: a resting place. It was also said: a cushion. Al-Qutabi said: a sitting place. The meanings are close, and its origin is from reclining, as it is said: "irtafaqtu," meaning I leaned on the elbow. The poet said:

She said to him, and she leaned, "Is there not a youth
who drives the people with the gazelles of the forenoon?" [[The gazelle of the forenoon and its gazelles: after the sun has spread and become bright. It was said: it is the beginning of the forenoon until the greater extension of the day, when about a fifth of the day has passed.]]

It is also said: "irtafaqa al-rajul" means a man slept on his elbow, unable to sleep. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

The one at ease slept, while I spent the night propped on my elbow,
as if my eyes, within them, were struck with bitter aloe. [[The version in the Diwan reads "mushtajiran." Al-mushtajir is one who has pressed himself and placed his hand under a tree on his jaw or mouth. Al-shajr is what is between the two jaws. "Madhbuh" means split open/cracked.]]

*Al-Sabb* (الصَّابُ): the sap of a bitter tree.

When He mentioned what He had prepared for the disbelievers of humiliation, He also mentioned what is for the believers of reward. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: "We do not waste the reward of those among them who do good deeds." As for one who does better deeds than the believers, from among non-believers, his deed is nullified. "ʿAmalan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and if you wish, "aḥsana" may govern it. It has also been said: "Innā lā nuḍīʿu ajra man aḥsana ʿamalan" is a parenthetical clause (kalam muʿtaraḍ), and the predicate (khabar) is His saying: ﴿Those, for them are Gardens of Eden﴾. "Jannātu ʿadnin" is the navel (surrat) of Paradise, meaning its middle, and the rest of the gardens surround it. It is mentioned in the plural form because of its vastness, since every part of it is fit to be a garden. It has also been said: "al-ʿadn" means residence. One says: "ʿadana bi-l-makān" when he resides in the place; "ʿadantu al-balad" means I settled in the town; "ʿadanat al-ibil bi-makān kadhā" means the camels stayed at such a place and did not leave it. From this comes "Jannāt ʿadn," meaning gardens of residence. From this the mine (al-maʿdin, with a kasra on the dal) is named, because people reside in it in summer and winter; and the center of everything is its maʿdin. Al-ʿādin: the she-camel that remains in the pastures. "ʿAdan" is a town, as said by al-Jawhari.

﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾: this has been discussed in more than one place [see vol. 1, p. 239].

﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾: this is the plural of siwar (bracelet). Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: each one of them has three bracelets: one of gold, one of silver, and one of pearls. I say: this is stated explicitly in the Qur'an. Here He said "min dhahab" (of gold), and in Surat al-Hajj [see vol. 12, p. 28] and Fatir [see vol. 14, p. ...] "min dhahabin wa lu'lu'an" (of gold and pearls), and in al-Insan [see vol. 19, p. 141] "min fiḍḍa" (of silver). Abu Hurayra said: I heard my close friend (ﷺ) say: "The ornament of the believer reaches as far as the ablution reaches." Recorded by Muslim.

al-Farra' related: "yuḥallawna" with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the ha', and a light fatha on the lam. It is said: "ḥaliyat al-mar'a taḥlā, fa-hiya ḥāliyah" when a woman wears ornaments; and "ḥalia al-shay' bi-ʿaynayya yaḥlā" (I found the thing pleasing to my eyes). Al-Nahhas mentioned this. Al-siwar is the woman's bracelet, its plural is asāwira, and the plural of the plural is asāwira. Also read: "fa-lawlā ulqiya ʿalayhi asāwiratun min dhahab" [see vol. 16, p. 100]; the plural may also be asāwir. Allah the Exalted said: "yuḥallawna fīhā min asāwira min dhahab," as al-Jawhari said. Ibn ʿUzayr said: asāwir is the plural of asāwira, and asāwira is the plural of siwār and siwār, which is worn on the forearm, of gold. If it is of silver, it is qilb, and its plural is qilab; if it is of horn or ivory, it is maskah, and its plural is masak. Al-Nahhas said: Qutrub related for the singular of asāwir the form iswār, but Qutrub is an odd (shādhdh) authority, whom Yaʿqub and others left and did not mention.

I say: it has come in al-Sihah, and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: its singular is iswār. The commentators said: since in this world the bracelets and crowns were [symbols of rank], Allah the Exalted gave these to the people of Paradise.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade﴾: "Sundus" is the thin and delicate, its singular is sundusah, said al-Kisa'i. "Istabraq" is what is thick of it, according to Ikrima, and it is silk. The poet said:

"You see them at times wearing the cloaks, and at times their garment is istabraq brocade."

So istabraq is brocade. Ibn Bahr: the woven with gold. Al-Qutabi: it is a Persian word that has been Arabized. Al-Jawhari: its diminutive is ubayriq. It has also been said: it is istaf'al from al-bariq (sheen). The correct view is that it is common to both languages, since there is nothing in the Qur'an that is not from the language of the Arabs, as previously stated; and Allah knows best. The green is singled out for mention because it is the most agreeable to the sight, since white dazzles the gaze and causes pain, black is disliked, and green lies between white and black, and it gathers the rays. And Allah knows best.

al-Nasa'i related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: While we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a man came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us about the garments of Paradise: are they something created or something woven?" Some of the people laughed. He said to them: "Why do you laugh at an ignorant man who asks a learned one?" Then he sat for a little while, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Where is the one who asked about the garments of Paradise?" He said: "Here I am, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "No, rather they split forth from the fruits of Paradise," and he said it three times. Abu Hurayra said: The abode of the believer is a hollow pearl, in the middle of which is a tree that produces garments, and he takes with his finger, or he said with his two fingers, seventy garments arranged with pearls and coral. Yahya ibn Sallam mentioned it in his Tafsir, and Ibn al-Mubarak in his Raqa'iq. We have mentioned its chain in the book al-Tadhkira. It is mentioned in the hadith that on each of them there is a garment with two faces, each face of a different color, and they speak with a voice that pleases the hearer; one of the two faces says to the other: "I am more honored before the friend of Allah than you; I attend to his body, and you do not." And the other says: "I am more honored before the friend of Allah than you; I look upon his face, and you do not."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾: "al-arā'ik" is the plural of arika, which are thrones in canopies (al-ḥijāl). It has been said: they are cushions in the canopies, as said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn ʿAbbas: they are beds of gold, adorned with pearls and rubies, with canopies over them. The arika is what lies between Sanaa and Ayla, and between Aden and al-Jabiya. The origin of mutaki'in is mu-tuka'in, and similarly ittaka'a originally was awta'a or tuka'a; the root of tuka'a is wuka'a, from which comes tawakku' for leaning heavily on something; then the waw was changed to ta and assimilated. A man who leans much is called wuka'a.

﴿How excellent the reward, and how good a resting place﴾: this refers to the Gardens, the opposite of ﴿and how evil a resting place﴾, which has been discussed before. Had it been "ni'mat," it would be permissible, since it is a name for Paradise. And upon this, "wa-ḥasunat murtafaqan." Al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib related that a Bedouin stood before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the Farewell Pilgrimage, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing at ʿArafat on his she-camel al-ʿAḍbāʾ, and he said: "I am a Muslim man, so inform me about this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ — the verse." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are not far from them, nor are they far from you; they are these four: Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, and ʿAli. So inform your people that this verse was revealed concerning them." Al-Mawardi mentioned it, and al-Nahhas traced its chain in his book Maʿani al-Qur'an, saying: Abu ʿAbd Allah Ahmad ibn ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn al-Daris narrated to us from Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiya from Ibn Ishaq from al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, who said: A Bedouin stood up... and he mentioned it. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And set forth for them the parable of two men﴾. This is a parable for one who takes pride in the world and disdains sitting with the believers, and it is connected to His saying, "And keep yourself patient" (18:28). Scholars differ about the names of these two men and about identifying them. Al-Kalbi said: They were revealed concerning two brothers from Makkah, of the clan of Makhzum. It was also said: They inherited it from their father, and they were brothers, and they divided it. One of them bought land for a thousand dinars. His companion said: "O Allah, so-and-so has bought land for a thousand dinars, and I have bought from You land in Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave it in charity. Then his companion built a house for a thousand dinars, and he said: "O Allah, so-and-so has built a house for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave [a thousand dinars] in charity. He then married a woman and spent a thousand dinars on her, and he said: "O Allah, so-and-so has married a woman for a thousand dinars, and I propose to You for a woman of the women of Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then he bought servants and goods for a thousand dinars, and he said: "I buy from You servants and goods from Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then a severe need befell him, and he said: "Perhaps my companion will bestow his kindness upon me." He came to him and said: "What has become of your wealth?" He told him his story. He said: "Are you truly one of those who believe this report? By Allah, I will not give you anything." Then he said to him: "You worship the God of the heavens, and I worship only an idol." His companion said: "By Allah, I will admonish him." So he admonished him, reminded him, and warned him. He said: "Come, let us go fishing; whoever catches more is in the right." He said to him: "O my brother, indeed this world is too insignificant in the sight of Allah for Him to make it a reward for the good or a punishment for the unbeliever." He said: He compelled him to go out with him, and Allah tested them both. The unbeliever began casting his net and calling upon the name of his idol, and fish came up in abundance. The believer began casting his net and calling upon the name of Allah, and nothing came up for him in it. Then he said to him: "How do you see it? I have more than you in this world in wealth, position and followers. Likewise, I shall be better than you in the Hereafter, if what you say is true according to your claim." He said: The angel appointed over them both cried out, so Allah, may He be exalted, commanded Gabriel to take him and go with him to the Gardens, and show him the dwellings of the believer there. When he saw what Allah had prepared for him, he said: "By Your might, what he obtained of the world will not harm him, since his final destination is this." And He showed him the dwellings of the unbeliever in Hell, and he said: "By Your might, what he obtained of the world will not benefit him, since his final destination is this." Then Allah, may He be exalted, took the believer to Himself and destroyed the unbeliever with a punishment from Him. When the believer settled in Paradise and saw what Allah had prepared for him, he and his companions began to ask one another, and he said: "Indeed, I had a companion" (37:51), saying: "Are you truly among those who believe?" (37:52), and so on. A caller called out: "O people of Paradise! Would you like to look down?" So he looked down into Hell and saw him in the midst of the blazing fire, and then this was revealed: "And set forth for them a parable" (18:32). One of them sold his share to the other, and he spent it in obedience to Allah until the other changed [his condition]. Conversation took place between them, and Allah drowned them in a single night, and it was these that this verse refers to. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had surrounded the two with date palms﴾, that is, We enclosed them on their sides with date palms. The ḥifāf is the side, and its plural is aḥiffah. It is said: "The people encircled so-and-so (ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān), yaḥuffūna ḥaffan," meaning they went around him. From this is His saying: "encircling the Throne" (39:75) [[See vol. 15, p. 84, part 2 onward.]]. "And We placed between them a field of crops" means that We placed the date palms around the vines, and the crops in the middle of the vines.

"Both the gardens" means each of the two gardens, "yielded its produce" in full, and therefore He did not say "yielded their produce." Scholars differed over whether the word kilā and kiltā is singular or dual. The Basrans said: It is singular, because kilā and kiltā, when used to emphasise the dual, correspond to kull used with the plural, and it is a singular noun, not dual. When it is followed by an apparent noun, it has one form in the nominative, accusative and genitive. You say: "I saw kilā al-rajulayn (both the two men), and kilā al-rajulayn came to me, and I passed by kilā al-rajulayn." When it is attached to a pronoun, the alif becomes yā' in the genitive and accusative positions. You say: "I saw kilayhimā, and I passed by kilayhimā," just as you say ʿalayhimā. Al-Farra' said: It is dual, and it is derived from kull, with the lam lightened and the alif added to form the dual. Likewise kiltā is for the feminine, and neither of them is used except in construction (as the first term of an idāfa), and one does not speak of a single one of them. If one did speak of a single one, one would say: kil, kilt, kilān, kiltān. He argued with the poet's verse:

"In the one of her two feet are single phalanges (sulāmā), both joined to an extra one."

He meant "in one of her two feet," and so used the singular. This view is weak according to the Basrans, because if it were dual, its alif would have to become yā' in the accusative and genitive with an apparent noun. Also, the meaning of kilā differs from the meaning of kull, because kilā is for comprehensiveness of two, whereas kull refers to a specific thing. As for this poet, he omitted the alif out of poetic necessity and assumed it was extra, and what is a necessity cannot be made evidence. Thus it is established that it is a singular noun like miʿan, except that it was put in place to indicate the dual, just as their saying "naḥnu" (we) is a singular noun that indicates two or more. The verse of Jarir proves this:

"Both days of Umamah are a day of separation,
and even if we do not visit them except briefly."

Here he reported about "kilā" with a single "day," just as he used a singular predicate with His saying "yielded" (ātat), and had it been dual he would have said ātatā, and yawman [would be yawmayn]. Scholars also differed about the alif of "kiltā." Sibawayh said: the alif of "wa-kiltā" is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the lam of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original was kilwā. The wāw was changed into tā' because the tā' carries the sign of the feminine, and the alif in "kiltā" may become yā' with a pronoun, so it would leave the sign of the feminine; therefore, the replacement of the wāw by tā' became an emphasis for the feminine. Abu Umar al-Jarmi said: the tā' is an added letter, and the alif is the lam of the verb, and its pattern in his view is fiʿtal. If the matter were as he claimed, they would say in the relative form kiltawī, but since they said kilawī and dropped the tā', it shows that they treated it as the tā' in ukht (sister), where if you form the relative you say ukhawī. Al-Jawhari mentioned this. Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: The grammarians permitted, outside the Qur'an, interpretation according to meaning, and that you say: "Kiltā al-jannatayn ātatā ukulahumā," because the preferred meaning is "kiltāhumā ātatā" [in another copy: "al-jannatān kiltāhumā"]. Al-Farra' permitted: "Kiltā al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu," and he said: because the meaning is "kull al-jannatayn" (each of the two gardens). He said: In the reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) it is "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu." The meaning according to al-Farra' is: everything of the two gardens yielded its produce.

Al-Ukul (with a dammah on the hamzah) is the fruit of the date palm and of trees, and everything that is eaten is ukul. From this is His saying: "its food is eternal" (13:35), and it has been mentioned before [[See vol. 9, p. 324.]].

"And did not fall short in it at all" means it did not diminish. His saying, may He be exalted: "And We caused a river to gush forth between them" means: We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens.

(And he had fruit.) Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "thamar" (ثَمَرٌ) with a fatha on the ثـ and the م, and likewise in His words "and his fruit was encompassed" (وَأُحِيطَ بثمره), which is the plural of thamara (ثَمَرَة). Al-Jawhari said: "Thamara is the singular of thamar and thamarat, and the plural of thamar is thimar (ثِمَار), like jabal and jibal." Al-Farra' said: "The plural of thimar is thamar, like kitab and kutub, and the plural of thumur (ثُمُر) is athmar (أَثْمَار), like a'naq and 'unuq." Thamar also means wealth that has been made to yield profit, and it may be pronounced with light or heavy emphasis. Abu 'Amr read "wa-kana lahu thumr" (وَكَانَ لَهُ ثُمْرٌ) with a damma on the ثـ and a sukun on the م, and he interpreted it as meaning kinds of wealth. The rest read it with a damma on both letters in both places. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Gold, silver and property." Something similar to this has already been explained in detail in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 49.]].

al-Nahhas reported: Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb narrated to us, saying: 'Imran ibn Bakkar informed me, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-'Ala' al-Zubaydi narrated to us, saying: Shu'ayb ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: [Harun informed us [[In manuscript j, and in ya: "narrated to us."]]], saying: Aban narrated to me, from Tha'lab, from al-A'mash, that al-Hajjaj said: "If I hear anyone reading 'wa-kana lahu thamar,' I will cut out his tongue." I said to al-A'mash: "Do you adopt this reading?" He said: "No, by the blessing of the eye [[This word has twelve dialectal forms: ni'm, 'ayn, ni'mah, na'am, na'im (with two fathas), ni'ma, na'ma, na'ima (with two dammas), ni'mah, na'am (with a kasra). All of them are put in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: I do that as a delight to your eye and as an honour.]]." So he read "thamar" and took it from the plural of thamara. al-Nahhas said: "The reckoning according to this view is that he formed the plural of thamara as thimar, and then formed the plural of thimar as thumur, which is good in Arabic. However, the first view is more likely, and God knows best, because His words 'Both gardens brought forth their produce' (كِلْتَا الْجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ أُكُلَهَا) indicate that he had fruit."

His words, exalted is He: "So he said to his companion while he was conversing with him" (فَقالَ لِصاحِبِهِ وَهُوَ يُحاوِرُهُ), meaning he was returning speech to him and answering him. Al-muhawara (المُحَاوَرَة) is answering, and al-tahawur (التَّحَاوُر) is mutual answering. It is said: "I spoke to him, but he did not return an answer to me, nor did he come back to me with a reply, nor a response, nor a reply at all," meaning he did not return an answer.

"I have more wealth than you and am mightier in followers" (أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنْكَ مَالًا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَراً). Al-nafar (النَّفَر) is a group, which is fewer than ten. Here it means followers, servants and children, as has been explained earlier.

"And did not fall short in it at all" means it did not diminish. His saying, may He be exalted: "And We caused a river to gush forth between them" means: We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens.

(And he had fruit.) Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "thamar" (ثَمَرٌ) with a fatha on the ثـ and the م, and likewise in His words "and his fruit was encompassed" (وَأُحِيطَ بثمره), which is the plural of thamara (ثَمَرَة). Al-Jawhari said: "Thamara is the singular of thamar and thamarat, and the plural of thamar is thimar (ثِمَار), like jabal and jibal." Al-Farra' said: "The plural of thimar is thamar, like kitab and kutub, and the plural of thumur (ثُمُر) is athmar (أَثْمَار), like a'naq and 'unuq." Thamar also means wealth that has been made to yield profit, and it may be pronounced with light or heavy emphasis. Abu 'Amr read "wa-kana lahu thumr" (وَكَانَ لَهُ ثُمْرٌ) with a damma on the ثـ and a sukun on the م, and he interpreted it as meaning kinds of wealth. The rest read it with a damma on both letters in both places. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Gold, silver and property." Something similar to this has already been explained in detail in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 49.]].

al-Nahhas reported: Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb narrated to us, saying: 'Imran ibn Bakkar informed me, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-'Ala' al-Zubaydi narrated to us, saying: Shu'ayb ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: [Harun informed us [[In manuscript j, and in ya: "narrated to us."]]], saying: Aban narrated to me, from Tha'lab, from al-A'mash, that al-Hajjaj said: "If I hear anyone reading 'wa-kana lahu thamar,' I will cut out his tongue." I said to al-A'mash: "Do you adopt this reading?" He said: "No, by the blessing of the eye [[This word has twelve dialectal forms: ni'm, 'ayn, ni'mah, na'am, na'im (with two fathas), ni'ma, na'ma, na'ima (with two dammas), ni'mah, na'am (with a kasra). All of them are put in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: I do that as a delight to your eye and as an honour.]]." So he read "thamar" and took it from the plural of thamara. al-Nahhas said: "The reckoning according to this view is that he formed the plural of thamara as thimar, and then formed the plural of thimar as thumur, which is good in Arabic. However, the first view is more likely, and God knows best, because His words 'Both gardens brought forth their produce' (كِلْتَا الْجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ أُكُلَهَا) indicate that he had fruit."

His words, exalted is He: "So he said to his companion while he was conversing with him" (فَقالَ لِصاحِبِهِ وَهُوَ يُحاوِرُهُ), meaning he was returning speech to him and answering him. It is said: "I spoke to him, but he did not return an answer to me, nor did he come back to me with a reply, nor a response, nor a reply at all," meaning he did not return an answer.

"I have more wealth than you and am mightier in followers" (أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنْكَ مَالًا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَراً). Al-nafar (النَّفَر) is a group, which is fewer than ten. Here it means followers, servants and children, as has been explained earlier.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And set forth for them the parable of two men﴾. This is a parable for one who takes pride in the world and disdains sitting with the believers, and it is connected to His saying, "And keep yourself patient" (18:28). Scholars differ about the names of these two men and about identifying them. Al-Kalbi said: They were revealed concerning two brothers from Makkah, of the clan of Makhzum. One of them was a believer, Abu Salamah Abdullah ibn Abd al-Asad ibn Hilal ibn Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, the former husband of Umm Salamah before the Prophet ﷺ. The other was an unbeliever, al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad. They are the two brothers mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: "One of them said, 'Indeed, I had a companion'" (37:51) [[See vol. 15, p. 81 onward.]]. Each of them inherited four thousand dinars. One of them spent his wealth in the way of Allah, and his brother asked him for something, and he said what he said... This was related by al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri. It was also said: It was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ and the people of Makkah. It was also said: It is a parable for all who believe in Allah and all who disbelieve. It was also said: It is a parable for Uyaynah ibn Hisn and his companions in relation to Salman and Suhayb and their companions. Allah likened them to two men from the Children of Israel, two brothers, one of whom was a believer, named Yahudha according to the view of Ibn Abbas. Muqatil said: his name was Tamlikha. The other was an unbeliever, named Qartush. They are the two whom Allah described in Surat al-Saffat. Likewise, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri' mentioned: the name of the good one of them was Tamlikha, and the other was Qartush, and they were partners, then they divided the wealth so that each of them had three thousand dinars. The believer bought slaves with one thousand and freed them; with the second thousand he bought garments and clothed the naked; with the third thousand he bought food and fed the hungry; he also built mosques and did good. As for the other, he married women of means with his money, bought beasts and cattle and had them breed, so their offspring multiplied greatly, and he traded with the remainder and profited until he surpassed the people of his time in wealth. The first one was overtaken by need, so he wanted to hire himself out to work in a garden that he would tend. He said: "If I go to my partner and companion and ask him to employ me in some of his gardens, I hope that will be better for me." So he came to him, but he could hardly reach him because of the harshness of the chamberlains. When he entered upon him, recognised him, and asked him for his need, he said to him: "Did I not divide the wealth with you equally? What have you done with your wealth?" He said: "I have bought with it from Allah, may He be exalted, what is better than it and more lasting." Then the rich one said: "Are you truly among those who believe? I do not think the Hour will come, and I do not see you except as a fool, and what is your reward from me for your folly except deprivation? Do you not see what I have done with my wealth, until it has come to what you see of abundance and good condition? That is because I earned and you were foolish. Get out of my sight!" Then the matter of this wealthy man was what Allah mentioned in the Qur'an: the destruction of his fruits and their complete loss by what He sent upon them from the sky, a reckoning (ḥusbān) [[See vol. 15, p. 84, part 2 onward.]]. Al-Tha'labi related this story in different wording, though the meaning is close. Ata said: They were partners, and they had eight thousand dinars. It was also said: They inherited it from their father, and they were brothers, and they divided it. One of them bought land for a thousand dinars. His companion said: "O Allah, so-and-so has bought land for a thousand dinars, and I have bought from You land in Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave it in charity. Then his companion built a house for a thousand dinars, and he said: "O Allah, so-and-so has built a house for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave [a thousand dinars] in charity. He then married a woman and spent a thousand dinars on her, and he said: "O Allah, so-and-so has married a woman for a thousand dinars, and I propose to You for a woman of the women of Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then he bought servants and goods for a thousand dinars, and he said: "I buy from You servants and goods from Paradise for a thousand dinars," and he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then a severe need befell him, and he said: "Perhaps my companion will bestow his kindness upon me." He came to him and said: "What has become of your wealth?" He told him his story. He said: "Are you truly one of those who believe this report? By Allah, I will not give you anything." Then he said to him: "You worship the God of the heavens, and I worship only an idol." His companion said: "By Allah, I will admonish him." So he admonished him, reminded him, and warned him. He said: "Come, let us go fishing; whoever catches more is in the right." He said to him: "O my brother, indeed this world is too insignificant in the sight of Allah for Him to make it a reward for the good or a punishment for the unbeliever." He said: He compelled him to go out with him, and Allah tested them both. The unbeliever began casting his net and calling upon the name of his idol, and fish came up in abundance. The believer began casting his net and calling upon the name of Allah, and nothing came up for him in it. Then he said to him: "How do you see it? I have more than you in this world in wealth, position and followers. Likewise, I shall be better than you in the Hereafter, if what you say is true according to your claim." He said: The angel appointed over them both cried out, so Allah, may He be exalted, commanded Gabriel to take him and go with him to the Gardens, and show him the dwellings of the believer there. When he saw what Allah had prepared for him, he said: "By Your might, what he obtained of the world will not harm him, since his final destination is this." And He showed him the dwellings of the unbeliever in Hell, and he said: "By Your might, what he obtained of the world will not benefit him, since his final destination is this." Then Allah, may He be exalted, took the believer to Himself and destroyed the unbeliever with a punishment from Him. When the believer settled in Paradise and saw what Allah had prepared for him, he and his companions began to ask one another, and he said: "Indeed, I had a companion" (37:51), saying: "Are you truly among those who believe?" (37:52), and so on. A caller called out: "O people of Paradise! Would you like to look down?" So he looked down into Hell and saw him in the midst of the blazing fire, and then this was revealed: "And set forth for them a parable" (18:32). Allah explained the state of the two brothers in this world in this surah, and explained their state in the Hereafter in Surat al-Saffat, in His saying: "Indeed, I had a companion. He used to say, 'Are you truly among those who believe?'" (37:51–52), up to His saying: "For the like of this let the workers work" (37:61). Ibn Atiyyah said: Ibrahim ibn al-Qasim al-Katib mentioned in his book on the wonders of the lands that the lake of Tinnis was these two gardens, and that they belonged to two brothers. One of them sold his share to the other, and he spent it in obedience to Allah until the other changed [his condition]. Conversation took place between them, and Allah drowned them in a single night, and it was these that this verse refers to. It has also been said that this is a parable that Allah set forth for this community, and it is not a report about a past state, so that they would renounce the world and desire the Hereafter, and it was intended as a warning and admonition. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. But the context of the verse indicates otherwise, and Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had surrounded the two with date palms﴾, that is, We enclosed them on their sides with date palms. The ḥifāf is the side, and its plural is aḥiffah. It is said: "The people encircled so-and-so (ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān), yaḥuffūna ḥaffan," meaning they went around him. From this is His saying: "encircling the Throne" (39:75) [[See vol. 15, p. 84, part 2 onward.]]. "And We placed between them a field of crops" means that We placed the date palms around the vines, and the crops in the middle of the vines.

"Both the gardens" means each of the two gardens, "yielded its produce" in full, and therefore He did not say "yielded their produce." Scholars differed over whether the word kilā and kiltā is singular or dual. The Basrans said: It is singular, because kilā and kiltā, when used to emphasise the dual, correspond to kull used with the plural, and it is a singular noun, not dual. When it is followed by an apparent noun, it has one form in the nominative, accusative and genitive. You say: "I saw kilā al-rajulayn (both the two men), and kilā al-rajulayn came to me, and I passed by kilā al-rajulayn." When it is attached to a pronoun, the alif becomes yā' in the genitive and accusative positions. You say: "I saw kilayhimā, and I passed by kilayhimā," just as you say ʿalayhimā. Al-Farra' said: It is dual, and it is derived from kull, with the lam lightened and the alif added to form the dual. Likewise kiltā is for the feminine, and neither of them is used except in construction (as the first term of an idāfa), and one does not speak of a single one of them. If one did speak of a single one, one would say: kil, kilt, kilān, kiltān. He argued with the poet's verse:

"In the one of her two feet are single phalanges (sulāmā), both joined to an extra one."

He meant "in one of her two feet," and so used the singular. This view is weak according to the Basrans, because if it were dual, its alif would have to become yā' in the accusative and genitive with an apparent noun. Also, the meaning of kilā differs from the meaning of kull, because kilā is for comprehensiveness of two, whereas kull refers to a specific thing. As for this poet, he omitted the alif out of poetic necessity and assumed it was extra, and what is a necessity cannot be made evidence. Thus it is established that it is a singular noun like miʿan, except that it was put in place to indicate the dual, just as their saying "naḥnu" (we) is a singular noun that indicates two or more. The verse of Jarir proves this:

"Both days of Umamah are a day of separation,
and even if we do not visit them except briefly."

Here he reported about "kilā" with a single "day," just as he used a singular predicate with His saying "yielded" (ātat), and had it been dual he would have said ātatā, and yawman [would be yawmayn]. Scholars also differed about the alif of "kiltā." Sibawayh said: the alif of "wa-kiltā" is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the lam of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original was kilwā. The wāw was changed into tā' because the tā' carries the sign of the feminine, and the alif in "kiltā" may become yā' with a pronoun, so it would leave the sign of the feminine; therefore, the replacement of the wāw by tā' became an emphasis for the feminine. Abu Umar al-Jarmi said: the tā' is an added letter, and the alif is the lam of the verb, and its pattern in his view is fiʿtal. If the matter were as he claimed, they would say in the relative form kiltawī, but since they said kilawī and dropped the tā', it shows that they treated it as the tā' in ukht (sister), where if you form the relative you say ukhawī. Al-Jawhari mentioned this. Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: The grammarians permitted, outside the Qur'an, interpretation according to meaning, and that you say: "Kiltā al-jannatayn ātatā ukulahumā," because the preferred meaning is "kiltāhumā ātatā" [in another copy: "al-jannatān kiltāhumā"]. Al-Farra' permitted: "Kiltā al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu," and he said: because the meaning is "kull al-jannatayn" (each of the two gardens). He said: In the reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) it is "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu." The meaning according to al-Farra' is: everything of the two gardens yielded its produce.

Al-Ukul (with a dammah on the hamzah) is the fruit of the date palm and of trees, and everything that is eaten is ukul. From this is His saying: "its food is eternal" (13:35), and it has been mentioned before [[See vol. 9, p. 324.]].

"And did not fall short in it at all" means it did not diminish. His saying, may He be exalted: "And We caused a river to gush forth between them" means: We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens.

(And he had fruit.) Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 35–36:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he entered his garden﴾. It was said: he took his believing brother by the hand, walking around with him in it and showing him it.

﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ means: by his disbelief. It is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). Whoever causes himself to enter the Fire by his disbelief is one who wrongs himself.

﴿He said: "I do not think that this will ever perish."﴾ He denied the perishing of the abode.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will be established.﴾ That is, I do not reckon that the Resurrection will occur.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord...﴾ That is, even if there is a resurrection, just as He has given me these blessings in this world, He will give me something better than them, because of my honour before Him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿I will surely find better than them as a return.﴾ He only said that when his brother invited him to belief in the gathering and the resurrection.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is "minhuma" (from both of them). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is "minha" (from it), in the singular. The dual is preferable, because the pronoun is closer to the two gardens.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 37–38:

His words, exalted is He: (His companion said to him). He was Yahudha or Tamlikha, according to the disagreement about his name.

(Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you as a man?) He admonished him and made clear to him that what he admitted of these matters, which no one denies, is more wondrous than the return (to life). And "fashioned you as a man" means He made you of balanced stature and form, sound in your limbs, male.

(But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord.) Thus it was recited by Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Abu al-'Aliyah. It is also reported from al-Kisa'i as "Lakinna Huwa Allah," meaning "but the matter is that He is Allah, my Lord," so its subject (the pronoun of the alif-less form) is elided within it. The rest recited "Lakinna" with the alif affirmed. Al-Kisa'i said: "There is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in it. Its estimated form is: 'But Allah, He is my Lord, I.' The hamza of 'ana' (I) was dropped for lightness because of frequent use, one of the two nuns was assimilated into the other, and the alif of 'ana' was dropped in continuous recitation (wasl) and affirmed in pause (waqf)." Al-Nahhas said: "The view of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is 'lakinna ana,' so the vowel of the hamza was placed on the nun of 'lakinna,' the hamza was dropped, and the nun was assimilated into the nun. So the pause on it is 'lakinna,' and its alif is the alif of 'ana,' to show the vowel." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The original is 'lakinna ana,' the alif was dropped, two nuns met, and so it came with the shaddah (doubling) for that reason." Al-Kisa'i recited to us:

"Lahinnaka min 'Absiyyatin la-wasimatun
'ala hanawatin kadhibun man yaquluha"

He meant: "Lillahi innaka" (By Allah, indeed you), so he dropped one of the two lams from "lillah" and dropped the alif from "innaka." Another said, and brought it in its original form:

"Wa-tarminini bi-l-tarfi ay anta mudhnibu
wa-taqlinani lakinna iyyaka la aqli"

That is, "lakinna ana" (but I). Abu Hatim said: "They related from 'Asim, 'Lakinna huwa Allah rabbi,' and he claimed that this is a grammatical error (lahn), meaning the affirmation of the alif in continuous recitation." Al-Zajjaj said: "Affirming the alif in 'Lakinna huwa Allah rabbi' in continuous recitation is good, because the alif of 'ana' was dropped, so they brought it back as a substitute." He said: "In the recitation of Ubayy it is 'Lakinna ana huwa Allah rabbi.'" Ibn 'Amir and al-Masili [he is Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id; this nisba is to Masila (on the pattern of Safina), a town in the Algerian region], from Nafi' and Ruways from Ya'qub, recited "Lakinna" with the alif affirmed in both pause and continuous recitation. The poet said:

"Ana sayfu al-'ashirati fa-'rifuni
Humaydan qad tadharraytu al-sanama"

And al-A'sha said:

"Fa-kayfa ana wa-intihali al-qawafi
ba'da al-mashibi kafa dhaka 'aran"

There is no disagreement about affirming it in pause.

(He is Allah, my Lord.) "He" is the pronoun of the matter, the affair and the situation, like His words: "Then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare" [see vol. 11, p. 340], and His words: "Say: He is Allah, the One" [see vol. 20, p. 244].

(And I will not associate anyone with my Lord.) Its implication indicates that the other brother was a polytheist, worshipping other than Allah, exalted is He. It may also mean: I do not see wealth and poverty except from Him, and I know that if He wished to strip the owner of worldly wealth of his wealth, He would be able to do so, and He is the One who gave me poverty. It may also mean that your denial of the Resurrection leads to the belief that Allah, exalted is He, is unable to do it, and this is an attribution of incapacity (ta'jiz) to the Lord, glorified and exalted is He. Whoever attributes incapacity to Him, glorified and exalted is He, has likened Him to His creation, and that is association (shirk).
