(But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord.) Thus it was recited by Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Abu al-'Aliyah. It is also reported from al-Kisa'i as "Lakinna Huwa Allah," meaning "but the matter is that He is Allah, my Lord," so its subject (the pronoun of the alif-less form) is elided within it. The rest recited "Lakinna" with the alif affirmed. Al-Kisa'i said: "There is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in it. Its estimated form is: 'But Allah, He is my Lord, I.' The hamza of 'ana' (I) was dropped for lightness because of frequent use, one of the two nuns was assimilated into the other, and the alif of 'ana' was dropped in continuous recitation (wasl) and affirmed in pause (waqf)." Al-Nahhas said: "The view of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is 'lakinna ana,' so the vowel of the hamza was placed on the nun of 'lakinna,' the hamza was dropped, and the nun was assimilated into the nun. So the pause on it is 'lakinna,' and its alif is the alif of 'ana,' to show the vowel." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The original is 'lakinna ana,' the alif was dropped, two nuns met, and so it came with the shaddah (doubling) for that reason." Al-Kisa'i recited to us:

"Lahinnaka min 'Absiyyatin la-wasimatun
'ala hanawatin kadhibun man yaquluha"

He meant: "Lillahi innaka" (By Allah, indeed you), so he dropped one of the two lams from "lillah" and dropped the alif from "innaka." Another said, and brought it in its original form:

"Wa-tarminini bi-l-tarfi ay anta mudhnibu
wa-taqlinani lakinna iyyaka la aqli"

That is, "lakinna ana" (but I). Abu Hatim said: "They related from 'Asim, 'Lakinna huwa Allah rabbi,' and he claimed that this is a grammatical error (lahn), meaning the affirmation of the alif in continuous recitation." Al-Zajjaj said: "Affirming the alif in 'Lakinna huwa Allah rabbi' in continuous recitation is good, because the alif of 'ana' was dropped, so they brought it back as a substitute." He said: "In the recitation of Ubayy it is 'Lakinna ana huwa Allah rabbi.'" Ibn 'Amir and al-Masili [he is Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id; this nisba is to Masila (on the pattern of Safina), a town in the Algerian region], from Nafi' and Ruways from Ya'qub, recited "Lakinna" with the alif affirmed in both pause and continuous recitation. The poet said:

"Ana sayfu al-'ashirati fa-'rifuni
Humaydan qad tadharraytu al-sanama"

And al-A'sha said:

"Fa-kayfa ana wa-intihali al-qawafi
ba'da al-mashibi kafa dhaka 'aran"

There is no disagreement about affirming it in pause.

(He is Allah, my Lord.) "He" is the pronoun of the matter, the affair and the situation, like His words: "Then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare" [see vol. 11, p. 340], and His words: "Say: He is Allah, the One" [see vol. 20, p. 244].

(And I will not associate anyone with my Lord.) Its implication indicates that the other brother was a polytheist, worshipping other than Allah, exalted is He. It may also mean: I do not see wealth and poverty except from Him, and I know that if He wished to strip the owner of worldly wealth of his wealth, He would be able to do so, and He is the One who gave me poverty. It may also mean that your denial of the Resurrection leads to the belief that Allah, exalted is He, is unable to do it, and this is an attribution of incapacity (ta'jiz) to the Lord, glorified and exalted is He. Whoever attributes incapacity to Him, glorified and exalted is He, has likened Him to His creation, and that is association (shirk).

**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 18, verses 39–41:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except in Allah"?﴾ In this there are two issues (masalah).

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What Allah wills; there is no power except in Allah"?﴾ "Or, that is, in the heart." This is a rebuke and an admonition from the believer to the disbeliever, and a refutation of him, when he said, ﴿I do not think this will ever perish.﴾ The word *ma* (ما) in *ma sha'a Allah* is in the nominative position (fi mawdi' raf'), its implied sense being: "This garden is what Allah wills." Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: "The matter is what Allah wills," or "It is what Allah wills," meaning the matter is the will of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said that the response (jawab) is implied, meaning: "What Allah wills comes to pass, and what He does not will does not come to pass." ﴿There is no power except in Allah﴾ means: whatever wealth has gathered for you is by the power and might of Allah, exalted is He, not by your power and might; and if He willed, He would strip the blessing from it, and it would not have gathered.

**The second issue:** Ashhab said: Malik said, "It is fitting for everyone who enters his home to say this." Ibn Wahb said: Hafs ibn Maysarah told me, "I saw written on the door of Wahb ibn Munabbih: *ma sha'a Allah, la quwwata illa billah* (What Allah wills; there is no power except in Allah)."

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to Abu Hurayrah: "Shall I not direct you to a word from the treasures of Paradise—or he said, a treasure from the treasures of Paradise?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah. When the servant says it, Allah, mighty and majestic, says: 'My servant has submitted and surrendered.'" Muslim transmitted it in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa. In it: He said, "O Abu Musa, or O Abdullah ibn Qays, shall I not direct you to a word from a treasure of Paradise—in one narration, 'from a treasure of the treasures of Paradise'?" I said: "What is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah."

And from him (Abu Musa), he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Shall I not direct you to a word from the treasures of Paradise, or he said, a treasure from the treasures of Paradise?" I said: "Yes." He said: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah, the Most High, the Mighty."

It is also related that whoever enters his home or leaves it and says: *Bismillah, ma sha'a Allah, la quwwata illa billah* (In the name of Allah, what Allah wills; there is no power except in Allah), the devils will be driven away from before him, and Allah, exalted is He, will send down blessings upon him.

Aisha said: When a man leaves his house and says *Bismillah*, the angel says: "You are guided." When he says *ma sha'a Allah*, the angel says: "You are sufficed." When he says *la quwwata illa billah*, the angel says: "You are protected." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says—meaning when he leaves his house—*Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah* (In the name of Allah, I have put my trust in Allah; there is no might and no power except in Allah)—it is said to him: 'You are sufficed and protected,' and Satan withdraws from him." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except through this route. Abu Dawud also transmitted it and added in it: he said to him: "You are guided, sufficed and protected." Ibn Majah transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a man leaves the door of his house or the door of his dwelling, two angels appointed to him are with him. When he says *Bismillah*, they say: 'You are guided.' When he says *la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah*, they say: 'You are protected.' When he says *tawakkaltu 'ala Allah*, they say: 'You are sufficed.' Then his two companions meet him and say: 'What do you want of a man who has been guided, protected and sufficed?'"

Al-Hakim Abu Abdullah said in *Ulum al-Hadith*: Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah was asked about the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Paradise and Hell disputed. Hell said: 'The arrogant will enter me.' Paradise said: 'This—meaning Paradise—the weak will enter me.'" He was asked: "Who is the weak one?" He said: "The one who disowns from himself might and power"—meaning twenty or fifty times a day.

Anas ibn Malik said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees something and is pleased with it, then says *ma sha'a Allah, la quwwata illa billah*, the evil eye will not harm him."

Some people have said: No one says *ma sha'a Allah* and then something befalls him, except that he is content with it.

It is also related that whoever says four things is safe from four things: whoever says *hadhihi* (this) is safe from the evil eye; whoever says *hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil* (Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs) is safe from the plotting of Satan; whoever says *wa ufawwidu amri ila Allah* (and I entrust my affair to Allah) is safe from the schemes of people; and whoever says *la ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu mina al-zalimin* (there is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers) is safe from distress.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. *In* (إن) is the conditional particle; *tarani* (ترني) is jussive by it; the response is ﴿then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾. *Ana* (أنا) is a separating pronoun (fasilah) with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis); it may also be in the accusative position as an emphasis for the *nun* and the *ya'* (of the first person object).

Isa ibn Umar recited *in tarani ana aqallu minka* with the nominative, making *ana* the subject (mubtada') and *aqallu* its predicate; the clause is in the position of the second object, and the first object is the *nun* and the *ya'*, except that the *ya'* was omitted because the kasrah indicates it. Retaining it is good and eloquent, and it is the original form, since it is the noun in reality. *Fa'asa* (فعسى) here has the meaning of *la'alla* (perhaps), i.e., *fa la'alla rabbi* (then perhaps my Lord).

﴿to give me something better than your garden﴾: that is, in the Hereafter. It was also said: in this world.

﴿and send upon it﴾: that is, upon your garden.

﴿a thunderbolt (husban)﴾: that is, missiles from the sky. Its singular is *husbanah*, as said by al-Akhfash, al-Qutabi and Abu Ubaydah. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-husbanah* is a cloud; *al-husbanah* is a cushion; *al-husbanah* is a thunderbolt. Al-Jawhari said: *al-husban* (with a damma) is punishment. Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi said: "A husban struck the earth," meaning a locust swarm. *Al-husban* also means reckoning, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by reckoning﴾, and the word *husban* has been interpreted here in this sense. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-husban* is from *al-hisab* (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it the punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned; it is thus from the omission of the annexed noun (hadhf al-mudaf). *Al-husban* also means short arrows shot in one direction, which was from the shooting of the Akasirah (Persian kings). And "missiles from the sky" is a punishment.

﴿so it becomes a bare, slippery ground (sa'idan zalaqa)﴾: meaning a white land in which no plant grows and upon which no foot stands firm. It is the most barren land, after it had been a garden, the most fruitful land. *Zalaqan* is an emphasis on the description of *sa'id*, meaning: and feet will slip upon it because of its smoothness. It is said: *makan zalaq* (with fatha on the lam, in the sense of *dahd*), meaning a slippery place. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying: *zalaqat rijluhu* (his foot slipped), *yazlaqu zalaqan*, and *azlaqaha* (he made it slip) was used by others. *Al-zalaq* also means the rump of an animal. Ru'bah said:

*Ka'annaha haqba'u balqa'u al-zalaq*
*(As if she were a white-spotted mare, white in the rump)*

*Al-mazlaqah* and *al-muzlaqah* mean a place upon which no foot remains firm, and likewise *al-zallaqah*. *Al-zalq* means shaving: *zalaqa ra'sahu yazlaquhu zalqan* (he shaved his head), said al-Jawhari; and *al-zaliq* is the shaved one, like *al-naqd* and *al-naqad*. The intended meaning is not that it becomes a slide, but that no vegetation remains in it, like a head that has been shaved, on which no hair remains. Al-Qushayri said this.

﴿or its water sinks away (ghawran)﴾: meaning sunk and gone away, so it becomes the land most devoid of water, after having been the land most abundant in water. *Al-ghawr* is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, as one says: *rajulun sawmun* (a man who fasts), *fitrun* (who breaks the fast), *adlun* (just), *ridan*, *fadlun*, *zawrun* (false), and *nisa'un nawhun* (women who wail). It is used for masculine, feminine, dual and plural alike. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*Tazallu jiyaduhu nawhan 'alayhi ... muqallidatan a'innatuha sufunan*
*(His horses remain wailing over him, their reins hung with [their] standing forms)*

Another said:

*Hariqi min dumu'ihima sijaman ... Dubā'u wa jawibi nawhan qiyaman*
*(Pour out from their tears a flood, O Dubā'; and answer with standing lamentation)*

That is, wailing women. It was also said: *aw yusbihama'uha dha ghawr* (or its water becomes sunk), with the omission of the annexed noun. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas. Al-Kisa'i said: *ma'un ghawr* (water that has sunk). It is said: *ghara al-ma'u yaghuru ghawran wa ghu'uran*, meaning it went down into the earth; the hamzah is permissible because of the damma of the waw. *Ghārat 'aynuhu taghuru ghawran wa ghu'uran* means it entered into the head. *Ghārat taghār* is a dialectal form of it. And he said:

*Aghārat 'aynuhu am lam taghārā*
*(Did his eye sink, or did it not sink?)*

*Ghārati al-shamsu taghūru ghiyaran*, meaning it set. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*Hal al-dahru illa laylatan wa nahāruhā ... wa illa tulū'u al-shamsi thumma ghiyāruhā*
*(Is time anything but a night and its day, and the rising of the sun, then its setting?)*

﴿then you will not be able to seek it (talaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to restore the sunken water, nor will you be able to bring it back by any stratagem. It was also said: you will not be able to seek anything else in its place. And with this word the admonition and warning of his brother ended.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except in Allah"?﴾ In this there are two issues (masalah).

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What Allah wills; there is no power except in Allah"?﴾ "Or, that is, in the heart." This is a rebuke and an admonition from the believer to the disbeliever, and a refutation of him, when he said, ﴿I do not think this will ever perish.﴾ The word *ma* (ما) in *ma sha'a Allah* is in the nominative position (fi mawdi' raf'), its implied sense being: "This garden is what Allah wills." Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: "The matter is what Allah wills," or "It is what Allah wills," meaning the matter is the will of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said that the response (jawab) is implied, meaning: "What Allah wills comes to pass, and what He does not will does not come to pass." ﴿There is no power except in Allah﴾ means: whatever wealth has gathered for you is by the power and might of Allah, exalted is He, not by your power and might; and if He willed, He would strip the blessing from it, and it would not have gathered.

**The second issue:** Ashhab said: Malik said, "It is fitting for everyone who enters his home to say this." Ibn Wahb said: Hafs ibn Maysarah told me, "I saw written on the door of Wahb ibn Munabbih: *ma sha'a Allah, la quwwata illa billah* (What Allah wills; there is no power except in Allah)."

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to Abu Hurayrah: "Shall I not direct you to a word from the treasures of Paradise—or he said, a treasure from the treasures of Paradise?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah. When the servant says it, Allah, mighty and majestic, says: 'My servant has submitted and surrendered.'" Muslim transmitted it in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa. In it: He said, "O Abu Musa, or O Abdullah ibn Qays, shall I not direct you to a word from a treasure of Paradise—in one narration, 'from a treasure of the treasures of Paradise'?" I said: "What is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah."

And from him (Abu Musa), he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Shall I not direct you to a word from the treasures of Paradise, or he said, a treasure from the treasures of Paradise?" I said: "Yes." He said: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah, the Most High, the Mighty."

It is also related that whoever enters his home or leaves it and says: *Bismillah, ma sha'a Allah, la quwwata illa billah* (In the name of Allah, what Allah wills; there is no power except in Allah), the devils will be driven away from before him, and Allah, exalted is He, will send down blessings upon him.

Aisha said: When a man leaves his house and says *Bismillah*, the angel says: "You are guided." When he says *ma sha'a Allah*, the angel says: "You are sufficed." When he says *la quwwata illa billah*, the angel says: "You are protected." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says—meaning when he leaves his house—*Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah* (In the name of Allah, I have put my trust in Allah; there is no might and no power except in Allah)—it is said to him: 'You are sufficed and protected,' and Satan withdraws from him." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except through this route. Abu Dawud also transmitted it and added in it: he said to him: "You are guided, sufficed and protected." Ibn Majah transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a man leaves the door of his house or the door of his dwelling, two angels appointed to him are with him. When he says *Bismillah*, they say: 'You are guided.' When he says *la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah*, they say: 'You are protected.' When he says *tawakkaltu 'ala Allah*, they say: 'You are sufficed.' Then his two companions meet him and say: 'What do you want of a man who has been guided, protected and sufficed?'"

Al-Hakim Abu Abdullah said in *Ulum al-Hadith*: Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah was asked about the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Paradise and Hell disputed. Hell said: 'The arrogant will enter me.' Paradise said: 'This—meaning Paradise—the weak will enter me.'" He was asked: "Who is the weak one?" He said: "The one who disowns from himself might and power"—meaning twenty or fifty times a day.

Anas ibn Malik said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees something and is pleased with it, then says *ma sha'a Allah, la quwwata illa billah*, the evil eye will not harm him."

Some people have said: No one says *ma sha'a Allah* and then something befalls him, except that he is content with it.

It is also related that whoever says four things is safe from four things: whoever says *hadhihi* (this) is safe from the evil eye; whoever says *hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil* (Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs) is safe from the plotting of Satan; whoever says *wa ufawwidu amri ila Allah* (and I entrust my affair to Allah) is safe from the schemes of people; and whoever says *la ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu mina al-zalimin* (there is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers) is safe from distress.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. *In* (إن) is the conditional particle; *tarani* (ترني) is jussive by it; the response is ﴿then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾. *Ana* (أنا) is a separating pronoun (fasilah) with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis); it may also be in the accusative position as an emphasis for the *nun* and the *ya'* (of the first person object).

Isa ibn Umar recited *in tarani ana aqallu minka* with the nominative, making *ana* the subject (mubtada') and *aqallu* its predicate; the clause is in the position of the second object, and the first object is the *nun* and the *ya'*, except that the *ya'* was omitted because the kasrah indicates it. Retaining it is good and eloquent, and it is the original form, since it is the noun in reality. *Fa'asa* (فعسى) here has the meaning of *la'alla* (perhaps), i.e., *fa la'alla rabbi* (then perhaps my Lord).

﴿to give me something better than your garden﴾: that is, in the Hereafter. It was also said: in this world.

﴿and send upon it﴾: that is, upon your garden.

﴿a thunderbolt (husban)﴾: that is, missiles from the sky. Its singular is *husbanah*, as said by al-Akhfash, al-Qutabi and Abu Ubaydah. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-husbanah* is a cloud; *al-husbanah* is a cushion; *al-husbanah* is a thunderbolt. Al-Jawhari said: *al-husban* (with a damma) is punishment. Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi said: "A husban struck the earth," meaning a locust swarm. *Al-husban* also means reckoning, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by reckoning﴾, and the word *husban* has been interpreted here in this sense. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-husban* is from *al-hisab* (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it the punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned; it is thus from the omission of the annexed noun (hadhf al-mudaf). *Al-husban* also means short arrows shot in one direction, which was from the shooting of the Akasirah (Persian kings). And "missiles from the sky" is a punishment.

﴿so it becomes a bare, slippery ground (sa'idan zalaqa)﴾: meaning a white land in which no plant grows and upon which no foot stands firm. It is the most barren land, after it had been a garden, the most fruitful land. *Zalaqan* is an emphasis on the description of *sa'id*, meaning: and feet will slip upon it because of its smoothness. It is said: *makan zalaq* (with fatha on the lam, in the sense of *dahd*), meaning a slippery place. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying: *zalaqat rijluhu* (his foot slipped), *yazlaqu zalaqan*, and *azlaqaha* (he made it slip) was used by others. *Al-zalaq* also means the rump of an animal. Ru'bah said:

*Ka'annaha haqba'u balqa'u al-zalaq*
*(As if she were a white-spotted mare, white in the rump)*

*Al-mazlaqah* and *al-muzlaqah* mean a place upon which no foot remains firm, and likewise *al-zallaqah*. *Al-zalq* means shaving: *zalaqa ra'sahu yazlaquhu zalqan* (he shaved his head), said al-Jawhari; and *al-zaliq* is the shaved one, like *al-naqd* and *al-naqad*. The intended meaning is not that it becomes a slide, but that no vegetation remains in it, like a head that has been shaved, on which no hair remains. Al-Qushayri said this.

﴿or its water sinks away (ghawran)﴾: meaning sunk and gone away, so it becomes the land most devoid of water, after having been the land most abundant in water. *Al-ghawr* is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, as one says: *rajulun sawmun* (a man who fasts), *fitrun* (who breaks the fast), *adlun* (just), *ridan*, *fadlun*, *zawrun* (false), and *nisa'un nawhun* (women who wail). It is used for masculine, feminine, dual and plural alike. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*Tazallu jiyaduhu nawhan 'alayhi ... muqallidatan a'innatuha sufunan*
*(His horses remain wailing over him, their reins hung with [their] standing forms)*

Another said:

*Hariqi min dumu'ihima sijaman ... Dubā'u wa jawibi nawhan qiyaman*
*(Pour out from their tears a flood, O Dubā'; and answer with standing lamentation)*

That is, wailing women. It was also said: *aw yusbihama'uha dha ghawr* (or its water becomes sunk), with the omission of the annexed noun. This was mentioned by al-Nahhas. Al-Kisa'i said: *ma'un ghawr* (water that has sunk). It is said: *ghara al-ma'u yaghuru ghawran wa ghu'uran*, meaning it went down into the earth; the hamzah is permissible because of the damma of the waw. *Ghārat 'aynuhu taghuru ghawran wa ghu'uran* means it entered into the head. *Ghārat taghār* is a dialectal form of it. And he said:

*Aghārat 'aynuhu am lam taghārā*
*(Did his eye sink, or did it not sink?)*

*Ghārati al-shamsu taghūru ghiyaran*, meaning it set. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*Hal al-dahru illa laylatan wa nahāruhā ... wa illa tulū'u al-shamsi thumma ghiyāruhā*
*(Is time anything but a night and its day, and the rising of the sun, then its setting?)*

﴿then you will not be able to seek it (talaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to restore the sunken water, nor will you be able to bring it back by any stratagem. It was also said: you will not be able to seek anything else in its place. And with this word the admonition and warning of his brother ended.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 42:

Allah's words: ﴿وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِ﴾ The subject of the passive verb (ism ma lam yusamma fa'iluh, the unnamed agent) is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun (al-masdar), meaning the destruction. It is also permissible that the word in the genitive (al-makhfud, here "bi-thamarihi," "with its fruit") is in the place of the nominative. The meaning of ﴿وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِ﴾ is: his entire wealth was destroyed. This was the first way in which Allah fulfilled the warning of his brother.

﴿فَأَصْبَحَ يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ﴾ That is, the disbelieving man began to strike one of his hands against the other out of regret, because this is what the regretful person does. It has also been said: he turns over his property, and sees in it no return for what he spent. This is because "hand" may be used to refer to ownership, as in the expression "fi yadihi mal" (he has wealth in his hand), meaning he possesses wealth. The words ﴿فَأَصْبَحَ﴾ indicate that this destruction took place at night, like His saying: ﴿فَطَافَ عَلَيْهَا طَائِفٌ مِنْ رَبِّكَ وَهُمْ نَائِمُونَ. فَأَصْبَحَتْ كَالصَّرِيمِ﴾ [see vol. 18, p. 238]. It is said: "anfaqtu fi hadhihi al-dar kadha wa anfaqtu 'alayha" (I spent such-and-such on this house, and I spent on it).

﴿وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَى عُرُوشِهَا﴾ That is, empty, with some of it having fallen upon the rest. It is derived from "khawat al-nujum takhwa khayyan," meaning the stars became barren, which is when they set and did not bring rain in their season; "akhwat" is similar to it. "Khawat al-dar khawa'an" means it became desolate, and likewise when it collapsed. From this is His saying: ﴿فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خَاوِيَةً بِمَا ظَلَمُوا﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 216 onward]. It is also said: "fallen," as one says "fa-hiya khawiya 'ala 'urushiha," meaning fallen upon its roofs. Thus he combined in it the destruction of the fruit and the root, and this is among the greatest of calamities, as a recompense for his transgression.

﴿وَيَقُولُ يَا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّي أَحَداً﴾ That is, "Would that I had recognized the blessings of Allah upon me, and recognized that they were by the power of Allah, and had not disbelieved in Him." This is regret on his part at a time when regret no longer benefits him.

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he had no company to support him against Allah﴾. "Fi'ah" (company) is the subject of "takun" (was), and "lahu" (for him) is the predicate. "Yansuruna-hu" (they support him) is in the position of a qualifier, meaning a supporting company. It is also permissible for "yansuruna-hu" to be the predicate. The first reading is preferred by Sibawayh, since "lahu" has come before it. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) disagrees with him and argues from the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "And there is none comparable to Him" [see vol. 20, p. 344 and following]. Sibawayh also permitted the latter. "Yansuruna-hu" is in accordance with the meaning of "fi'ah," because its meaning is peoples (aqwam). Had it been according to the wording, it would have said: "And he had no company that supports him," meaning a group and an assembly to which he could take refuge.

"Wa ma kana muntasiran" means: unable to defend himself (mumtani'an), said by Qatadah. It was also said: one who would recover what was lost from him. The derivation of "fi'ah" has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 24]. The "ha'" (in fi'ah) is a substitute for the "ya'" that was dropped from its middle; its original form is like "fi'alah" (fi'ah), because it derives from "fa'a" (to return). Its plural is "fi'un" and "fi'at," like "shiyat," "lidat," and "mi'at." The meaning: he had no clan to protect him from the punishment of Allah, and what he had boasted of, namely the servants and children, went astray from him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the True﴾. Scholars differed regarding the governing element (al-'amil) of His saying "there" (hunalika), which is an adverb of place (zarf). It was said: the governing element of it is "and he had no company (fi'ah) to aid him," and it was not there (la kana hunalika), meaning: he was not helped and did not help himself there, that is, due to the punishment that had befallen him. It was also said: the sentence is complete at His saying "victorious (muntasiran)." The governing element of "there" is "guardianship" (al-walayah). Its construction, with inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), is: guardianship belongs to Allah, the True, there, that is, on the Day of Resurrection.

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "al-haqqu" (the True) with a raised vowel (raf'), as an adjective (na't) of "guardianship." The people of Medina and Hamzah read "al-haqqi" with a lowered vowel (khafd), as an adjective of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, and the construction is: to Allah, the Possessor of truth (dhi al-haqq). Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "al-haqqa" with a fathah, as an infinitive (masdar) and an emphasis (tawkid), as you say: "this is yours, truly (haqqan)."

Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "al-wilayah" with a kasrah on the waw, while the rest read it with a fathah. Both have the same meaning, like "al-radla'ah" and "al-rida'ah." It was also said: "al-walayah" with a fathah means from "al-muwalah" (allegiance/alliance), as in His saying: "Allah is the Guardian (wali) of those who believe" and His saying: "That is because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe." With a kasrah it means sovereignty, power and command, as in His saying: "And the command on that Day belongs to Allah," meaning that to Him belong the dominion and the judgment on that Day, that is, His command is not referred to anyone else. Dominion belongs to Allah at all times, but claims and illusions will vanish on the Day of Resurrection. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is with a fathah on the waw for the Creator, and with a kasrah for the created.

﴿He is best in reward﴾: that is, Allah is best in reward, in this world and the Hereafter, for whoever believes in Him, and there is no other from whom one may hope for reward. Rather, He intends this according to the assumption of the ignorant, that is, He is the best of those from whom hope is placed.

﴿And best in outcome﴾: 'Asim, al-A'mash, Hamzah and Yahya read "'uqban" with a sukun on the qaf, while the rest read it with a dammah. Both have the same meaning, that is, He is the best outcome for whoever hopes in Him and believes in Him. It is said: this is the outcome (aqibah) of so-and-so's affair, and its 'uqba and 'uqb, meaning its end.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And set forth to them the parable of the life of this world﴾. That is, describe to these arrogant people, who asked you to drive away the poor among the believers, the likeness of the life of this world, i.e., liken it.

(﴿like water We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it﴾), that is, with the water.

(﴿plants of the earth﴾) until they flourished. It has been said that the plants intermingled with one another when the water fell upon them, because plants intermingle and grow thick only with rain. This meaning has already been explained in Surah Yunus [[see vol. 8, p. 326]].

The sages said: God likened the world to water for several reasons. Water does not settle in one place, and likewise the world does not remain in one state. Water does not stay in one condition, and likewise the world. Water does not last but goes away, and likewise the world perishes. No one can enter water without getting wet, and likewise no one who enters the world is safe from its trials and its afflictions. Water, when it is in measure, is beneficial and makes things grow, but when it exceeds the measure, it is harmful and destructive; likewise, the sufficiency of the world benefits, while its excess harms.

In a hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ), a man said to him: "O Messenger of God, I want to be among the successful." He said: "Leave the world and take from it like still water, for little of it suffices, and much of it makes one rebellious."

In Sahih Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "He has succeeded who has embraced Islam, been given sustenance sufficient for him, and whom God has made content with what He has given him."

(﴿then it becomes dry stalks﴾), that is, the plants become broken and crumbling from dryness, meaning when the water is cut off from them. This is omitted for brevity, the meaning being understood from the context. Al-hashm is breaking a dry thing. Al-hashim is dry, broken vegetation, and a dead tree may be taken by the wood-gatherer as he wishes. From this comes their saying: "So-and-so is nothing but a broken vine-stalk," when he is generous. A "hashim" man is one weak in body. Tahashshama 'alayhi fulan means he showed kindness toward him. Ihtashama what is in the udder of the she-camel means he milked it entirely. It is also said: hashama al-tharid (he crumbled the bread in broth), and from this Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf was named, whose name was 'Amr. Concerning him 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara said:

"'Amr al-'Ula crumbled bread in broth for his people,
while the men of Mecca were in years of drought, emaciated."

The reason for this was that the Quraysh were struck by years of drought which consumed their wealth. Hashim set out for Syria, ordered a great quantity of bread to be baked, and carried it on camels in sacks until he reached Mecca. He crumbled that bread, that is, broke it and made it into tharid, slaughtered those camels, then ordered the cooks to cook, and then poured the cooking pots over the platters, feeding the people of Mecca. This was the first feast after the year of drought that had struck them, and for this he was named Hashim.

(﴿the winds scatter it﴾), that is, they disperse it. This is the explanation of Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn Qutayba said: they blow it away. Ibn Kaysan said: they carry it away and bring it back. Ibn 'Abbas said: they turn it around. The meanings are close. Talha ibn Musarrif read "tudhriyhi al-rih" (تُذْرِيهِ الرِّيحُ). Al-Kisa'i said: in the reading of Abdullah it is "tudhriyhi" (تُذْرِيهِ). It is said: dharat-hu al-rih tadhruhu dharwan, and tudhriyhi dhariyan, and adhraytu-hu tudhrihi idhra' idha tarat bihi (when the wind carried it away). Al-Farra' related: adhraytu al-rajul 'an farasihi, meaning I threw him off his horse, i.e., I turned him over. Sibawayh and al-Farra' cited the verse:

"I said to him: aim straight and do not overexert him,
lest he be thrown from the back of the sand-grouse and slip off."

[[In Sibawayh's book the reading is "fayudnika" (فيدنك), another version of the line, which Sibawayh attributed to 'Amr ibn 'Ammar al-Ta'i. The meaning of "sawwib" is: take a moderate pace in traveling, be gentle with the horse, and do not tire him. "Ukhra al-qata" is its last part. "Al-qata" is the rear of the saddle.]] (i.e., the back part of the horse where the rider's rear sits). He says this to his servant, whom he had mounted on his horse to hunt for him.

[[Refer to al-Shantamari's commentary on Sibawayh's book.]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God is ever Capable of everything﴾, of bringing into being, annihilating, and giving life. Glory be to Him.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾. It is permissible to read *zīnatā* (in the dual), since it is the predicate (*khabar al-ibtida'*, the predicate of the subject) and can agree in dual or singular. Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life because wealth brings beauty and benefit, and children bring strength and defence, so the two became the adornment of the worldly life. But the qualifier [*ṣifah*] applies to wealth and children together with the contextual indication [*qarīnat al-ṣifah*], because the meaning is: wealth and children are the adornment of this lowly life, so do not let your souls follow them. This was a rebuttal of 'Uyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn and those like him, when they boasted of riches and nobility. The Almighty informed that whatever is of the adornment of the worldly life is a delusion that passes away and does not last, like dry stubble when the wind scatters it. Only what is provision for the grave and preparation for the Hereafter remains. It was said: "Do not attach your heart to wealth, for it departs; nor to women, for today they are with you and tomorrow with someone else; nor to the ruler, for today he is yours and tomorrow he belongs to another." Sufficient in this is the saying of Allah the Almighty: "Your wealth and your children are only a trial" [[See vol. 18, p. 140.]] and His saying: "Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them" [[See vol. 18, p. 140.]].

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And the lasting good deeds﴾, meaning what Salman and Suhayb and the poor Muslims perform of acts of obedience.

(﴿are better in the sight of your Lord for reward﴾), meaning more excellent.

(﴿and better in hope﴾), meaning better than the one who has wealth and children without righteous deeds. There is no good in the adornment of this world, but it came in the form of His saying: "The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in their resting place" [[See vol. 13, p. 21 and following.]]. It was also said: it is better in reality than what the ignorant suppose it to be in their assumption.

The scholars differed concerning "the lasting good deeds." Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, Abū Maysarah and ʿAmr ibn Sharḥabīl said: they are the five daily prayers. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: they are every righteous deed, whether saying or action, that remains for the Hereafter. Ibn Zayd said this, and al-Ṭabarī preferred it, and it is the correct view, Allah willing, because whatever its reward endures may rightly be called by this name. He [my teacher] said to me, may Allah be pleased with him: "Tilth is of two kinds: the tilth of this world is wealth and children, and the tilth of the Hereafter is the lasting good deeds; and Allah may gather both for some people." The majority said: they are the words reported to have excellent merit: Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, Allāhu akbar, and lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh al-ʿAliyy al-ʿAẓīm. Mālik transmitted it in his *Muwaṭṭaʾ* (al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, the Mālik collection of hadith) from ʿUmārah ibn Ṣayyād, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, that he heard him say concerning the lasting good deeds: they are the servant's saying Allāhu akbar, Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh.

al-Nasāʾī traced it back [to the Prophet] from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Increase from the lasting good deeds." It was asked: "And what are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The glorification (*takbīr*), the declaration of unity (*tahlīl*), the glorification of God (*tasbīḥ*), praise of Allah, and there is no power nor strength except by Allah." Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq authenticated it, may Allah have mercy on him.

Qatādah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took a branch and stripped it until its leaves fell, and said: "When the Muslim says: Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar, his sins fall away as this branch has shed its leaves. Take them for yourself, Abū al-Dardāʾ, before you are prevented from them, for they are from the treasures of Paradise and the choicest words, and they are the lasting good deeds." al-Thaʿlabī mentioned it. Ibn Mājah transmitted its meaning from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hold fast to Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar, for they remove sins as a tree sheds its leaves."

al-Tirmidhī transmitted from the hadith of al-Aʿmash, from Anas ibn Mālik, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by a tree whose leaf had dried, struck it with his staff, and the leaves scattered, and he said: "Indeed, al-ḥamdu lillāh, Subḥān Allāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar will surely cause the sins of the servant to fall away as the leaves of this tree fall." He said: this is a strange (*gharīb*) hadith, and we do not know that al-Aʿmash heard from Anas, nor that he saw him and looked at him.

al-Tirmidhī also transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I met Ibrahim, peace be upon him, on the night I was taken on the Night Journey, and he said: O Muhammad, convey my greetings to your community and inform them that Paradise has pure soil, sweet water, and that it is an empty plain, and its planting is Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar." He said: this is a fair strange hadith. al-Māwardī transmitted its meaning. In it: I said: What are the plantings of Paradise? He said: "There is no power nor strength except by Allah."

Ibn Mājah transmitted from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by him while he was planting a seedling, and said: "O Abū Hurayrah, what are you planting?" I said: seedlings. He said: "Shall I not direct you to a planting better than this: Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar; for each one a tree is planted for you in Paradise."

It has been said that the lasting good deeds are the intentions and resolutions, because by them deeds are accepted and raised; al-Ḥasan said this. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: they are the daughters, indicated by the beginning of the verse, for Allah says: "Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life," then He says: "And the lasting good deeds," meaning the righteous daughters, who are with Allah for their fathers as a better reward and better hope in the Hereafter for whoever treats them well. This is supported by what ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, related: "A poor woman came to me..." the hadith, which we have mentioned in Surah al-Naḥl in His saying: "He hides from the people" [[See p. 117 of this part.]]. It is also related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I saw a man from my community who was ordered to the Fire, and his daughters clung to him, crying out and saying: 'O Lord, he used to be kind to us in the world,' so Allah had mercy on him because of them." Qatādah said concerning His saying: "So We desired that their Lord would replace him with one better than him in purity and nearer in mercy" [[See vol. 21, p. 33 and following.]]: He replaced them with a daughter, whom a prophet married, and she bore him twelve sons, all of them prophets.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾. Some of the grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) said: The implied sense is, "And the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord, on the day We set the mountains in motion." Al-Nahhas said: This is an error because of the waw (conjunction). It was also said: The meaning is, "Remember the day We set the mountains in motion," that is, We remove them from their places on the face of the earth and move them as We move the clouds, as He said in another verse: ﴿And they pass by like the passing of clouds﴾ [see vol. 13]. Then they are broken and return to the earth, as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust, and become scattered particles of dust﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 194 onward].

Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, Abu Amr and Ibn Amir recited wa-yawma tusayyaru, with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ya', and al-jibalu in the nominative, as an impersonal passive verb. Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid recited wa-yawma tasiru al-jibalu, with a fatha on the ta' and the verb in its light form (mukhaffafan) from sara, with al-jibalu in the nominative. The evidence for Abu Amr's reading is ﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾ [see vol. 19, p. 225 onward]. The evidence for Ibn Muhaysin's reading is ﴿And the mountains will move with a [true] movement﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 194 onward]. Abu Ubayd preferred the first reading, nusayyiru with the nun, because of His saying "and We gathered them."

Bariza means manifest, with nothing upon it to cover it, no mountain, tree or building. That is, its fruits are plucked, its mountains uprooted and its buildings demolished, so it is bare and manifest. The exegetes hold this view. It was also said: "and you see the earth laid bare" means that what is in it of treasures and the dead has come out, as He said: ﴿And the earth will cast out what is within it and empty itself﴾ [see vol. 19, p. 267 onward], and He said: ﴿And the earth will bring forth its burdens﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 147]. This is the view of Ata'.

(And We gathered them): that is, to the place of standing (al-mawqif).

(And We left out none of them): that is, We did not leave any behind. It is said: ghadartu kadha, meaning "I left such-and-such." Antarah said:

"I left him rolling in the dust, his limbs scattered, while the people were between wounded and felled."

That is, I left him. Al-mughadara means leaving, and from it comes al-ghadr (betrayal), because it is leaving fidelity. A pool of water is called ghadir only because the water departed and left it. From the same root come a woman's ghada'ir (braids), because she places them behind her.

He says: We gathered their righteous and their wicked, their jinn and their humankind.

Allah's statement: ﴿They will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾.

"Ṣaffan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Muqatil said: They will be presented row after row, like the rows in prayer, each nation and group in its own row, not that they will be one single row. It was also said: "Ṣaffan" means all together, as in His statement ﴿then come in rows﴾ [Q 20:64], meaning all together. It was also said: standing. The memorizer (al-Ḥāfiẓ) Abū al-Qāsim ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mandah transmitted in the Book of Tawḥīd, from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, will call out on the Day of Resurrection with a loud voice, not a frightening one: O My servants, I am Allah; there is no god but I, the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Just of judges, and the Swiftest of reckoners. O My servants, there is no fear for you today, nor will you grieve. Bring forward your proofs and prepare your answers, for you are to be questioned and called to account. O My angels, arrange My servants in rows, standing on the tips of their toes, for the reckoning." I say: This ḥadīth is a clear explanation of this verse, and many of the exegetes did not mention it. We have recorded it in the Kitāb al-Tadhkira, and from there we have quoted it, all praise be to Allah.

﴿You have come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾. That is, it will be said to them: You have certainly come to Us barefoot, naked, with no wealth or children with you. It was also said: alone (furādā). Its evidence is His statement ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [Q 6:94], which has already passed. Al-Zajjāj said: That is, We resurrected you just as We created you.

﴿Rather, you claimed﴾.

This is an address to those who deny the Resurrection, meaning: you claimed in the world that you would never be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you an appointed time for resurrection. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised (ghurlan)." I said: O Messenger of Allah! Men and women will look at one another? He said: "O ʿĀʾisha, the matter is too grave for them to look at one another."

"Ghurlan" means uncircumcised. Its explanation has already been given in al-Anʿām.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾. "al-Kitab" (the Book) is a generic noun (ism jins), and in it there are two views. The first: they are the books of deeds in the hands of the servants; this was said by Muqatil. The second: that the reckoning (al-hisab) will be placed; this was said by al-Kalbi, and he called the reckoning "the Book" because they will be called to account for their recorded deeds. The first view is the more apparent, and it was mentioned by Ibn al-Mubarak, who said: Al-Hakam or Abu al-Hakam informed us (Nu'aym was unsure which) from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from a man of the Banu Asad, who said: 'Umar said to Ka'b: "Woe to you, O Ka'b! Tell us some of the news of the Hereafter." He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful! When the Day of Resurrection comes, the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) will be lifted up, and none of the creatures will remain without looking at his deed." He said: "Then the scrolls in which the deeds of the servants are recorded will be brought and scattered around the Throne. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, 'Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great but it has counted it?'﴾" Al-Asadi said: "The small sin is what is less than shirk, and the great sin is shirk; ﴿except it has counted it﴾." Ka'b said: "Then the believer will be called, and his book will be given to him in his right hand. He will look into it, and his good deeds will be apparent to the people while he reads his bad deeds, lest he say, 'I had good deeds that were not mentioned.' So God wills to show him all his deeds, until, when he has gone through what is in the Book and finds at the end of all of it that he is forgiven and that you are among the people of Paradise, at that point he will turn to his companions and say: ﴿Here, read my book. Indeed, I thought that I would encounter my reckoning.﴾ Then the disbeliever will be called and his book will be given to him in his left hand, then it will be rolled up and placed behind his back and his neck will be twisted; this is His saying: ﴿But as for he who is given his book behind his back﴾."

﴿He will look into his book, and his bad deeds will be apparent to the people, and he will look at his good deeds, lest he say, "Will I be rewarded for the bad deeds?"﴾

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, when he recited this verse, would say: "Woe to us! Cry out to God, the Exalted, over the small sins before the great sins."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The small sin is the smile, and the great sin is laughter," meaning whatever of that occurs in disobedience to God, mighty and majestic. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Al-Mawardi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the small sin is laughter. I say: It is possible that it is a small sin when it is not in disobedience, for laughter at a sin is approval of it, and approval of disobedience is itself disobedience; and on this basis it would be a great sin. So this is the way of reconciling them, and God knows best. Or the laughter mentioned by al-Mawardi is to be understood as smiling, and God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿So she smiled, laughing at her words﴾.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The small sins are the lamam (minor lapses), like touching and kissing; and the great sin is intercourse and fornication." The explanation of this has already passed in "al-Nisa'" (see vol. 5, p. 158).

Qatadah said: "The people complained of the counting, but no one complained of injustice. So beware of belittled sins, for they accumulate upon their doer until they destroy him." This has already passed.

The meaning of ﴿ahsaha﴾ is that it counted it and encompassed it, and the counting is attributed to the Book figuratively (tawassu'an).

(﴿And they will find what they did present﴾) i.e., they will find the counting of what they did present. It was also said: they will find the recompense for what they did present. (﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾) i.e., He does not seize anyone for the crime of another, nor punish them for what they did not do; said by al-Dahhak. It was also said: He does not diminish the reward of the obedient, nor increase the punishment of the disobedient.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 18, verse 50:**

God Most High says: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord.﴾ This has been covered fully in "al-Baqarah."[^1] Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: There is a question about this verse, namely, what is the meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾? There are two views on this:

The first, which is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is that the meaning is: defiance came upon him when he was commanded and he disobeyed. So the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say, "I fed him out of hunger" (*aṭamtuhu 'an jū'*).

The second view, which is the view of Muhammad ibn Qutrub, is that the meaning is: he defied by rejecting the command of his Lord. Then the Mighty and Majestic addressed the disbelievers by way of reproach, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me?﴾ O children of Adam, ﴿while they are an enemy to you﴾, that is, enemies. So it is a collective noun. ﴿How evil is this exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, that is, how evil is the worship of Satan as a substitute for the worship of God; or, how evil is Iblis as a substitute for God.

Scholars differed as to whether Iblis has offspring from his own loins. al-Sha'bi said: A man asked me, "Does Iblis have a wife?" I said, "That would be a wedding I did not attend." Then I recalled His saying, ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies?﴾, and I knew that offspring can only come from a wife, so I said, "Yes."

Mujahid said: Iblis inserted his private part into his own private part and laid five eggs, and this is the origin of his offspring.

It was also said: God Most High created for him a male organ in his right thigh and a female organ in his left, and he mates this with that, and every day ten eggs are hatched for him; from each egg come seventy devils, male and female. He goes out flying. The greatest of them in rank with their father is the greatest of them in tempting the sons of Adam.

Others said: He has no children or offspring, and his offspring are his helpers among the devils.

al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: The sum of the matter is that God Most High has informed us that Iblis has followers and offspring, and that they whisper to the children of Adam while they are their enemies. The manner of reproduction among them and the emergence of offspring from Iblis is not established for us, so the matter must rest on a sound transmission.

I say: What has been established from the authentic reports in this field is what al-Humaydi mentioned in *al-Jam' bayn al-Sahihayn*, from the Imam Abu Bakr al-Barqani, that he recorded in his book, with a chain going back to Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Hafiz, from the narration of Asim, from Abu Uthman, from Salman, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not be the first to enter the marketplace, nor the last to leave it, for the devil lays his eggs and hatches his brood there." This indicates that the devil has offspring from his own loins, and God knows best.

Ibn Atiyya said: The phrase ﴿and his offspring﴾, by its apparent meaning, refers to the devils who whisper, who bring evil and incite to falsehood. al-Tabari and others mentioned that Mujahid said: The offspring of Iblis are the devils, and he would enumerate them: Zalanbur, the lord of the markets, who places his banner in every market between heaven and earth, and sets that banner over the shop of the first to open and the last to close. Thabr, the lord of calamities, who orders the striking of faces, the tearing of garments, and the calling for woe and war. Al-A'war, the lord of the gates of adultery. Musawwat (in one copy: Washt), the lord of news, who brings it and casts it into people's mouths, so they find no basis for it. Dasim, who, when a man enters his house without greeting and without mentioning God's name, causes him to see the goods in it that are not put away and not placed well; and when he eats without mentioning God's name, he eats with him.

al-A'mash said: Indeed, I have often entered a house without mentioning God or greeting, and I saw a water-jug, and I said, "Remove this," and I argued with them. Then I remembered and said, "Dasim, Dasim, I seek refuge in God from him."

al-Tha'labi and others added, from Mujahid: and al-Abyad, who whispers to the prophets. And Sakhr, who stole the ring of Solomon, peace be upon him. And al-Walhan, the lord of purification, who whispers in it. And al-Aqyas, the lord of prayer, who whispers in it. And Murrah, the lord of musical instruments, and he is known by this kunya. And al-Haffaf, who dwells in the deserts, misleading people and making them lost. And among them are the ghouls.

Abu Mut'i Makhul ibn al-Fadl al-Nasafi related in the book *al-Lu'lu'iyyat* from Mujahid that al-Haffaf is the lord of drink, and Laqs is the lord of incitement, and al-A'war is the lord of the gates of rulers.

He said: al-Darani said: Iblis has a devil called al-Mutaqadi, who demands from the son of Adam an account of a deed he did in secret twenty years ago, and so he is made to speak of it openly.

Ibn Atiyya said: These and what resembles them are not reported by a sound chain. al-Naqqash lengthened the discussion on this subject and brought accounts that are far from soundness. Nothing sound has come to me in this matter except what is in the *Sahih* of Muslim, that for prayer there is a devil called Khanzab. And al-Tirmidhi mentioned that for ablution there is a devil called al-Walhan.

I say: As for what was mentioned about the naming, it is sound. As for his having followers, helpers and troops, this is certain. We have already mentioned the sound hadith that he has children from his own loins, as Mujahid and others said.

In the *Sahih* of Muslim, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: Indeed the devil takes the form of a man, comes to a people and tells them a lying tale, and they disperse. Then one of them says: "I heard a man whose face I recognize, but I do not know his name, telling it."

In the *Musnad* of al-Bazzar, from Salman al-Farisi, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not, if you can help it, be the first to enter the marketplace nor the last to leave it, for it is the battlefield of the devil, and there he plants his banner."

In the *Musnad* of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, he said: Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: When Iblis rises in the morning, he spreads out his troops and says, "Whoever has misled a Muslim, I will place the crown upon him." Then one of them says to him, "I did not cease to work on so-and-so until he divorced his wife." He says, "He will soon marry again." Another says, "I did not cease to work on so-and-so until he disobeyed his parents." He says, "He will soon be dutiful." Another says, "I did not cease to work on so-and-so until he drank wine." He says, "You! You!" Another says, "I did not cease to work on so-and-so until he committed adultery." He says, "You!" Another says, "I did not cease to work on so-and-so until he killed." He says, "You! You!"

In the *Sahih* of Muslim, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Iblis sets his throne upon the water, then he sends out his armies. The nearest of them to him in rank is the greatest of them in temptation. One of them comes and says, 'I did such and such.' He says, 'You have done nothing.' Then another comes and says, 'I did not leave him until I separated him from his wife.' He says, 'Then he draws him near,' or he said, 'he embraces him, and says, "Yes, you!"'"

This has been mentioned before. I also heard our shaykh, the Imam Abu Muhammad Abd al-Mu'ti, in the frontier city of Alexandria, say: There is a devil called al-Bayda'i who appears to the poor who persist in [their devotions]...

**Volume Eleven**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

[Continuation of the commentary on Surah al-Kahf]

The Qur'an verse 51–53 of Surah 18 (Al-Kahf), with al-Qurtubi's commentary from *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*

**Allah's words: ﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves﴾.** It has been said: the pronoun refers to Iblis and his offspring, meaning: I did not consult them about the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor about the creation of themselves; rather, I created them as I willed. It has also been said: "I did not make Iblis and his offspring witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of their own selves," meaning the selves of the polytheists, so how did they take them as allies besides Me? It has also been said: the pronoun in "I did not make them witnesses" refers to the polytheists and to people in general, so the verse includes a refutation of groups of astrologers (*munajjimin*), adherents of the natural temperaments (*ahl al-tabai'*), and self-appointed authorities among physicians and others, from everyone who plunges (*yatakhawwadu* [[In ج: yankhariṭu; in ا: yankhariṭu; in ك وى والبحر: yatakharraṣu.]]) into these matters.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I heard my father, may Allah be pleased with him, say: I heard the jurist Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad [[In ك: Abu 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah.]] ibn Mu'adh al-Mahdawi in al-Mahdiyya say: I heard 'Abd al-Haqq al-Siqilli say this statement and interpret this verse in this way, and that it is a refutation of these groups." Some of the scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*, scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence) also mentioned this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I say: the primary intended purpose of the verse is Iblis and his offspring, and in this way the refutation of the aforementioned groups is properly directed, as well as the refutation of the soothsayers, the Arabs, and those who revere the jinn, when they say: 'I seek refuge in the mighty one of this valley,' since all of these groups are attached to Iblis and his offspring, and they have misled all of them. So they are the primary target of 'the misleaders,' and these groups fall within their meaning."

Al-Tha'labi said: "Some of the people of knowledge said: ﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a refutation of the astrologers who claim that the spheres (*aflak*) produce effects on the earth and on some things relative to others. And His words ﴿and the earth﴾ are a refutation of the people of geometry (*handasa*), who said that the earth is spherical and the spheres move beneath it, and that people are attached to it and beneath it. And His words ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾ are a refutation of the naturalists (*tabai'iyyun*), who claimed that natures are the agents in souls."

Abu Ja'far recited: "﴿ma ashhadnahum﴾" with a nun and an alif, as a form of glorification (*ta'zim*). The rest recited it with a ta' (*ma ashhadtuhum*), based on His words ﴿and I did not take [them] as helpers﴾ [[Arabic: wa-ma kuntu muttakhidha]]. This means: I did not seek their help in the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor did I consult them.

**﴿And I would not have taken the misleaders as helpers﴾**, meaning the devils. It has also been said: the disbelievers.

**(ʿaḍudan)**, meaning helpers. It is said: *i'taḍadtu bi-fulan* when I sought his help and strengthened myself by him. The original meaning is "the upper arm" (*'aḍud al-yad*), then it is used in place of "help," because the arm is sustained by the upper arm. It is said: *'aḍadahu* and *'āḍadahu 'ala kadha* when he helped him and strengthened him. From this is His words: ﴿We will strengthen your arm with your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35], meaning: We will help you with your brother. The word "upper arm" is used in a figurative manner, and Allah, glorified and exalted is He, does not need anyone's help. He singled out the misleaders for mention to increase the blame and rebuke.

Abu Ja'far al-Jahdari recited: "wa-ma kuntu" with a fatha on the ta' [i.e., wa-ma kunta], meaning: "and you would not have taken, O Muhammad, the misleaders as helpers."

There are eight forms of the word *'aḍud*: ʿaḍudan with a fatha on the ʿayn and a damma on the ḍad, which is the recitation of the majority and is the most eloquent of them. ʿaḍdan with a fatha on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ḍad, which is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. ʿuḍudan with a damma on the ʿayn and the ḍad, which is the recitation of Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan. ʿuḍdan with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the ḍad, which is the recitation of 'Ikrima. ʿiḍadan with a kasra on the ʿayn and a fatha on the ḍad, which is the recitation of al-Dahhak. ʿaḍadan with a fatha on the ʿayn and the ḍad, which is the recitation of 'Isa ibn 'Umar. Harun the reciter transmitted ʿaḍidan. The eighth dialect is ʿiḍdan, according to the dialect of one who says *kitf* and *fakhdh* (shoulder, thigh).

**Allah's words: ﴿And [remember] the Day He will say: "Call My partners whom you claimed"﴾**, meaning: remember the Day when Allah says: "Where are My partners?" That is, call upon those whom you associated with Me, so that they may protect you from My punishment. He says this only to the worshippers of idols. Hamza, Yahya and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited *naqulu* with a nun. The rest recited it with a ya', in accordance with His words "shurakai-ya" [My partners], and He did not say "shurakana" [our partners].

**(So they called upon them)**, meaning: they did that.

(And man is ever most contentious) meaning, most disputatious and argumentative. What is intended is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his disputing about the Quran. It is also said that the verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the disbeliever is most contentious. The evidence that he meant the disbeliever is His saying: "And those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood." Anas reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A man from among the disbelievers will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and God will say to him, 'What did you do concerning what I sent to you?' He will say, 'My Lord, I believed in You, I affirmed Your messengers, and I acted upon Your Book.' God will say to him, 'This is your record; there is nothing of that in it.' He will say, 'My Lord, I do not accept what is in this record.' It will be said to him, 'These are the recording angels, who bear witness against you.' He will say, 'I do not accept them either, my Lord. How could I accept them, when they are neither from me nor from my side?' God, Exalted, will say, 'This is the Preserved Tablet, the Mother of the Book; it has testified to this.' He will say, 'My Lord, did You not protect me from injustice?' He will say, 'Yes.' He will say, 'My Lord, I do not accept what is in this record.' It will be said to him, 'These are the recording angels, who bear witness against you.' He will say, 'I do not accept them either, my Lord. How could I accept them, when they are neither from me nor from my side?' God, Exalted, will say, 'This is the Preserved Tablet, the Mother of the Book; it has testified to this.' He will say, 'My Lord, did You not protect me from injustice?' He will say, 'Yes.' O Abu Mundhir, you wished for fidelity, so you feared it,
