It is also said that the verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the disbeliever is most contentious. The evidence that he meant the disbeliever is His saying: "And those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood." Anas reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A man from among the disbelievers will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and God will say to him, 'What did you do concerning what I sent to you?' He will say, 'My Lord, I believed in You, I affirmed Your messengers, and I acted upon Your Book.' God will say to him, 'This is your record; there is nothing of that in it.' He will say, 'My Lord, I do not accept what is in this record.' It will be said to him, 'These are the recording angels, who bear witness against you.' He will say, 'I do not accept them either, my Lord. How could I accept them, when they are neither from me nor from my side?' God, Exalted, will say, 'This is the Preserved Tablet, the Mother of the Book; it has testified to this.' He will say, 'My Lord, did You not protect me from injustice?' He will say, 'Yes.' He will say, 'My Lord, I accept no witness against me except from myself.' God, Exalted, will say, 'Now We shall send against you a witness from yourself.' He will then ponder who among himself would bear witness against him. His mouth will be sealed, and then his limbs will speak of his associating partners, and then he will be left free to speak. He will enter the Fire. Indeed, some of him will curse others. He will say to his limbs, 'May God curse you! It was for you that I used to contend.' His limbs will say, 'May God curse you! Do you not know that God has the power to make speech?' That is His saying: '(And man is ever most contentious).'" Muslim reported it in its meaning from the hadith of Anas also. In Sahih Muslim, from Ali, that the Prophet ﷺ visited him and Fatimah at night, and said: "Will you not pray?" I said: "O Messenger of God, our souls are only in the hand of God; when He wills to raise us, He raises us." The Messenger of God ﷺ turned away when I said that to him. Then I heard him as he was leaving, striking his thigh and saying: "(And man is ever most contentious)."

His saying, Exalted is He: (And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them) meaning the Quran, Islam, and Muhammad, peace be upon him. (And from asking forgiveness of their Lord) (except that there come to them the way of the former peoples) meaning Our custom in destroying them. That is, nothing prevented them from faith except My judgment against them in that matter; and had I judged them to believe, they would have believed. "The way of the former peoples" is the habit of the former peoples in punishment that uproots. It is also said: the meaning is, "And nothing prevented the people from believing except seeking that there come to them the way of the former peoples," and the phrase has been elided. "The way of the former peoples" is the direct witnessing of punishment, and so the polytheists sought it and said: "O God, if this is indeed the truth from You…" [al-Anfal: 32], to the end of the verse.

(Or that the punishment should come to them face to face) [[This is the reading of Nafi', which the commentator, may God have mercy on him, used to recite.]] It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its meaning is "openly," as said by Ibn Abbas. Al-Kalbi said: it is the sword on the day of Badr. Muqatil said: suddenly. Abu Ja'far, Asim, al-A'mash, Hamzah, Yahya, and al-Kisa'i recited "qubulan" with two dammahs, intending by it all kinds of punishment, the plural of qabil, like sabil and subul. Al-Nahhas said: the view of al-Farra' is that "qubulan" is the plural of qabil, that is, dispersed, following one another. It is permissible in his view that the meaning be "openly." Al-A'raj said: his reading was "qubulan," meaning all together. Abu Amr said: his reading was "qubulan," and its meaning is "openly."

His saying, Exalted is He: (And We do not send the messengers except as bringers of good news) that is, of Paradise for whoever believes, (and as warners) that is, warning with punishment against disbelief. This has been discussed earlier.

(And those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood in order to refute thereby the truth.) It is said: it was revealed concerning the Muqtasimun, who used to dispute about the Messenger ﷺ, saying: "He is a sorcerer, a madman, a poet, and a soothsayer," as was mentioned earlier [[See vol. 10, p. 58.]]. The meaning of "yudhdahu" (refute) is to remove and nullify. The root of al-dahd is slipping. It is said: "his foot slipped" (dahadat rijluhu), meaning it slipped; it slips, dahdan. "The sun slipped from the middle of the sky" (dahadat al-shams 'an kabid al-sama'), meaning it declined. "His argument slipped" (dahadat hujjatuhu duhudan), meaning it became void, and God made it slip (adhdahaha Allah). Al-idhdah is causing to slip. In the description of the bridge (sirat): (The bridge is laid over Hell, and intercession is permitted, and they say: O God, grant safety, grant safety.) It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is the bridge?" He said: "A slippery place (dahd), a place where the foot slides." Tarafah said:

O Abu Mundhir, you wished for fidelity, so you feared it,
and you swerved as a camel swerves from the slippery ground.

(And they take My signs) meaning the Quran.

(And what they are warned of) of threats, (in mockery.) "Ma" here is in the sense of the verbal noun, that is, "and the warning." It is also said: it is in the sense of "that which," meaning they took the Quran and what they were warned of, namely the threat, in mockery, that is, as play and falsehood. Its explanation has been given earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 156 onward.]]. It is said: it is the saying of Abu Jahl about the butter and dates: "This is the zaqqum." It is also said: it is their saying about the Quran: "It is sorcery, confused dreams, and tales of the ancients," and they said to the Messenger: "Is this not but a human like you?" [al-Anbiya': 3], and "Why was this Quran not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?" [al-Zukhruf: 31], and "What did God intend by this as an example?" [al-Muddaththir: 31].

His saying, Exalted is He: (And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them?) That is, there is no one more unjust to himself than one who is admonished with the signs of his Lord, then treats them lightly and turns away from accepting them.

(And forgets what his hands have sent forward) that is, he abandoned his disbelief and his disobediences and did not repent of them. So "forgetting" here means abandoning. It is said: the meaning is "he forgot what he had sent forward for himself and what he had gained of punishment," and the meanings are close.

(Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness.) Because of their disbelief; that is, We are the ones who prevented faith from entering their hearts and their hearing.

(And if you call them to guidance) that is, to faith, (they will never be guided, ever.) It was revealed concerning specific people, and it refutes the Qadariyyah [[The Qadariyyah are a early theological school who affirmed human free will in a way the commentator considered deviant.]] in their saying. The meaning of this verse has been discussed in "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 271.]] [al-Isra': 1] and elsewhere.

His saying, Exalted is He: (And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy.) That is, for sins. This is specific to the people of faith, not the disbelievers, by the evidence of His saying: "Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him" [[See vol. 5, p. 245.]] [al-Nisa': 48]. "Possessor of mercy" has four interpretations: first, possessor of pardon; second, possessor of reward. On these two meanings it is specific to the people of faith, not disbelief. Third, possessor of blessing; fourth, possessor of guidance. On these two meanings it encompasses both the people of faith and disbelief, because He bestows blessings in this world upon the disbeliever just as He bestows them upon the believer, and He has made His guidance clear to the disbeliever as He has made it clear to the believer, though only the believer is guided by it and not the disbeliever. The meaning of His saying: (Were He to seize them for what they earned) that is, of disbelief and disobedience,

(He would have hastened for them the punishment), but He gives respite.

(Rather, for them there is an appointed time) that is, a fixed term to which they are deferred. Its parallel is: "For every news there is a fixed time" [al-An'am: 67], and "For every term there is a Book" [al-Ra'd: 38]. That is, when it arrives, it will not be delayed from them, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

(They will never find from other than Him a refuge.) That is, a place of shelter. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, and al-Jawhari related it in al-Sihah. The verb is "wa'ala, ya'ilu, wa'lan, wu'ulan," on the pattern fu'ul, meaning he took refuge. "Wa'ala minhu" on the pattern fa'ala means he sought deliverance. Mujahid said: a shelter. Qatadah said: a protector. Abu Ubaydah said: a place of escape. It is also said: a refuge, and the meaning is one. The Arabs say: "May his soul not be saved" (la wa'alat nafsuhu), meaning may it not escape, and from this is the poet's saying:

May your soul not be saved; you left it
to the two men of 'Amir, and you were not wounded.

al-A'sha said:

I have indeed stolen upon the lord of the house in his heedlessness,
and though he guards against me, he does not escape.

that is, he does not escape.

His saying, Exalted is He: (And those cities We destroyed when they wronged, and We appointed for their destruction a fixed time.) "Tilka" (those) is in the nominative position as the subject. "Al-qura" (the cities) is an epithet or an apposition. "Ahlaknahum" (We destroyed them) is in the position of the predicate, and it is construed according to meaning, since what is meant is the people of the cities. It is also permissible that "tilka" be in the accusative position according to the view of one who says: "Zaydan, I struck him," meaning: and those cities of which We have related to you the account, such as the cities of 'Ad, Thamud, Madyan, and the people of Lut, whom We destroyed when they did wrong and disbelieved.

(And We appointed for their destruction a fixed time) [[This is the reading of the majority, as in al-Bahr and elsewhere.]] that is, a known time that they could not exceed. "Muhlak" derives from "uhlikū" (they were destroyed). Asim recited "mahlakihim" with a fatha on the mim and the lam, which is the verbal noun of halaka. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted "limahlikihim" with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the mim. Al-Nahhas said: [al-Kisa'i said] and this is more beloved to me, because it derives from halaka. Al-Zajjaj said: [mahlak] is a noun of time, and the implied meaning is "for the time of their destruction," just as it is said: "the she-camel came to her mating-place" [[Lit., the stallion mounted the she-camel; "came upon her mating-place" means at the time the stallion mounted her, so they treated time as place.]].

**Issue 1.** Concerning this verse there are several matters.

**The first:** the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant (fata)﴾ (18:60). Most scholars and historians hold that this is Moses son of Imran, who is the Moses mentioned in the Qur'an; there is no other Moses in it. A group, among them Nawf al-Bikali, said: he is not the son of Imran but Moses son of Manshа son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub, and he was a prophet before Moses son of Imran. This view was refuted by Ibn Abbas in Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere. His servant (fata) is Yusha' ibn Nun, whose mention has already passed in "al-Ma'ida" [[See vol. 6, p. 130 onward.]] and at the end of "Yusuf" [[See vol. 9, p. 270 onward.]]. Whoever says he is the son of Manshа, the servant is not Yusha' ibn Nun.

﴿I will not cease﴾ (18:60): that is, I will not stop traveling. The poet said: [[It is Khidash ibn Zuhayr who says: "I will not cease leading my noble horse." It is said that he intended a saying praised for its praise of my people; in al-Lisan it reads "against the enemies," (by the praise of God).]]

*"And I will not cease, as long as God preserves my people, / By the praise of God, girded and excellent."*

It is also said: "I will not cease" means: I will not part from you.

﴿Until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾ (18:60): that is, their junction. Qatadah said: it is the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome, and Mujahid said the same. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an arm that extends from the Ocean from north to south in the land of Persia, beyond Azerbaijan; so the corner where the two seas meet on the side of the land of Sham is the meeting place of the two seas according to this view. It is said: they are the Jordan Sea and the Sea of al-Qulzum. It is said: the meeting place of the two seas is at Tangier; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. It was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that it is in Africa (Ifriqiya). Al-Suddi said: al-Kurr and al-Rass [[al-Kurr and al-Rass: two rivers.]] are in Armenia. Some scholars said: it is the sea of al-Andalus from the Ocean, related by al-Naqqash, and this is much mentioned. A group said: the two are only Moses and al-Khidr. This is a weak view, reported from Ibn Abbas, and it is not sound, for the matter is clear from the hadiths that what was indicated to him was a sea of water.

The cause of this story is what the two Sahihs narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Moses (peace be upon him) stood up to preach among the Children of Israel, and he was asked: Who is the most knowledgeable of people? He said: I am. God rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge to Him. God revealed to him: Indeed I have a servant at the meeting place of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you. Moses said: O Lord, how can I reach him? He said: Take a fish with you and put it in a basket; wherever you lose the fish, he is there." And he mentioned the hadith; the wording is that of al-Bukhari.

Ibn Abbas said: "When Moses and his people prevailed over the land of Egypt, he settled his people in Egypt. When the dwelling became settled for them, God commanded him to remind them of the Days of God. So he addressed his people and reminded them of the good and blessing God had given them when He saved them from the family of Pharaoh, destroyed their enemy, and made them successors in the earth. Then he said: God spoke to your Prophet with direct speech, chose him for Himself, cast love for me from Him upon him, gave you all that you asked of Him, made you the most excellent people of the earth, granted you honour after humiliation, wealth after poverty, and the Torah after you had been ignorant. A man from the Children of Israel said to him: We understood what you say; is there on the face of the earth anyone more knowledgeable than you, O Prophet of God? He said: No. So God rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge to Him, and God sent Gabriel: O Moses, what makes you know where I place My knowledge? Indeed, I have a servant at the meeting place of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you." And he mentioned the hadith.

Our scholars said: his saying in the hadith, "he is more knowledgeable than you," means in judgments of particular events and rulings on specific occurrences, not absolutely. The evidence is al-Khidr's saying to Moses: "You have a knowledge that God taught you which I do not know, and I have a knowledge that He taught me which you do not know." On this basis, each of them is truly more knowledgeable than the other with respect to what he knows and the other does not. When Moses heard this, his noble soul and lofty aspiration yearned to acquire knowledge of what he did not know, and to meet the one of whom it was said he was more knowledgeable than him. So he resolved, and asked, in the manner of one humbly seeking the way, and he was commanded to set out in every circumstance. He was told: Carry with you a salted fish in a basket, which is the zanbil; wherever it comes back to life and you miss it, there is the way. So he set out with his servant when he came to him, striving in earnest, saying: "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" (18:60).

﴿Or I will journey on for a long time﴾ (18:60): with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and the qāf, which is the age (dahr), and its plural is aḥqāb. Its qāf may also be sukun, so it is said ḥuqb. It is eighty years. It is also said: more than that. Its plural is ḥiqāb. And ḥiqba, with a kasra on the ḥā', is the singular of ḥuqb, which means years. [[In al-Bahr: al-ḥuqb means years.]]

**Second issue:** In this there is from jurisprudence (fiqh) the journeying of the scholar in pursuit of increase in knowledge, seeking assistance in that through a servant and a companion, and seizing the opportunity to meet the excellent and the scholars even when their regions are distant. This was the practice of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), and through this those who travelled attained the superior portion and achieved the successful striving. Firm footing in the sciences was established for them, and they obtained the best shares of remembrance, reward and virtue. Al-Bukhari said: Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah travelled a month's journey to 'Abd Allah ibn Unays in a hadith.

**Third issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant (fata)﴾ (18:60). The scholars have three opinions regarding this.

The first: he was with him serving him. In the language of the Arabs, *fata* is a young man, and since servants are mostly young men, the servant was called *fata* as a matter of good manners. The Sharia recommended this in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my maid'; let him say 'my young man' (fataya) and 'my young woman' (fatati)." This is a recommendation toward humility, and this has already been mentioned in "Yusuf" [[See vol. 9, p. 194, p. 176 and p. 222.]]. The *fata* in the verse is the servant, who is Yusha' ibn Nun ibn Ifra'im ibn Yusuf (peace be upon him). It is also said he is the son of Moses's sister (peace be upon him). It was also said: he was called the *fata* of Moses only because he stayed with him to learn from him, even though he was free; and this is the meaning of the first view.

It was said: he called him *fata* because he took the place of the *fata*, who is the slave. God the Exalted said: ﴿And he said to his servants (fityan): place their merchandise in their saddlebags﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 194, p. 176 and p. 222.]], and He said: ﴿She sought to seduce her servant (fata) from himself﴾ (12:30) [[See vol. 9, p. 194, p. 176 and p. 222.]].

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires that he was a slave. In the hadith, he was Yusha' ibn Nun. In the (exegetical) books, he was the son of his sister. All of this is not something that can be decided with certainty, and suspending judgment regarding it is safer.

**Fourth issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿Or I will journey on for a long time﴾ (18:60). 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said: a ḥuqb is eighty years. Mujahid said: seventy autumns. Qatadah said: a period of time. Al-Nahhas said: What the people of the language know is that ḥuqb and ḥiqba are a period of time from the age, indefinite and unbounded, just as rahṭ and qawm are indefinite and unbounded. Its plural is aḥqāb.

﴿So when they reached the meeting-place of the two seas, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, making a passage.﴾ The pronoun in His words "between them" (bayni-himā) refers to the two seas. This is the view of Mujahid. The *sarab* is the path or way, also according to Mujahid [also]. Qatadah said: the water froze and became like a *sarab* (a tunnel or passage). Most of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) hold that the fish left its path empty, and that Musa walked along it following the fish, until the way led him to an island in the sea, where he found al-Khadir. The apparent meaning of the narrations and of the Book is that he found al-Khadir on the bank of the sea. His words "they forgot their fish" are said of both, though the forgetting was only the young man's. It is said that the meaning is: he forgot to inform Musa of what he had seen of the fish's condition, and so the forgetting is attributed to both of them because they were companions, as in His words: ﴿From them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas it comes out of the salt water only. And as in His words: "O company of jinn and humans, did there not come to you messengers from among you?" [al-An'am: 130], whereas the messengers are from humankind, not from the jinn. [See vol. 17, p. 161.] [See vol. 7, p. 85.]

In al-Bukhari: [Musa] said to his young man, "I will not burden you except that you tell me the place where the fish will leave you." He said, "You have not burdened me greatly." That is the meaning of His Mighty and Majestic words: ﴿And when Musa said to his young man﴾ [60], Yusha' ibn Nun. [The naming of the young man is not from Sa'id; i.e., Ibn Jurayj, who is one of the narrators of the hadith, said this. The naming of the young man is not from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. (Al-Qastallani).] He said: "While he was in the shade of a rock in a damp place [tharyan; it is said a place is tharyan and land is thariyya when there is moisture and dew in its soil], the fish stirred [tadarraba; i.e., moved and shook, as when it came to life in the basket] while Musa was asleep. His young man said, 'I will not wake him.' When he awoke, he forgot to inform him. The fish moved until it entered the sea, and Allah held back the flow of the sea from it, until its trace was like a trace on a stone." Amr [i.e., Ibn Jurayj said, "Amr told me"] said: "It was like this," and he made a circle with his two thumbs and the two fingers next to them. And in another narration: "Allah held back from the fish the flow of the water, so that above it there became something like an arch (tāq). When [Musa] awoke, his companion forgot to inform him about the fish. So they set off for the rest of their day and night, until the next day, when Musa said to his young man: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; we have suffered much fatigue from this journey of ours﴾ [62]. Musa had not felt the fatigue until he had passed the place Allah had commanded him to reach. His young man said to him: ﴿Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it﴾ [63]."

It is also said that the forgetting was from both of them, because of His words: "they forgot," so the forgetting is attributed to them both. The reason is that the fish's movement was from Musa, since he was the one commanded with it. When they set out, the young man was the one carrying it until they reached the rock and stopped there. The fish was "forgotten" there, that is, left behind. When Musa asked for the morning meal, the young man attributed the forgetting to himself in addressing him. Allah mentioned their forgetting when they reached the meeting-place of the two seas, which is the rock. Musa was a partner in the forgetting, because forgetting means delay, as in the supplication: "May Allah postpone (ansa'a) your term." When they left the rock, they delayed their fish from being carried, so neither of them carried it, and it was permissible to attribute the forgetting to both of them, because they had both left and abandoned the fish.

His words: ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾. There is one issue here: taking provisions on journeys. This is a refutation of the ignorant, inexperienced Sufis who venture into the wastelands and deserts, claiming that this is trust in Allah, the One, the Subduer. Here is Musa, the prophet of Allah and His interlocutor, one of the people of the earth, who took provisions while knowing his Lord and trusting in the Lord of the servants. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari: Some people from Yemen used to perform the Hajj without taking provisions, saying, "We are the trusters in Allah." When they arrived they would ask people [for food], so Allah revealed: ﴿And take provisions﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. This has already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* [see vol. 2, p. 411 onward].

Scholars differed about what Musa's provision was. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a salted fish in a basket, and they would eat from it at morning and evening. When they reached the rock on the shore of the sea, his companion [in some texts: "his companion" is in K] placed the basket down. The flow of the sea reached the fish, and it moved in the basket, overturned the basket, and slipped away into the sea, and the young man forgot to mention the story of the fish to Musa. It is also said: the fish was only a sign for the location of al-Khadir, because of his words in the hadith: "Carry with you a fish in a basket; wherever you lose the fish, he is there." On this view, they took with them something other than the fish as provision. This was mentioned by our shaykh, the Imam Abu al-'Abbas, who preferred it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: My father, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say in his sermon: Musa walked to the private conversation (munajah) and remained for forty days without needing food, but when he walked to Bishr he was hungry for part of a day.

His words: (*nasaban*), meaning fatigue. *Nasab* is weariness and hardship. It is said that what is meant here is hunger. This is evidence for the permissibility of reporting what a person experiences of pain and sickness, and that this does not detract from contentment or from submission to Allah's decree, provided it does not come from impatience or anger.

In His words: ﴿and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it﴾: *an* with the verb is interpreted as a verbal noun (*masdar*), and it is in the accusative as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for the pronoun in *ansanihu*. It is a noun substituting for a pronoun, meaning: "and none but Satan made me forget mentioning it." In the Mushaf of Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud]: "and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it." Yusha' mentioned this only as an excuse, in response to Musa's words: "I will not burden you except that you tell me where the fish will leave you." He said, "You have not burdened me greatly," and so he offered this excuse.

His words: ﴿And it took its way into the sea, a wonder﴾. It is possible that this is the words of Yusha' to Musa, meaning: the fish took its path into the sea as a wonder for people. It is also possible that His words "and it took its way into the sea" complete the report, and then He begins an expression of wonder, saying from Himself: "a wonder" at this matter. The wonder lies in that the fish had died, and part of it was eaten, and then it came to life after that. Abu Shuja' said in the book of al-Tabari: "I saw it, it was brought to me: it was half a fish with one eye, and the other half had nothing." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: I too saw it, and the half that had nothing had a thin skin over it, with no bone beneath it. It is also possible that His words "and it took its way" are a report from Allah, in two ways: either He reports about Musa that he took the fish's path in the sea as a wonder, that is, he marveled at it; or He reports about the fish that it took its path as a wonder for people. Among the strange narrations in al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Abbas about the story of this verse: the fish came to life only because water from a spring there, called the Spring of Life, touched it, and it never touched anything without bringing it to life. In the exegesis: the sign was that the fish would come to life. It is said: when Musa came down after the journey had exhausted him, at a rock beside which was the water of life, some of that water touched the fish and it came to life. Al-Tirmidhi said in his hadith: Sufyan said: some people claim that beneath that rock is the Spring of Life, and its water does not touch anything dead without it coming to life. He said: the fish had been partly eaten, and when the water dripped on it, it came to life. The author of the book *al-'Arus* mentioned that Musa, peace be upon him, performed ablution from the Spring of Life, and a drop from his beard fell onto the fish and it came to life. And Allah knows best.

His words: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾ [the reading (*nabghi*) with a *ya* is that of Nafi'.] Meaning: Musa said to his young man, "The matter of the fish and its loss is what we were seeking, for the man we came for is there." So they returned, retracing their steps, lest they miss their path. In al-Bukhari: they found Khadir on a green carpet (*tanfisa*) on the edge of the sea, covered with his garment, having put one end under his feet and the other under his head. [See vol. 17, p. 161.] [See vol. 7, p. 85.]

His young man said, 'I will not wake him.' When he awoke, he forgot to inform him. The fish moved until it entered the sea, and Allah held back the flow of the sea from it, until its trace was like a trace on a stone." Amr [i.e., Ibn Jurayj said, "Amr told me"] said: "It was like this," and he made a circle with his two thumbs and the two fingers next to them. And in another narration: "Allah held back from the fish the flow of the water, so that above it there became something like an arch (tāq). **Al-Qurtubi's commentary on verses 66–70 (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran)**

Allah's statement: ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [as] guidance?"﴾ [This contains two issues.] The first: Allah's statement ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you?"﴾ is a question of courtesy and gentle address, spoken by one who seeks to bring someone down to his level and who exaggerates in good manners. The meaning is: "Will it happen for you, and will it be easy for you?" This is like the hadith: "Can you show me how the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to perform wudu'?" According to some interpretations, Allah's statement ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112] is of the same kind, as its explanation was already given in "al-Ma'idah" [see vol. 6, p. 365].

The second: this verse is evidence that the student follows the scholar, even if their ranks differ. One should not think that in Moses' learning from al-Khidr there is anything indicating that al-Khidr was superior to him. The lesser may know something that the greater does not, and excellence belongs to those whom Allah has granted it. If al-Khidr was a saint (wali), then Moses is more excellent than him, because he is a prophet, and a prophet is more excellent than a saint. If he was a prophet, then Moses was distinguished by his messengerhood. And Allah knows best. "Rushdan" (guidance) is the second object of "tu'allimanni" (you teach me).

(Al-Khidr) said: ﴿"Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me."﴾ That is: O Moses, you cannot bear to be patient with what you see of my knowledge, because the outward matters, which are your knowledge, do not give it. How can you be patient with what you see as wrong, while you have not been informed of its wisdom or the path of correctness? This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿"And how can you have patience over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"﴾ Prophets do not approve of wrongdoing; it is not permissible for them to tolerate it. That is, silence does not suit you, continuing according to your habit and your judgment. "Khubran" is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the subject. It was also said that it is an accusative of the verbal noun implied in meaning, because His statement "lam tuhit" (you did not encompass) means "lam tukhbirhu" (you did not inform yourself about it), so it is as if He said: "You did not test it as a test." Mujahid pointed to this. A person knowledgeable in matters (khabir) is one who knows their hidden aspects and what is tested from them.

Allah's statement: ﴿He said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient."﴾ That is: I will be patient by the will of Allah.

(And I will not disobey you in any matter.) That is: I have committed myself to obeying you. There is disagreement about the exception (istithna'), whether it covers his statement "and I will not disobey you in any matter" or not. It was said that it covers it, like His statement: ﴿And the men who remember Allah often and the women who remember [Him]﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. It was also said: he made an exception regarding patience, and so he was patient, but he made no exception in his statement "and I will not disobey you in any matter," and so he objected and asked. Our scholars said: this came from him because patience is a future matter, and one does not know what his state will be in it, whereas the negation of disobedience is a firm resolve and is present in the present moment. So the exception in it contradicts the resolve. It may be distinguished between them by saying that patience is not acquired by us, unlike the doing or abandoning of disobedience, for all of that is acquired by us. And Allah knows best.

Allah's statement: ﴿He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾ [70] That is: until I myself explain it to you. This is from al-Khidr a form of discipline and guidance toward what requires the continuation of companionship. Had he been patient and persevered, he would have seen marvels, but he objected too much, so separation and turning away became necessary.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 71–73:

The Exalted said: ﴿So they set out until, when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it.﴾ [In this there are two issues.]

The first issue: In the Sahih of Muslim and al-Bukhari: "They set out walking along the seashore. A ship passed by, and they spoke to its people to carry them. They recognized al-Khidr, so they carried him without a fare. When the two of them boarded the ship, [Musa [[Addition from al-Bukhari.]]] was not taken by surprise except that al-Khidr had pulled out a plank from the planks of the ship with an adze. Musa said to him: 'These people carried us without a fare, and you deliberately went to their ship and made a hole in it, to drown its people. You have certainly done a grave thing.' He said: 'Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?' He said: 'Do not blame me for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.'"

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first [objection] from Musa was forgetfulness." He said: "A sparrow came and perched on the edge of the ship and pecked once into the sea. Al-Khidr said to him: 'My knowledge and your knowledge, compared with the knowledge of Allah, are no more than what this sparrow has taken from this sea.'"

Our scholars said: The edge (harf) of the ship is its side, and the harf of anything is its end, [and from it comes the harf of a mountain [[Addition from the lexicon books.]]], which is its sharp, highest point. Here "knowledge" means "the known," as in the Exalted's words: ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], meaning of His known things. This is an analogy from al-Khidr: my known things and your known things have no effect on the knowledge of Allah, just as what this sparrow has taken from this sea has no effect relative to the water of the sea. The sea was used as the example because it is what we most often see of what is before us. The use of the word "decrease" here is a figurative expression intended for illustration and understanding, since there is no decrease in the knowledge of Allah, and His known things have no limit. Al-Bukhari also clarified this meaning, saying: "By Allah, my knowledge and your knowledge, in comparison with the knowledge of Allah, are only like what this bird has taken with its beak from the sea."

In al-Tafsir, it is reported from Abu al-'Aliyah: No one saw al-Khidr when he made a hole in the ship except Musa, and he was a servant whom no one sees except the eye of the one whom Allah wills to show him. Had the people seen him, they would have prevented him from making a hole in the ship.

It was also said: The people of the ship had gone out to an island, and al-Khidr stayed behind and made a hole in the ship. Ibn 'Abbas said: "When al-Khidr made a hole in the ship, Musa withdrew to one side and said to himself: 'What was I doing keeping company with this man! I used to recite the Book of Allah to the Children of Israel morning and evening, and they obeyed me!' Al-Khidr said to him: 'O Musa, do you want me to tell you what you said to yourself?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Such and such,' and he said: 'You are right.'" Al-Tha'labi mentioned this in his book al-'Ara'is.

The second issue: The making of a hole in the ship is evidence that the guardian (waliyy) may diminish the property of an orphan when he sees it as beneficial, such as when he fears that a tyrant will seize its yield, so he damages part of it. Abu Yusuf said: It is permissible for the guardian to placate the ruler by giving up part of the orphan's property to protect the rest.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "li-yughraqa" with a ya' (the verb in the passive), and "ahluha" with a raf' as the subject of yughraqa. According to the reading of the majority, "li-tughriqa," the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-ma'al, the lam indicating outcome), like the Exalted's words: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. According to Hamzah's reading, the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay). He did not say "li-tughriqanni" ("to drown me") because what overcame him at that moment was extreme compassion for them and regard for their rights. [See vol. 13, p. 252.]

(*Imran*) means "a wonder," said al-Qutabi. It was also said: "something abhorrent," said Mujahid. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-Imr* is a great calamity. He recited:

"The rivals have met from me a disaster, a great calamity, a grave affair"

Al-Akhfash said: It is said *amira amruhu ya'maru amran* when it becomes severe, and the noun is *al-imr*.

The Exalted's words: ﴿He said: Do not blame me for what I forgot﴾. Regarding its meaning there are two views. One of them is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This is one of the *ma'arid al-kalam*" (indirect or allusive speech, in which a statement is made that admits more than one meaning). The other is that he forgot and then apologized, and in this there is evidence that forgetfulness does not entail blame, and that it does not fall under legal obligation, and that no ruling of divorce or other rulings attach to it. This has already been discussed. Had he forgotten in the second instance, he would have apologized.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "When al-Khidr made a hole in the ship, Musa withdrew to one side and said to himself: 'What was I doing keeping company with this man! I used to recite the Book of Allah to the Children of Israel morning and evening, and they obeyed me!' Al-Khidr said to him: 'O Musa, do you want me to tell you what you said to yourself?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Such and such,' and he said: 'You are right.'" Al-Tha'labi mentioned this in his book al-'Ara'is.

The second issue: The making of a hole in the ship is evidence that the guardian (waliyy) may diminish the property of an orphan when he sees it as beneficial, such as when he fears that a tyrant will seize its yield, so he damages part of it. Abu Yusuf said: It is permissible for the guardian to placate the ruler by giving up part of the orphan's property to protect the rest.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "li-yughraqa" with a ya' (the verb in the passive), and "ahluha" with a raf' as the subject of yughraqa. According to the reading of the majority, "li-tughriqa," the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-ma'al, the lam indicating outcome), like the Exalted's words: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. According to Hamzah's reading, the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay). He did not say "li-tughriqanni" ("to drown me") because what overcame him at that moment was extreme compassion for them and regard for their rights. [See vol. 13, p. 252.]

(*Imran*) means "a wonder," said al-Qutabi. It was also said: "something abhorrent," said Mujahid. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-Imr* is a great calamity. He recited:

"The rivals have met from me a disaster, a great calamity, a grave affair"

Al-Akhfash said: It is said *amira amruhu ya'maru amran* when it becomes severe, and the noun is *al-imr*.

The Exalted's words: ﴿He said: Do not blame me for what I forgot﴾. Regarding its meaning there are two views. One of them is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This is one of the *ma'arid al-kalam*" (indirect or allusive speech, in which a statement is made that admits more than one meaning). The other is that he forgot and then apologized, and in this there is evidence that forgetfulness does not entail blame, and that it does not fall under legal obligation, and that no ruling of divorce or other rulings attach to it. This has already been discussed. Had he forgotten in the second instance, he would have apologized.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 74–76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him﴾. In al-Bukhari, Ya'la said: Sa'id said: he found boys playing, so he seized a boy who was a disbeliever, laid him down, and then slaughtered him with a knife. "Have you killed a pure soul, not in retaliation for another soul?" — he had not committed wrongdoing (al-hinth) [[Because he had not reached puberty, and this is an explanation of his saying (zakiyyah), i.e., "Have you killed a pure soul who had not committed wrongdoing, not in retaliation for a soul?" According to Abu Dharr: "had not committed wrongdoing" (al-khubth), with a kha' with a dot and a ba' with a dot, both with a fatha. Al-Qastallani; so it is in K.]]. In the two Sahihs and the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi: "Then they both got out of the boat, and while they were walking along the shore, he saw al-Khadir (Khidr) a boy playing with the boys, so al-Khadir took his head in his hand, pulled it off with his hand, and killed him. Musa said to him: 'Have you killed a pure soul, not in retaliation for another soul? Indeed you have done a dreadful thing.' He said: 'Did I not say to you that you would not be able to have patience with me?'" He [Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna] said [[It is Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, as in al-Qastallani. It was said: this (remark) was harsher than the first, because of the addition of (lak, "to you").]] and this was harsher than the first. "He said: 'If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me company; you have reached an excuse from my side.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari. And in the (Tafsir): al-Khadir passed by boys playing, and he took by the hand [[In K and Ya: by the hand of a boy.]] a boy who was the most handsome of them, and took a stone and struck his head with it until it was crushed, and killed him. Abu al-'Aliyah said: No one saw him except Musa; and had they seen him, they would have prevented him from [killing] the boy.

I say: There is no contradiction among these three accounts, for it is possible that he first crushed him with a stone, then laid him down and slaughtered him, then pulled off his head. And Allah knows best what took place; and what has come in the Sahih is sufficient for you.

The majority read "zakiyyatan" with an alif. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read "zakiyyatan" without an alif and with a shaddah on the ya'. It was said: the meaning is one, as stated by al-Kisa'i. Tha'lab said: al-zakiyyah is more emphatic. Abu 'Amr said: al-zakiyah is the one who has never sinned at all, and al-zakiyyah is the one who sinned and then repented.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a boy﴾. The scholars differed concerning the boy: was he mature (baligh) or not? Al-Kalbi said: he was mature, cutting off the road between two villages; his father was among the notables of one of the two villages, and his mother among the notables of the other village. Al-Khadir seized him, threw him down, and wrenched his head from his body. Al-Kalbi said: the boy's name was Shim'un. Al-Dahhak said: Haysun. Wahb said: his father's name was Silas and his mother's name was Ruhma. Al-Suhayli related that his father's name was Kazir and his mother's name was Sahwa. The majority said: he was not mature, and for this reason Musa said "zakiyyah" (one who has not sinned); and this is what the word "boy" requires, for "ghulam" among males is applied to one who has not reached puberty, and its counterpart among females is "jariyah." Al-Khadir killed him because he knew what he would become, and that he was created a disbeliever, as in the sound hadith, and that if he had lived he would have burdened his parents with disbelief. Killing a child is not impossible when Allah permits it, for Allah, may He be exalted, is the Doer of what He wills, the Capable of what He pleases. In the book al-'Ara'is: when Musa said to al-Khadir, "Have you killed a pure soul..." — the verse — al-Khadir became angry, tore out the boy's left shoulder, stripped the flesh from it, and found written on the bone of his shoulder: "A disbeliever who never believes in Allah." The proponents of the first view argued that the Arabs keep the name "ghulam" for a youth, and from it is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah: [[The verse is from a poem in which she praised al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, and before it:

When al-Hajjaj alighted in a sickly land ... he followed the furthest extent of its disease and healed it.]]

He healed her of the fatal disease that was in her, a youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives her drink.

And Safwan said to Hassan: [[Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, had recited a poem satirizing Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal and the Arabs of Aslam from Mudar; so Ibn al-Mu'attal confronted him, struck him with the sword, and said the verse.

(See the story in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.)]]

Meet the edge of the sword on my behalf, for I am a youth who, when provoked, is no poet.

In a report: this boy used to cause corruption on the earth, and would swear to his parents that he had not done it, and they would confirm his oath and protect him from whoever sought him. They said: his saying "not in retaliation for a soul" implies that if it had been in retaliation for a killing, there would have been no harm; and this indicates the boy's maturity, for otherwise, if he had not reached puberty, killing him would not be obligatory for a soul; and killing him was permissible only because he was mature and rebellious. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was a young man who cut off the road. Ibn Jubayr held that he had reached the age of obligation, based on the reading of Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas: "As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, and his parents were believers." Disbelief and belief are attributes of the responsible (mukallaf), and are not applied to one who is not responsible except by way of following his parents; and the boy's parents were believers by the text, so the name of disbeliever applies to him only upon reaching maturity, so it is necessary to take this meaning. And "ghulam" is from al-ightilam, which is intensity of sexual desire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿an abomination (nukran)﴾. People differed over which is more emphatic: "imran" or His saying "nukran." One group said: this is a clear killing, and there is an expectation [of something]; so "nukran" is more emphatic. Another group said: this is the killing of one person and that is the killing of a group; so "imran" is more emphatic. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: in my view they carry two different meanings: "imran" is more dreadful and terrifying, since it is an awaited great matter; and "nukran" is clear in corruption, since its harm has already occurred, and this is evident. His saying: (If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me company) is a condition, and it is binding, and "the Muslims are at their conditions"; and the most deserving of conditions to be fulfilled are those which the prophets undertook and which were undertaken towards the prophets. His saying: (you have reached an excuse from my side) indicates that an excuse is established by the first instance absolutely, and that the proof is established by the second instance decisively; this was said by Ibn al-'Arabi. Ibn 'Atiyyah: It may be that this story is also a basis for the terms in rulings, which are three, and the days of the one who is given a delay (al-mutalawwim) are three; so consider this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿do not keep me company﴾. Thus the majority read it, meaning "follow me." Al-A'raj read (tasbahanni) with a fatha on the ta' and ba' and a shaddah on the nun. It was also read (tasbahni), meaning "follow me." Ya'qub read (tushbihni) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', and Sahl related it from Abu 'Amr. Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is "do not leave me so that I accompany you." "You have reached from my side an excuse" means you have reached a point by which you are excused in not keeping company with me. The majority read "min ladunni" with a damma on the dal; except that Nafi' and 'Asim lightened the nun, so it is "ladun," to which is joined the ya' of the speaker, as in "ghulami" and "farasi," and the letter before the ya' is kasra, as it is in this (word). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ladni" with a fatha on the lam, sukun on the dal, and lightening of the nun. It is also reported from 'Asim "ludni" with a damma on the lam and sukun on the dal; Ibn Mujahid said: it is an error. Abu 'Ali said: this censure may be from the side of transmission; but according to Arabic analogy it is sound. The majority read "'udhran" (excuse). 'Isa read "'uduran" with a damma on the dhal. Al-Dani related that Ubayy narrated from the Prophet ﷺ "'udhri" with a kasra on the ra' and a ya' after it. 

Issue: al-Tabari related with a chain: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed for anyone, he began with himself, and one day he said: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon Musa; had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen the wonder; but he said: 'do not keep me company; you have reached from my side an excuse.'" And what is in the Sahih of Muslim: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon Musa; had he not hurried, he would have seen the wonder; but he was seized by a sense of shame (dhamamah) before his companion; and had he been patient, he would have seen the wonder." He said: And whenever he mentioned any of the prophets, he began with himself: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon my brother so-and-so." And in al-Bukhari, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "May Allah have mercy upon Musa; we wished that he had been patient until he related to us their matter."

Al-dhamamah, with a dhal with a dot and a fatha, has the same meaning as al-madhammah with a fatha or kasra on the dhal, and it means a sense of obligation and shame arising from that respect; one says: "I was seized by a dhamamah / madhammah / dhimmah from you." It seems he was ashamed at repeating his opposition, and at what came from him of harsh rebuke.

They said: his saying "not in retaliation for a soul" implies that if it had been in retaliation for a killing, there would have been no harm; and this indicates the boy's maturity, for otherwise, if he had not reached puberty, killing him would not be obligatory for a soul; and killing him was permissible only because he was mature and rebellious. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was a young man who cut off the road. Ibn Jubayr held that he had reached the age of obligation, based on the reading of Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas: "As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, and his parents were believers." Disbelief and belief are attributes of the responsible (mukallaf), and are not applied to one who is not responsible except by way of following his parents; and the boy's parents were believers by the text, so the name of disbeliever applies to him only upon reaching maturity, so it is necessary to take this meaning. And "ghulam" is from al-ightilam, which is intensity of sexual desire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿an abomination (nukran)﴾. People differed over which is more emphatic: "imran" or His saying "nukran." One group said: this is a clear killing, and there is an expectation [of something]; so "nukran" is more emphatic. Another group said: this is the killing of one person and that is the killing of a group; so "imran" is more emphatic. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: in my view they carry two different meanings: "imran" is more dreadful and terrifying, since it is an awaited great matter; and "nukran" is clear in corruption, since its harm has already occurred, and this is evident. His saying: (If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me company) is a condition, and it is binding, and "the Muslims are at their conditions"; and the most deserving of conditions to be fulfilled are those which the prophets undertook and which were undertaken towards the prophets. His saying: (you have reached an excuse from my side) indicates that an excuse is established by the first instance absolutely, and that the proof is established by the second instance decisively; this was said by Ibn al-'Arabi. Ibn 'Atiyyah: It may be that this story is also a basis for the terms in rulings, which are three, and the days of the one who is given a delay (al-mutalawwim) are three; so consider this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿do not keep me company﴾. Thus the majority read it, meaning "follow me." Al-A'raj read (tasbahanni) with a fatha on the ta' and ba' and a shaddah on the nun. It was also read (tasbahni), meaning "follow me." Ya'qub read (tushbihni) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', and Sahl related it from Abu 'Amr. Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is "do not leave me so that I accompany you." "You have reached from my side an excuse" means you have reached a point by which you are excused in not keeping company with me. The majority read "min ladunni" with a damma on the dal; except that Nafi' and 'Asim lightened the nun, so it is "ladun," to which is joined the ya' of the speaker, as in "ghulami" and "farasi," and the letter before the ya' is kasra, as it is in this (word). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "ladni" with a fatha on the lam, sukun on the dal, and lightening of the nun. It is also reported from 'Asim "ludni" with a damma on the lam and sukun on the dal; Ibn Mujahid said: it is an error. Abu 'Ali said: this censure may be from the side of transmission; but according to Arabic analogy it is sound. The majority read "'udhran" (excuse). 'Isa read "'uduran" with a damma on the dhal. Al-Dani related that Ubayy narrated from the Prophet ﷺ "'udhri" with a kasra on the ra' and a ya' after it. 

Issue: al-Tabari related with a chain: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed for anyone, he began with himself, and one day he said: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon Musa; had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen the wonder; but he said: 'do not keep me company; you have reached from my side an excuse.'" And what is in the Sahih of Muslim: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon Musa; had he not hurried, he would have seen the wonder; but he was seized by a sense of shame (dhamamah) before his companion; and had he been patient, he would have seen the wonder." He said: And whenever he mentioned any of the prophets, he began with himself: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon my brother so-and-so." And in al-Bukhari, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "May Allah have mercy upon Musa; we wished that he had been patient until he related to us their matter."

Al-dhamamah, with a dhal with a dot and a fatha, has the same meaning as al-madhammah with a fatha or kasra on the dhal, and it means a sense of obligation and shame arising from that respect; one says: "I was seized by a dhamamah / madhammah / dhimmah from you." It seems he was ashamed at repeating his opposition, and at what came from him of harsh rebuke.

There are thirteen issues in this passage. The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they came to the people of a town﴾. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Base people" [[In K and W: "al-majalis."]] "...they wandered in the assembly, [and] asked the people for food, but they refused to host them. And they found in it a wall about to collapse." He said: "It was leaning." He said: "So al-Khadir raised it with his hand." Musa said to him: "People whom we came to, and they did not host us nor feed us. If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it." He said: "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Musa. I wish he had been patient until he related to us their stories."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the town. It was said: it is Ubullah. This was said by Qatadah, and likewise Muhammad ibn Sirin said it. It is the most miserly town and the farthest from the sky. It was also said: Antioch. It was said: it is in the island of al-Andalus, narrated from Abu Hurayrah and others, and it is mentioned that it is the Green Island. A group said: it is Bajirwan, which is in the region of Adharbayjan. Al-Suhayli related and said: it is Barqah. Al-Tha'labi said: it is a village among the villages of the Romans called Nasirah, and the Christians are attributed to it. All of this is according to the disagreement about which part of the earth the story of Musa took place in. And Allah knows best the reality of that.

The third: Musa, peace be upon him, when he watered [the flocks] for the two daughters of Shu'ayb, was more in need than when he came to the town with al-Khadir, and he did not ask for food but watered [them] at the outset, whereas in the town they asked for food. The scholars have many explanations for this, among them that Musa was alone in the story of Madyan, while in the story of al-Khadir he was following another. I say: according to this meaning, His saying at the beginning of the verse to his young man is consistent: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours﴾. So hunger afflicted him, out of consideration for his companion Yusha', and Allah knows best. It was also said: since this journey was a journey of discipline, he was left to bear hardship, and since that journey was a journey of emigration, he was left to [receive] help and support with food.

The fourth: In this verse is evidence for asking for food, and that whoever is hungry must seek what will repel his hunger, contrary to the ignorant among the Sufis. Al-istit'am is asking for food, and what is meant here is asking for hospitality, as evidenced by His saying: "...but they refused to host them." For this, the people of the town deserved to be censured and attributed with baseness and miserliness, as our Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, described them. Qatadah said concerning this verse: the worst of towns is the one that does not host the guest and does not acknowledge the right of the traveler. It is evident from this that hospitality was obligatory upon them, and that al-Khadir and Musa only asked for what was due to them of hospitality. This is the most fitting for the condition of the prophets and the rank of the excellent and the saints. The discussion of hospitality has already preceded in [the commentary on] Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 64 onward.]], and praise be to Allah.

May Allah pardon al-Hariri [[He is the author of the famous Maqamat, and the verse in which he alluded to this verse is from his maqama (al-Sa'diyyah). In K: "tasakhkhaf" (he made light of it).]], for he made light of this verse and was over-familiar with it, and uttered a foolish saying and slipped. He took it as evidence for begging (al-kudyah [[Al-kudyah: seeking alms from people.]]) and insistence in it, and that this is not blameworthy for its doer nor a defect in him. He said:
"Even if you are refused, there is no defect in the refusal for you; Musa was refused before, and al-Khadir."
I say: this is playing with religion and slipping away from respect for the prophets. It is a shameful habit and a frivolous lapse. May Allah have mercy on the righteous predecessors, for they went to great lengths in advising every man of sound intellect, saying: Whatever you are playing at, beware of playing with your religion.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a wall﴾. "Jidar" and "judr" have the same meaning. In a report: "until the water reaches the judr" [[The hadith concerns the dispute of al-Zubayr with a man from the Ansar over the torrents of Shurayj al-Harrah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the judr." He meant what is raised around a farm like a wall.]]. A place is "jadir" when a wall has been built around it, and its root meaning is elevation. "Ajdarat al-shajarah" means the tree put forth its shoots, and from this comes "al-judari" (smallpox).

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿about to collapse﴾, i.e., it was close to falling. This is figurative usage (majaz) and extension of meaning, and it has been explained in the hadith by the phrase "leaning." So there is in this evidence for the existence of figurative usage in the Qur'an, and this is the position of the majority of scholars (al-jumhur). Every action whose proper subject is a living, speaking being, when it is attributed to an inanimate object or an animal, is metaphorical: that is, if a human were in their place, he would be performing that action. This is abundant in the speech of the Arabs and their poetry. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:
"Will you desist, when no one who is unjust [[Al-shatt: oppression and wrong. He means: no one restrains the wrongdoer from his wrong except a deep thrust, in which the sap and the fibers are lost.]] restrains him... except the piercing thrust in which the oil and the fibers go."
He attributed the restraining to the thrust. And from it is the saying of another:
"The spear desires the chest of Abu Bara', and turns away from the blood of Banu 'Aqil."
And another said:
"Indeed, a time that gathers my scattered affairs with a company is a time that intends kindness."
And another said:
"In a desert whose heads it split, a split like that of axes when they desire to penetrate."
That is, lodging in the ground, from the saying "nasala al-sayf" when the sword lodges in the target. He likened the striking of the swords on their heads to the striking of axes in the ground, for the axe strikes in it and lodges, hardly ever coming out. Hassan ibn Thabit said:
"If baseness were inherited, he would be a slave, ugly of face, one-eyed, from Thaqif."
And 'Antarah said:
"It shied from the impact of spears at its flank, and complained to me with tears and neighing."
[The line continues: "Had it known speech, it would have spoken to me." (The poet's line is incomplete here in the source.)]
He explained this meaning by saying:
"Had it known what conversation is, it would have complained."
This meaning is very common. From it is the saying of people: "My house looks toward the house of so-and-so." And in a hadith: "The Fire complained to its Lord." Some people went to deny figurative usage in the Qur'an, among them Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini and Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Isfahani and others, for the speech of Allah, exalted and mighty is He, and the speech of His Messenger, should be taken in its literal sense, which is more fitting for one of virtue and religion, since it relates the truth as Allah, exalted is He, informed in His Book. Among what they argued with is their saying: If Allah addressed us with figurative speech, He would also be described as speaking figuratively, for turning away from the literal to the figurative implies inability to express the literal, and that is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur: 24] [[See vol. 12, p. 210.]]. And He, exalted is He, said: "...and it says, 'Is there any more?' [50:30]" [[See vol. 17, p. 18.]] [Qaf: 30]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging and roaring﴾ [Al-Furqan: 12] [[See vol. 13, p. 6.]]. And He, exalted is He, said: "It calls him who turned his back and withdrew [70:17]" [[See vol. 18, p. 286 onward.]] [Al-Ma'arij: 17]. And "The Fire complained to its Lord," and "The Fire and the Garden argued," and whatever is like these is literal, and their Creator who made every thing speak made them speak.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Anas on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A seal will be placed on his mouth, and it will be said to his thigh: speak! So his thigh, his flesh, and his bones will speak of his deeds, so that his excuse from himself is removed [[Li-yu'dhar: in the active voice, from i'dhar, meaning: that Allah may remove his excuse from himself.]]. That is the hypocrite, and that is the one with whom Allah is displeased." This is in the Hereafter. As for this world, in al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the Hour will not come until the wild beasts speak to mankind, and until a man is spoken to by the tip of his whip and the strap of his sandal, and his thigh informs him of what his family did after him." [Abu 'Isa said [[The addition is from the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi.]]: This is also narrated in the chapter from Abu Hurayrah, and this is a hasan gharib hadith.]

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he raised it﴾. It was said: he demolished it, then sat and began to build it. So Musa said to al-Khadir: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it," because it is an action that deserves a wage. Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, on the authority of Abu Bakr, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he recited: "They found in it a wall about to collapse, so he demolished it and then sat to build it." Abu Bakr said: This hadith, if its chain is sound, then it is, from the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, in the manner of tafsir (exegesis) of the Qur'an, and that some transmitters inserted a tafsir into a place of the Qur'an, so it appeared that this was Qur'an that was omitted from the codex of 'Uthman, as some critics said. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he wiped it with his hand and it stood up, and this view is the correct one and is more like the actions of the prophets, peace be upon them, and indeed the saints. In some reports: the height of that wall was thirty cubits by the cubit of that generation, and its length on the face of the earth was five hundred cubits, and its width fifty cubits. So al-Khadir, peace be upon him, raised it, that is, he straightened it with his hand, and it became upright. This was said by al-Tha'labi in his book al-'Ara'is. Then Musa said to al-Khadir: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it," that is, food that we could eat. In this is evidence for the miracles (karamat) of the saints, and likewise all that is described of the conditions of al-Khadir, peace be upon him, in this matter, are all extraordinary events that break customary norms. This is if we assume he is a saint and not a prophet. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾ [Al-Kahf: 82] indicates his prophethood, and that he was inspired with obligations and rulings, as the prophets, peace be upon them, were inspired, except that he was not a messenger. And Allah knows best.

The eighth: It is obligatory upon a person not to place himself to sit beneath a leaning wall that he fears may fall, but rather to hasten his walking if he passes by it, for in the hadith of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "If one of you passes by a leaning ṭirbal, let him hasten his walk." Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: Abu 'Ubaydah used to say: the ṭirbal resembles the manzarah (lookout) among the manāẓir of the non-Arabs, in the form of a minaret, and a high building. Jarir said:
"He led her away with the withered veins of a wasted one... so it was as if she had been placed upon a ṭirbal."
[[Alwā: he led her wherever he wished. Shadhb al-'uruq: the veins showing through due to scant flesh, from the saying: a man is mushadhdhab, meaning lean and thin of flesh.]]

The ninth issue: the karamat (marvels or extraordinary favours) of the awliya' (friends of God) are established, as the established reports and the widely transmitted verses indicate. None denies them except the innovator who rejects them, or the wicked deviant.

The verses concerning Maryam include God's report that winter fruits appeared in summer and summer fruits in winter, as has been mentioned earlier, and what appeared at her hands when she commanded the palm tree, which was dry, and it bore fruit. She was not a prophetess, according to the differing view. This is supported by what appeared at the hands of al-Khadir (peace be upon him): the piercing of the ship, the killing of the boy, and the rebuilding of the wall.

Some scholars said: It is not permissible to say that he was a prophet, because establishing prophethood cannot rest on single-narrator reports (akhbar al-ahad), especially since it has been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) without room for interpretation, and by the consensus of the Ummah, the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "There is no prophet after me." And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40]. Al-Khadir and Ilyas [[In the manuscripts: "Daniel", which is a distortion.]] both remain alive with this marvel, so it is necessary that they are not prophets, for if they were prophets, there would have to be a prophet after our Prophet (peace be upon him), except what is established by evidence concerning the descent of 'Isa, who will come down after him.

I say: The majority hold that al-Khadir was a prophet, as has been mentioned earlier, and there is no prophet after our Prophet (peace be upon him), meaning that no one claims prophethood after him in the sense of an original claim. And God knows best.

The tenth issue: People differed over whether it is permissible for the wali (friend of God) to know that he is a wali or not, on two views.

The first: It is not permissible, and whatever appears at his hands must be regarded with a watchful eye of fear of deception, because he cannot be safe that it is a deception and a gradual lure (istidraj) for him. It is reported from al-Sarri that he used to say: "If a man entered a garden and from the top of every tree a bird spoke to him in eloquent language: 'Peace be upon you, O friend of God,' then if he did not fear that this was a deception, he would be deceived by it. And because if he knew that he was a wali, fear would leave him and security would enter him. It is a condition of the wali that he continue in fear until the angels descend upon him, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿The angels descend upon them: Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. And because the wali is one whose end is sealed with happiness, and the outcomes are hidden, and no one knows with what he will be sealed. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Actions are only by their endings.'"

The second view: It is permissible for the wali to know that he is a wali. Do you not see that the Prophet (peace be upon him) may know that he is a wali? There is no disagreement that it is permissible for others to know [[In (k) and (w): "to recognise him".]] that he is a friend of God, so it is permissible for him to know that. The Prophet (peace be upon him) informed about ten of his Companions that they were among the people of Paradise, yet that did not remove their fear; rather they were greater in glorifying God, the Exalted, and more fearful and reverent. If that was permissible for the ten and did not take them out of fear, then it is so for others.

Al-Shibli used to say: "I am the security of this side." When he died and was buried, on that day the Daylamites crossed the Tigris and took control of Baghdad, and people said: "Two calamities: the death of al-Shibli and the crossing of the Daylamites."

It is not said that this may have been a gradual lure, because if that were permissible, it would be permissible that the Prophet did not know that he was a prophet and a friend of God, since it could be a lure. Since that is not permissible, because it would annul the miracles (mu'jizat), this is not permissible either, because it would annul the marvels.

As for what is reported of marvels appearing at the hands of Bal'am and his stripping away from religion afterwards, based on His saying: ﴿then he stripped himself from it﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 319.]] [al-A'raf: 175], there is nothing in the verse indicating that he was a wali and then the walaya was stripped from him. What is related, that things resembling marvels appeared at his hands, consists of single-narrator reports that do not establish knowledge. And God knows best.

The difference between a miracle (mu'jiza) and a marvel (karama) is that a marvel is conditioned by concealment, whereas a miracle is conditioned by manifestation. It is also said: a marvel is what appears without a claim, whereas a miracle is what appears at the claim of prophets, who are then challenged for proof, and the effect of that appears. The conditions of the miracle have been mentioned in the introduction of this book, and all praise is due to God alone, with no partner.

As for the hadiths narrated as evidence for the establishment of marvels, among them is what al-Bukhari transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyya) of ten men as scouts (ʿayn), and he appointed over them 'Asim ibn Thabit al-Ansari [[It is also said: Marthad ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi was appointed over them.]], who was the grandfather [[Al-Qastallani said: This is an error; he was rather the maternal uncle of 'Asim, because the mother of 'Asim was Jamilah bint Thabit.]] of 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. They set out until, when they were at al-Hada'ah, which lies between 'Usfan and Makkah, they were mentioned to a tribe of Hudhayl called Banu Lihyan. They rushed toward them, nearly two hundred foot-soldiers, all archers, and they followed their tracks until they found the remains of dates they had taken as provision from Madinah. They said: "These are the dates of Yathrib," and they followed their tracks. When 'Asim and his companions saw them, they retreated to a fadfad [[Fadfad: a high, elevated mound.]], and the people surrounded them. They said to them: "Come down and give us your hands, and you have our covenant and pledge that we will not kill any of you." 'Asim ibn Thabit, the commander of the detachment, said: "As for me, by God, I will not come down today into the protection of an unbeliever. O God, inform Your Prophet about us." They shot them with arrows and killed 'Asim with seven others. Then three men came down to them under the covenant and pledge: Khubayb al-Ansari, Ibn al-Dathinah, and another man [[The other man was 'Abd Allah ibn Tariq.]]. When they had them in their power, they loosened the strings of their bows and bound them. The third man said: "This is the first betrayal! By God, I will not accompany you. Surely in these (he meant the slain) there is an example for me." They dragged him and tried to make him go with them, but he refused, so they killed him. They took Khubayb and Ibn al-Dathinah away until they sold them in Makkah after the Battle of Badr. The sons of al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf bought Khubayb, for Khubayb was the one who had killed al-Harith ibn 'Amir on the day of Badr. Khubayb remained with them as a captive. 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Iyad reported that the daughter of al-Harith told him that when they gathered, Khubayb borrowed a razor from her to shave himself, and she gave it to him. "My little son took hold of him while I was unaware, until he reached him," she said. "I found him seating him on his thigh with the razor in his hand. I was terrified, and a terror that Khubayb recognised in my face. He said: 'Do you fear that I will kill him? I would never do that.'" She said: "By God, I have never seen a captive better than Khubayb. By God, I once found him eating from a bunch of grapes in his hand, while he was bound with iron, and there was no fruit in Makkah." She used to say: "It was a provision that God, the Exalted, gave to Khubayb." When they took him out of the sacred precinct (haram) to kill him outside it, in the non-sacred area (hill), Khubayb said to them: "Let me pray two rak'ahs." They left him, and he prayed two rak'ahs, then said: "Had I not feared that you would think my heart was in dread of death, I would have prolonged them [[In (k): "to lengthen them".]]." Then he said: "O God, count them, kill them one by one, and leave none of them." Then he said:

"I do not care, when I am slain as a Muslim,
On which side I fall for God's sake.
That is for the sake of God, and if He wills,
He will bless the scattered limbs of a torn body."

The Banu al-Harith killed him. Khubayb was the one who established the two rak'ahs of prayer for every Muslim man who is killed in cold blood (sabran). On the day Asim was struck, Allah answered him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions were informed of the news of them and of what had befallen them.

Some of the disbelievers of Quraysh sent people to Asim when they heard that he had been killed, so that they could bring back something of him that they would recognise. He had killed one of their great men on the day of Badr. Allah sent upon Asim something like a cloud of hornets (al-dabr) [[al-dabr: wasps or drones of the bees.]], which protected him from their messengers, so they could not cut off any of his flesh.

Ibn Ishaq said about this story: The Hudhayl, when Asim ibn Thabit was killed, wanted his head so that they could sell it to Sulafa bint Sa'd ibn Shahid [[In (j) and (waw): al-Shahid.]]. She had vowed, when her two sons were struck down at Uhud, that if she could get hold of his head she would drink wine from his skull [[al-qahf: the skull.]]. The hornets prevented them. When it came between him and them, they said: "Leave him until evening, when it will have gone from him, and then we will take him." But Allah sent the valley, which carried Asim away, and he was gone. Asim had given Allah a covenant that he would never touch a polytheist and no polytheist would ever touch him during his life, so Allah protected him after his death from what he had refused in his life.

And from Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent him alone as a spy. He said: "I came to the cross of Khubayb and climbed up it, while I was fearful of the spies. I cut him down, and he fell to the ground. Then I plunged in and moved away a little, then I turned and it was as if the earth had swallowed him."
