In another narration there is an addition: "Until this hour we have not mentioned any remains of Khubayb." Al-Bayhaqi related it.

The Eleventh: It is not denied that the guardian (wali) may have wealth and property with which he protects his honour [[From (j), (waw) and (kaf) and (waw). This is more likely.]] and his dependants. And it is enough for you to consider the Companions and their wealth, together with their guardianship (wilaya) and their merit, and they are the proof against others.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "While a man was in a barren land, he heard a voice in a cloud saying: 'Water the garden of so-and-so.' That cloud moved aside and poured its water onto a stony ground (harra), and there was a watercourse (shirja) among those watercourses which had absorbed all that water. He followed the water, and there was a man standing in his garden, diverting the water with his spade [[al-misha: the iron hoe.]]. He said: 'O servant of Allah, what is your name?' He said: 'So-and-so,' the name he had heard in the cloud. He said to him: 'O servant of Allah, why do you ask me my name?' He said: 'I heard a voice in the cloud whose water this is, saying: "Water the garden of so-and-so," using your name. What do you do with it?' He said: 'As you have said this, I look at what comes out of it, and I give a third of it in charity, and I and my dependants eat a third, and I return a third of it to it.'" In another narration: "And I put a third of it toward the poor, the beggars and the wayfarer."

I say: This hadith is not contradicted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not take up property (day'a) lest you incline to the world." Al-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud and said of it: "It is a good hadith." For it is to be understood as applying to one who takes it in order to accumulate and to enjoy and indulge in its splendour. As for one who takes it as a livelihood, by which he protects his religion and his dependants, then taking it with this intention is among the best of deeds, and it is among the best of wealth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How excellent is good wealth for a righteous man."

People have said much about the miracles (karamat) of the saints, and what we have mentioned about it is sufficient. And Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

The Twelfth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had you wished, you could have taken a fee for it﴾. In it is evidence for the validity of the permissibility of hiring (ijara) [[ijara: a contract of hire or wage.]], and it is the practice (sunna) of the prophets and the saints, as will come its explanation in the surah "al-Qasas" [[See vol. 13, p. 267.]], if Allah wills.

The majority read "la-ittakhadhta" (with the ta' of the first person), while Abu Amr read "la-ttakhidhta," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatada. The two are dialectal forms with one meaning from taking, like your saying "taba'a" and "ittaba'a," and "taqa" and "ittaqa." Some readers assimilated the dhal into the ta' (idgham), and some did not assimilate it.

In the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "If you had wished, you would have been given a wage." This question came from Musa as a request for explanation (ard), not as an objection (i'tiraḍ). At that point al-Khadir said to him: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾, in accordance with the condition you set on yourself. His repeating "between me and you," and his departing from "between us," is for the sake of emphasis. Sibawayh said: "Just as one says, 'May Allah disgrace the liar from me and from you,' meaning from us."

Ibn Abbas said: Musa's saying about the ship and the boy was for Allah, while his saying about the wall was for himself, seeking something of worldly gain, and so it was the cause of the parting. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: That wall was a wall whose height in the sky was a hundred cubits.

The Thirteenth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will inform you of the ta'wil of that about which you could not have patience﴾. The ta'wil of a thing is its outcome (ma'al), that is, he said to him: "I will tell you why I did what I did." It has been said, in explaining these verses which occurred between Musa and al-Khadir, that they were a proof against Musa and not a marvel for him. That is because when he denied the matter of the breaking of the ship, it was said to him: "O Musa, where was this planning of yours while you were a castaway in the chest upon the sea?" When he denied the matter of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is this denial of yours from your striking the Copt and your judgement against him?" When he denied the setting up of the wall, it was said to him: "Where is this from your lifting the stone of the well for the daughters of Shu'ayb without a wage?"

There are thirteen issues in this passage. The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they came to the people of a town﴾. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Base people" [[In K and W: "al-majalis."]] "...they wandered in the assembly, [and] asked the people for food, but they refused to host them. And they found in it a wall about to collapse." He said: "It was leaning." He said: "So al-Khadir raised it with his hand." Musa said to him: "People whom we came to, and they did not host us nor feed us. If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it." He said: "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Musa. I wish he had been patient until he related to us their stories."

The second: The scholars differed concerning the town. It was said: it is Ubullah. This was said by Qatadah, and likewise Muhammad ibn Sirin said it. It is the most miserly town and the farthest from the sky. It was also said: Antioch. It was said: it is in the island of al-Andalus, narrated from Abu Hurayrah and others, and it is mentioned that it is the Green Island. A group said: it is Bajirwan, which is in the region of Adharbayjan. Al-Suhayli related and said: it is Barqah. Al-Tha'labi said: it is a village among the villages of the Romans called Nasirah, and the Christians are attributed to it. All of this is according to the disagreement about which part of the earth the story of Musa took place in. And Allah knows best the reality of that.

The third: Musa, peace be upon him, when he watered [the flocks] for the two daughters of Shu'ayb, was more in need than when he came to the town with al-Khadir, and he did not ask for food but watered [them] at the outset, whereas in the town they asked for food. The scholars have many explanations for this, among them that Musa was alone in the story of Madyan, while in the story of al-Khadir he was following another. I say: according to this meaning, His saying at the beginning of the verse to his young man is consistent: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours﴾. So hunger afflicted him, out of consideration for his companion Yusha', and Allah knows best. It was also said: since this journey was a journey of discipline, he was left to bear hardship, and since that journey was a journey of emigration, he was left to [receive] help and support with food.

The fourth: In this verse is evidence for asking for food, and that whoever is hungry must seek what will repel his hunger, contrary to the ignorant among the Sufis. Al-istit'am is asking for food, and what is meant here is asking for hospitality, as evidenced by His saying: "...but they refused to host them." For this, the people of the town deserved to be censured and attributed with baseness and miserliness, as our Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, described them. Qatadah said concerning this verse: the worst of towns is the one that does not host the guest and does not acknowledge the right of the traveler. It is evident from this that hospitality was obligatory upon them, and that al-Khadir and Musa only asked for what was due to them of hospitality. This is the most fitting for the condition of the prophets and the rank of the excellent and the saints. The discussion of hospitality has already preceded in [the commentary on] Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 64 onward.]], and praise be to Allah.

May Allah pardon al-Hariri [[He is the author of the famous Maqamat, and the verse in which he alluded to this verse is from his maqama (al-Sa'diyyah). In K: "tasakhkhaf" (he made light of it).]], for he made light of this verse and was over-familiar with it, and uttered a foolish saying and slipped. He took it as evidence for begging (al-kudyah [[Al-kudyah: seeking alms from people.]]) and insistence in it, and that this is not blameworthy for its doer nor a defect in him. He said:
"Even if you are refused, there is no defect in the refusal for you; Musa was refused before, and al-Khadir."
I say: this is playing with religion and slipping away from respect for the prophets. It is a shameful habit and a frivolous lapse. May Allah have mercy on the righteous predecessors, for they went to great lengths in advising every man of sound intellect, saying: Whatever you are playing at, beware of playing with your religion.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a wall﴾. "Jidar" and "judr" have the same meaning. In a report: "until the water reaches the judr" [[The hadith concerns the dispute of al-Zubayr with a man from the Ansar over the torrents of Shurayj al-Harrah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the judr." He meant what is raised around a farm like a wall.]]. A place is "jadir" when a wall has been built around it, and its root meaning is elevation. "Ajdarat al-shajarah" means the tree put forth its shoots, and from this comes "al-judari" (smallpox).

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿about to collapse﴾, i.e., it was close to falling. This is figurative usage (majaz) and extension of meaning, and it has been explained in the hadith by the phrase "leaning." So there is in this evidence for the existence of figurative usage in the Qur'an, and this is the position of the majority of scholars (al-jumhur). Every action whose proper subject is a living, speaking being, when it is attributed to an inanimate object or an animal, is metaphorical: that is, if a human were in their place, he would be performing that action. This is abundant in the speech of the Arabs and their poetry. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:
"Will you desist, when no one who is unjust [[Al-shatt: oppression and wrong. He means: no one restrains the wrongdoer from his wrong except a deep thrust, in which the sap and the fibers are lost.]] restrains him... except the piercing thrust in which the oil and the fibers go."
He attributed the restraining to the thrust. And from it is the saying of another:
"The spear desires the chest of Abu Bara', and turns away from the blood of Banu 'Aqil."
And another said:
"Indeed, a time that gathers my scattered affairs with a company is a time that intends kindness."
And another said:
"In a desert whose heads it split, a split like that of axes when they desire to penetrate."
That is, lodging in the ground, from the saying "nasala al-sayf" when the sword lodges in the target. He likened the striking of the swords on their heads to the striking of axes in the ground, for the axe strikes in it and lodges, hardly ever coming out. Hassan ibn Thabit said:
"If baseness were inherited, he would be a slave, ugly of face, one-eyed, from Thaqif."
And 'Antarah said:
"It shied from the impact of spears at its flank, and complained to me with tears and neighing."
[The line continues: "Had it known speech, it would have spoken to me." (The poet's line is incomplete here in the source.)]
He explained this meaning by saying:
"Had it known what conversation is, it would have complained."
This meaning is very common. From it is the saying of people: "My house looks toward the house of so-and-so." And in a hadith: "The Fire complained to its Lord." Some people went to deny figurative usage in the Qur'an, among them Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini and Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Isfahani and others, for the speech of Allah, exalted and mighty is He, and the speech of His Messenger, should be taken in its literal sense, which is more fitting for one of virtue and religion, since it relates the truth as Allah, exalted is He, informed in His Book. Among what they argued with is their saying: If Allah addressed us with figurative speech, He would also be described as speaking figuratively, for turning away from the literal to the figurative implies inability to express the literal, and that is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur: 24] [[See vol. 12, p. 210.]]. And He, exalted is He, said: "...and it says, 'Is there any more?' [50:30]" [[See vol. 17, p. 18.]] [Qaf: 30]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging and roaring﴾ [Al-Furqan: 12] [[See vol. 13, p. 6.]]. And He, exalted is He, said: "It calls him who turned his back and withdrew [70:17]" [[See vol. 18, p. 286 onward.]] [Al-Ma'arij: 17]. And "The Fire complained to its Lord," and "The Fire and the Garden argued," and whatever is like these is literal, and their Creator who made every thing speak made them speak.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Anas on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A seal will be placed on his mouth, and it will be said to his thigh: speak! So his thigh, his flesh, and his bones will speak of his deeds, so that his excuse from himself is removed [[Li-yu'dhar: in the active voice, from i'dhar, meaning: that Allah may remove his excuse from himself.]]. That is the hypocrite, and that is the one with whom Allah is displeased." This is in the Hereafter. As for this world, in al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the Hour will not come until the wild beasts speak to mankind, and until a man is spoken to by the tip of his whip and the strap of his sandal, and his thigh informs him of what his family did after him." [Abu 'Isa said [[The addition is from the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi.]]: This is also narrated in the chapter from Abu Hurayrah, and this is a hasan gharib hadith.]

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he raised it﴾. It was said: he demolished it, then sat and began to build it. So Musa said to al-Khadir: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it," because it is an action that deserves a wage. Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, on the authority of Abu Bakr, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he recited: "They found in it a wall about to collapse, so he demolished it and then sat to build it." Abu Bakr said: This hadith, if its chain is sound, then it is, from the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, in the manner of tafsir (exegesis) of the Qur'an, and that some transmitters inserted a tafsir into a place of the Qur'an, so it appeared that this was Qur'an that was omitted from the codex of 'Uthman, as some critics said. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he wiped it with his hand and it stood up, and this view is the correct one and is more like the actions of the prophets, peace be upon them, and indeed the saints. In some reports: the height of that wall was thirty cubits by the cubit of that generation, and its length on the face of the earth was five hundred cubits, and its width fifty cubits. So al-Khadir, peace be upon him, raised it, that is, he straightened it with his hand, and it became upright. This was said by al-Tha'labi in his book al-'Ara'is. Then Musa said to al-Khadir: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it," that is, food that we could eat. In this is evidence for the miracles (karamat) of the saints, and likewise all that is described of the conditions of al-Khadir, peace be upon him, in this matter, are all extraordinary events that break customary norms. This is if we assume he is a saint and not a prophet. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾ [Al-Kahf: 82] indicates his prophethood, and that he was inspired with obligations and rulings, as the prophets, peace be upon them, were inspired, except that he was not a messenger. And Allah knows best.

The eighth: It is obligatory upon a person not to place himself to sit beneath a leaning wall that he fears may fall, but rather to hasten his walking if he passes by it, for in the hadith of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "If one of you passes by a leaning ṭirbal, let him hasten his walk." Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: Abu 'Ubaydah used to say: the ṭirbal resembles the manzarah (lookout) among the manāẓir of the non-Arabs, in the form of a minaret, and a high building. Jarir said:
"He led her away with the withered veins of a wasted one... so it was as if she had been placed upon a ṭirbal."
[[Alwā: he led her wherever he wished. Shadhb al-'uruq: the veins showing through due to scant flesh, from the saying: a man is mushadhdhab, meaning lean and thin of flesh.]]

The ninth issue: the karamat (marvels or extraordinary favours) of the awliya' (friends of God) are established, as the established reports and the widely transmitted verses indicate. None denies them except the innovator who rejects them, or the wicked deviant.

The verses concerning Maryam include God's report that winter fruits appeared in summer and summer fruits in winter, as has been mentioned earlier, and what appeared at her hands when she commanded the palm tree, which was dry, and it bore fruit. She was not a prophetess, according to the differing view. This is supported by what appeared at the hands of al-Khadir (peace be upon him): the piercing of the ship, the killing of the boy, and the rebuilding of the wall.

Some scholars said: It is not permissible to say that he was a prophet, because establishing prophethood cannot rest on single-narrator reports (akhbar al-ahad), especially since it has been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) without room for interpretation, and by the consensus of the Ummah, the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "There is no prophet after me." And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40]. Al-Khadir and Ilyas [[In the manuscripts: "Daniel", which is a distortion.]] both remain alive with this marvel, so it is necessary that they are not prophets, for if they were prophets, there would have to be a prophet after our Prophet (peace be upon him), except what is established by evidence concerning the descent of 'Isa, who will come down after him.

I say: The majority hold that al-Khadir was a prophet, as has been mentioned earlier, and there is no prophet after our Prophet (peace be upon him), meaning that no one claims prophethood after him in the sense of an original claim. And God knows best.

The tenth issue: People differed over whether it is permissible for the wali (friend of God) to know that he is a wali or not, on two views.

The first: It is not permissible, and whatever appears at his hands must be regarded with a watchful eye of fear of deception, because he cannot be safe that it is a deception and a gradual lure (istidraj) for him. It is reported from al-Sarri that he used to say: "If a man entered a garden and from the top of every tree a bird spoke to him in eloquent language: 'Peace be upon you, O friend of God,' then if he did not fear that this was a deception, he would be deceived by it. And because if he knew that he was a wali, fear would leave him and security would enter him. It is a condition of the wali that he continue in fear until the angels descend upon him, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿The angels descend upon them: Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. And because the wali is one whose end is sealed with happiness, and the outcomes are hidden, and no one knows with what he will be sealed. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Actions are only by their endings.'"

The second view: It is permissible for the wali to know that he is a wali. Do you not see that the Prophet (peace be upon him) may know that he is a wali? There is no disagreement that it is permissible for others to know [[In (k) and (w): "to recognise him".]] that he is a friend of God, so it is permissible for him to know that. The Prophet (peace be upon him) informed about ten of his Companions that they were among the people of Paradise, yet that did not remove their fear; rather they were greater in glorifying God, the Exalted, and more fearful and reverent. If that was permissible for the ten and did not take them out of fear, then it is so for others.

Al-Shibli used to say: "I am the security of this side." When he died and was buried, on that day the Daylamites crossed the Tigris and took control of Baghdad, and people said: "Two calamities: the death of al-Shibli and the crossing of the Daylamites."

It is not said that this may have been a gradual lure, because if that were permissible, it would be permissible that the Prophet did not know that he was a prophet and a friend of God, since it could be a lure. Since that is not permissible, because it would annul the miracles (mu'jizat), this is not permissible either, because it would annul the marvels.

As for what is reported of marvels appearing at the hands of Bal'am and his stripping away from religion afterwards, based on His saying: ﴿then he stripped himself from it﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 319.]] [al-A'raf: 175], there is nothing in the verse indicating that he was a wali and then the walaya was stripped from him. What is related, that things resembling marvels appeared at his hands, consists of single-narrator reports that do not establish knowledge. And God knows best.

The difference between a miracle (mu'jiza) and a marvel (karama) is that a marvel is conditioned by concealment, whereas a miracle is conditioned by manifestation. It is also said: a marvel is what appears without a claim, whereas a miracle is what appears at the claim of prophets, who are then challenged for proof, and the effect of that appears. The conditions of the miracle have been mentioned in the introduction of this book, and all praise is due to God alone, with no partner.

As for the hadiths narrated as evidence for the establishment of marvels, among them is what al-Bukhari transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyya) of ten men as scouts (ʿayn), and he appointed over them 'Asim ibn Thabit al-Ansari [[It is also said: Marthad ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi was appointed over them.]], who was the grandfather [[Al-Qastallani said: This is an error; he was rather the maternal uncle of 'Asim, because the mother of 'Asim was Jamilah bint Thabit.]] of 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. They set out until, when they were at al-Hada'ah, which lies between 'Usfan and Makkah, they were mentioned to a tribe of Hudhayl called Banu Lihyan. They rushed toward them, nearly two hundred foot-soldiers, all archers, and they followed their tracks until they found the remains of dates they had taken as provision from Madinah. They said: "These are the dates of Yathrib," and they followed their tracks. When 'Asim and his companions saw them, they retreated to a fadfad [[Fadfad: a high, elevated mound.]], and the people surrounded them. They said to them: "Come down and give us your hands, and you have our covenant and pledge that we will not kill any of you." 'Asim ibn Thabit, the commander of the detachment, said: "As for me, by God, I will not come down today into the protection of an unbeliever. O God, inform Your Prophet about us." They shot them with arrows and killed 'Asim with seven others. Then three men came down to them under the covenant and pledge: Khubayb al-Ansari, Ibn al-Dathinah, and another man [[The other man was 'Abd Allah ibn Tariq.]]. When they had them in their power, they loosened the strings of their bows and bound them. The third man said: "This is the first betrayal! By God, I will not accompany you. Surely in these (he meant the slain) there is an example for me." They dragged him and tried to make him go with them, but he refused, so they killed him. They took Khubayb and Ibn al-Dathinah away until they sold them in Makkah after the Battle of Badr. The sons of al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf bought Khubayb, for Khubayb was the one who had killed al-Harith ibn 'Amir on the day of Badr. Khubayb remained with them as a captive. 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Iyad reported that the daughter of al-Harith told him that when they gathered, Khubayb borrowed a razor from her to shave himself, and she gave it to him. "My little son took hold of him while I was unaware, until he reached him," she said. "I found him seating him on his thigh with the razor in his hand. I was terrified, and a terror that Khubayb recognised in my face. He said: 'Do you fear that I will kill him? I would never do that.'" She said: "By God, I have never seen a captive better than Khubayb. By God, I once found him eating from a bunch of grapes in his hand, while he was bound with iron, and there was no fruit in Makkah." She used to say: "It was a provision that God, the Exalted, gave to Khubayb." When they took him out of the sacred precinct (haram) to kill him outside it, in the non-sacred area (hill), Khubayb said to them: "Let me pray two rak'ahs." They left him, and he prayed two rak'ahs, then said: "Had I not feared that you would think my heart was in dread of death, I would have prolonged them [[In (k): "to lengthen them".]]." Then he said: "O God, count them, kill them one by one, and leave none of them." Then he said:

"I do not care, when I am slain as a Muslim,
On which side I fall for God's sake.
That is for the sake of God, and if He wills,
He will bless the scattered limbs of a torn body."

The Banu al-Harith killed him. Khubayb was the one who established the two rak'ahs of prayer for every Muslim man who is killed in cold blood (sabran). On the day Asim was struck, Allah answered him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions were informed of the news of them and of what had befallen them.

Some of the disbelievers of Quraysh sent people to Asim when they heard that he had been killed, so that they could bring back something of him that they would recognise. He had killed one of their great men on the day of Badr. Allah sent upon Asim something like a cloud of hornets (al-dabr) [[al-dabr: wasps or drones of the bees.]], which protected him from their messengers, so they could not cut off any of his flesh.

Ibn Ishaq said about this story: The Hudhayl, when Asim ibn Thabit was killed, wanted his head so that they could sell it to Sulafa bint Sa'd ibn Shahid [[In (j) and (waw): al-Shahid.]]. She had vowed, when her two sons were struck down at Uhud, that if she could get hold of his head she would drink wine from his skull [[al-qahf: the skull.]]. The hornets prevented them. When it came between him and them, they said: "Leave him until evening, when it will have gone from him, and then we will take him." But Allah sent the valley, which carried Asim away, and he was gone. Asim had given Allah a covenant that he would never touch a polytheist and no polytheist would ever touch him during his life, so Allah protected him after his death from what he had refused in his life.

And from Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent him alone as a spy. He said: "I came to the cross of Khubayb and climbed up it, while I was fearful of the spies. I cut him down, and he fell to the ground. Then I plunged in and moved away a little, then I turned and it was as if the earth had swallowed him."

In another narration there is an addition: "Until this hour we have not mentioned any remains of Khubayb." Al-Bayhaqi related it.

The Eleventh: It is not denied that the guardian (wali) may have wealth and property with which he protects his honour [[From (j), (waw) and (kaf) and (waw). This is more likely.]] and his dependants. And it is enough for you to consider the Companions and their wealth, together with their guardianship (wilaya) and their merit, and they are the proof against others.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "While a man was in a barren land, he heard a voice in a cloud saying: 'Water the garden of so-and-so.' That cloud moved aside and poured its water onto a stony ground (harra), and there was a watercourse (shirja) among those watercourses which had absorbed all that water. He followed the water, and there was a man standing in his garden, diverting the water with his spade [[al-misha: the iron hoe.]]. He said: 'O servant of Allah, what is your name?' He said: 'So-and-so,' the name he had heard in the cloud. He said to him: 'O servant of Allah, why do you ask me my name?' He said: 'I heard a voice in the cloud whose water this is, saying: "Water the garden of so-and-so," using your name. What do you do with it?' He said: 'As you have said this, I look at what comes out of it, and I give a third of it in charity, and I and my dependants eat a third, and I return a third of it to it.'" In another narration: "And I put a third of it toward the poor, the beggars and the wayfarer."

I say: This hadith is not contradicted by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not take up property (day'a) lest you incline to the world." Al-Tirmidhi related it from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud and said of it: "It is a good hadith." For it is to be understood as applying to one who takes it in order to accumulate and to enjoy and indulge in its splendour. As for one who takes it as a livelihood, by which he protects his religion and his dependants, then taking it with this intention is among the best of deeds, and it is among the best of wealth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How excellent is good wealth for a righteous man."

People have said much about the miracles (karamat) of the saints, and what we have mentioned about it is sufficient. And Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

The Twelfth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had you wished, you could have taken a fee for it﴾. In it is evidence for the validity of the permissibility of hiring (ijara) [[ijara: a contract of hire or wage.]], and it is the practice (sunna) of the prophets and the saints, as will come its explanation in the surah "al-Qasas" [[See vol. 13, p. 267.]], if Allah wills.

The majority read "la-ittakhadhta" (with the ta' of the first person), while Abu Amr read "la-ttakhidhta," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatada. The two are dialectal forms with one meaning from taking, like your saying "taba'a" and "ittaba'a," and "taqa" and "ittaqa." Some readers assimilated the dhal into the ta' (idgham), and some did not assimilate it.

In the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "If you had wished, you would have been given a wage." This question came from Musa as a request for explanation (ard), not as an objection (i'tiraḍ). At that point al-Khadir said to him: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾, in accordance with the condition you set on yourself. His repeating "between me and you," and his departing from "between us," is for the sake of emphasis. Sibawayh said: "Just as one says, 'May Allah disgrace the liar from me and from you,' meaning from us."

Ibn Abbas said: Musa's saying about the ship and the boy was for Allah, while his saying about the wall was for himself, seeking something of worldly gain, and so it was the cause of the parting. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: That wall was a wall whose height in the sky was a hundred cubits.

The Thirteenth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will inform you of the ta'wil of that about which you could not have patience﴾. The ta'wil of a thing is its outcome (ma'al), that is, he said to him: "I will tell you why I did what I did." It has been said, in explaining these verses which occurred between Musa and al-Khadir, that they were a proof against Musa and not a marvel for him. That is because when he denied the matter of the breaking of the ship, it was said to him: "O Musa, where was this planning of yours while you were a castaway in the chest upon the sea?" When he denied the matter of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is this denial of yours from your striking the Copt and your judgement against him?" When he denied the setting up of the wall, it was said to him: "Where is this from your lifting the stone of the well for the daughters of Shu'ayb without a wage?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 79–82 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾. From this verse, those who say that the miskin (the destitute) is in a better condition than the faqir (the poor) derive their evidence. This meaning has already been discussed in full in Surah Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 168 onwards.]]. It has also been said that they were merchants, but because they were travelling in the depths of a sea, in a state of peril (qilla [[In manuscripts j, k and y: that is, on the verge of destruction or in fear. In the first printed edition it is qilla, which is not correct.]]) and in a state of weakness to repel a calamity, they were described as miskin, since they were in a condition that caused pity for them. This is like when you say of a wealthy man who has fallen into a dread or a calamity: "Miskin!" Ka'b and others said: it belonged to ten brothers who were miskin; they had inherited it from their father, five of them were disabled and five worked on the sea. It was also said: they were seven, each of whom had a disability different from the others. Al-Naqqash mentioned their names. As for those who worked, one of them was leprous, the second was one-eyed, the third was lame, the fourth had a hernia (adar), and the fifth had a fever that never left him all his life, and he was the youngest of them. The five who could not work were: blind, deaf, mute, paralysed, and insane. The sea in which they worked lay between Persia and Byzantium, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi. A group read: "limassakin" with a doubled sin, and regarding this it was said: they were the sailors of the boat, because the mass­ak is the one who holds the rudder of the boat, and all the servants are suitable for holding it, so all of them were called massakin. Another group said: by the massakin he meant the tanners of hides (dabaghat al-musuk), and the musuk are hides, whose singular is mask. The more evident reading is "masakin" with a single sin, the plural of miskin, and its meaning is: the boat belonged to weak people, for whom compassion should be felt. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so I desired to damage it﴾. That is, to make it defective. One says: "I made the thing defective (ʿibtu al-shay'a), so it became defective (ʿāb), when it became faulty; it is then maʿīb and ʿāʾib." His saying: (and behind them was a king who seized every boat by force). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr read: (ṣaḥīḥa, sound), and Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan also read (ṣāliḥa, good). The original meaning of (warā') is "behind," and some exegetes said: he was behind them, and their return was past him. But most hold that the meaning of (warā') here is "in front of," supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr: "and there was in front of them a king who seized every sound boat by force." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "warāahum" according to me retains its proper sense, because these expressions are used with regard to time: the event that comes first and exists is "in front," and what comes after it is "behind," which is what is left behind. This is contrary to what appears at first glance. Examine these expressions in their places where they occur and you will find them consistent. So the meaning of this verse is: these people, their work and their effort, will be followed in time by the seizure of this king. Whoever reads "amamahum" means in place, i.e., as if they were travelling to a town. The saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "The prayer is in front of you" [[The hadith concerns combining Maghrib and ʿIsha at Muzdalifa.]] means in place; otherwise their being at that time was in front of the prayer in time. Consider this statement, for it relieves the confusion of these expressions. In Tabari's book, Qatada's reading is "wa-kana warahum malik," and Qatada said: "amamahum" (in front of them). Do you not see that He says: "from behind them is Jahannam" [45:10], while it lies before them? This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic speech that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to complain of, as Zajjaj said. I say: this imam's choice was anticipated in this by Ibn ʿArafa. Al-Harawi said: Ibn ʿArafa said: someone will say, how did He say "min warā'ihi" when it is "amamahu"? Abu ʿUbayd and Abu ʿAli Qutrub claimed that this is one of the words with contrary meanings (adhdad), and that warā' means qudam (in front). This is not well grounded, because amam is the opposite of warā'; this usage is only appropriate with regard to places and times, as when you say to a man who promised something in Rajab for Ramadan and then said: "and behind you is Sha'ban," it would be permissible though it is in front of him, because it follows him up to the time of his promise. Al-Qushayri also pointed to this view and said: this is said only of times, and one does not say to a man "amamaka" that it is "warāka." Al-Farra' said: others permitted it. The people did not know of the king's affair, so Allah informed al-Khidr so that he damaged the boat, as mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Al-Mawardi said: the grammarians differed about the use of warā' in place of amam in three views. First: it is permissible to use it in every case and in every place, and it is among the contrary-meaning words; Allah says: ﴿from behind them is Jahannam﴾ [45:10], meaning in front of them. The poet said: [[It is Sawwar ibn al-Mudrib.]]
"Do the sons of Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people, Tamim, and the wilderness are behind me?"
meaning in front of me. Second: warā' is used in place of amam only with respect to times and periods, because a person may pass them, so they become behind him, and it is not used otherwise. Third: it is permissible with bodies that have no front, such as two facing stones, each of which is behind the other, and it is not permissible with other things. This is the view of ʿAli ibn ʿIsa. The name of this king has been disputed: it was said Hudad ibn Budad; it was said al-Jalandi, which is what al-Suhayli said. Al-Bukhari mentioned the name of the king who seized every boat by force, saying: he is [Hudad ibn Budad, and the boy who was killed] named Jaysur; this is how we have vowelled it in the (Jami') from the narration of Yazid al-Marwazi, while in other narrations it is Hayswar with a ḥa', and in my margin of the book there is a third narration: Haysun. He used to seize every good boat by force, therefore al-Khidr found fault with it and damaged it. In this there is jurisprudence of acting upon public interest when its benefit is clearly established, and the permissibility of preserving the whole of property by damaging a part of it, which has already been discussed. In Sahih Muslim is the wisdom of damaging the boat, namely his saying: "When the one who commandeers it comes and finds it damaged, he will pass it by; they then repaired it with a plank," and so on. From this is derived an exhortation to patience in hardships, for how many benefits are contained within that disliked matter. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾ [2:216].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers﴾ [18:80]. It came in sound hadith: "He was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever," and the apparent meaning supports that he was not yet mature, though it may be a report about him while he was mature, as has already been mentioned. [This meaning [[From j, k and y.]]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so we feared that he would overburden them﴾ [18:80]. It has been said: this is from the words of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and it is what the context of the speech indicates; this is the view of many exegetes, meaning: we feared that he would overburden them ﴿with rebellion and disbelief﴾ [18:80]. Allah had permitted him to exercise independent judgement regarding the killing of souls in this respect. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, exalted is He, and it is by this that al-Khidr expressed himself. Tabari said: its meaning is "so We knew," and Ibn ʿAbbas likewise said: that is, "so We knew." This is like how knowledge is referred to by fear in His saying: ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah﴾ [2:229]. It is reported that Ubayy read: "so your Lord knew." It was also said: fear here means dislike, as one says: "I separated them, fearing that they would fight," meaning, disliking that. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the more evident interpretation in my view, though the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor, meaning according to the assumption of the created beings and the addressees: had they known his state, fear of the overburdening of the parents would have arisen in them. Ibn Mas'ud read: "so your Lord feared," and this is clear as a metaphor. This is similar to what occurs in the Qur'an regarding Allah, exalted is He, of "perhaps," "it may be," and "that"; all of this, with its expectation, apprehension and fear, is only in accordance with your reckoning, O addressees. And ﴿overburden them﴾ means to impose upon them and burden them; the meaning is that his love might cast them into following him, so that they would go astray and adopt his religion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so We desired that their Lord should replace them﴾. The majority read with a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the dal; ʿAsim read with a sukun on the ba' and a light dal, meaning: that Allah should grant them a child.

(better than him in purity) that is, in religion and righteousness. It is said: badala and abdala, like mahhala and amhala, and nazzala and anzala.

(and nearer in kinship) Ibn ʿAbbas read "ruhuman" with a ḍamma. The poet said:
"How can there be oppression against a girl, when gentleness and kinship (ruhum) are in her?"
The rest read it with a sukun. From this is the saying of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj:
"O you who sent down kinship (ruhm) upon Idris, and sent down the curse upon Iblis."
There is variation from Abu ʿAmr. "Ruhman" is coordinated with "zakatan," meaning mercy; one says: "rahimahu rahmatan wa ruhman," and its feminine marker is for the feminine, while its masculine is ruhm. It has also been said that ruhm here means rahim (womb); Ibn ʿAbbas read it: "wa-awsala ruhman," meaning rahiman (near in womb). He also read "azka minhu." It is reported from Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj that they were replaced with a girl. Al-Kalbi said: a prophet among the prophets married her, and she bore him a prophet, through whom Allah guided a nation among the nations. Qatada said: she bore twelve prophets. It is also reported from Ibn Jurayj that the mother of the boy, on the day he was killed, was pregnant with a Muslim boy, while the one killed was a disbeliever. From Ibn ʿAbbas: she bore a girl who bore a prophet; in another narration: Allah replaced him for them with a girl who bore seventy prophets. Ja'far ibn Muhammad said this on the authority of his father. Our scholars said: this is far-fetched, and the multitude of prophets is only known among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not among them. From this verse is derived the easing of calamities by the loss of children, even if they are pieces of the liver; and whoever submits to the decree, his outcome will reveal the white hand. Qatada said: his parents rejoiced at his birth and grieved over him when he was killed, and had he lived, their ruin would have been in him. So it is obligatory upon everyone to be content with Allah's decree, for Allah's decree for the believer in what he dislikes is better for him than His decree for him in what he loves.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two boys﴾. These two boys were young, as indicated by describing them as orphans. Their names were Asram and Sarim [[In j, k and y: Asyram.]]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "There is no orphanhood after puberty." This is the apparent meaning. It may also be that the name of orphanhood remains upon them after puberty, if they were orphans, in the sense of compassion for them. It has already been noted [[See vol. 2, p. 14.]] that orphanhood among people is from the loss of the father, and among other animals from the loss of the mother. His saying, "in the town," indicates that a village is called a town (madina), and from this is the hadith: "I have been commanded to go to a town that devours the villages" [[The town is the city of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; its devouring the villages means what is opened by the hands of its people from the cities, and they take from their spoils.]], and in the hadith of the emigration: "To whom do you belong?" The man said: "From the people of the town," meaning Mecca.

The Qur'anic verse: "And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them both" (18:82). People differed about the treasure. ʿIkrima and Qatada said it was great wealth, and this is the plain meaning of the word *kanz* (treasure), since in the language it means accumulated wealth. The discussion of this has already passed [[See vol. 8, p. 123.]]. Ibn ʿAbbas said it was knowledge in buried pages. He also said: it was a tablet of gold on which was written, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. I am amazed at the one who believes in destiny, how he can grieve. I am amazed at the one who believes in provision, how he can toil. I am amazed at the one who believes in death, how he can rejoice. I am amazed at the one who believes in reckoning, how he can be heedless. I am amazed at the one who believes in this world and its turning with its people, how he can feel secure in it. There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Something similar is narrated from ʿIkrima and from ʿUmar, the client of Ghufra. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The Qur'anic verse: "And their father was righteous" (18:82). The apparent meaning of the words, and what comes first to mind, is that he was their immediate father. It was said that he was their seventh forefather, as Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said. It was said that he was their tenth forefather, and that they were protected because of him even though he is not mentioned as righteous. He was called Kashih. This was said by Muqatil. The name of their mother was Dunya [[In Ruh al-Maʿani: Dahna.]], as mentioned by al-Naqqash [[In (ى): al-Nahhas.]]. In this there is evidence that Allah, exalted is He, protects the righteous man in himself and in his offspring, even if they are far removed from him. It has been narrated that Allah, exalted is He, protects the righteous man for seven generations of his descendants [[In the margin of (ج): dhawih (his kin).]]. The verse "Indeed my guardian is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He takes charge of the righteous" (7:196) also points to this [[See vol. 7, p. 342.]].

The Qur'anic verse: "And I did not do it of my own accord" (18:82). This implies that al-Khidr was a prophet, and the disagreement about this has already passed.

"That is the interpretation" (18:82): that is, the explanation.

"Of that which you could not bear with patience" (18:82). A group recited *tastatiʿ* (with the second letter *ta'*, "you could bear"). The majority recited *tasti'* (without that *ta'*). Abu Hatim said: "This is how we recite it, as it is written in the Mushaf."

Here there are five issues.

The first. If someone says: no mention of Musa's servant (fata) is made in the beginning of the verse or at its end. It is answered: this has been disputed. ʿIkrima said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "Musa's servant is not mentioned, though he was with him?" He said: "The young man drank from the water and became immortal. The Learned One (al-ʿalim) took him, and wrapped a boat around him, and then released him into the sea. It still moves with him in it until the Day of Resurrection. This was because he was not permitted to drink from it, but he drank from it."

Al-Qushayri said: "If this is established, then the servant is not Yusha ibn Nun, for Yusha ibn Nun lived long after Musa and was his successor. It is more likely that Musa dismissed his servant when he met al-Khidr."

Our shaykh, the Imam Abu al-ʿAbbas, said: "It may be that mention of the one followed was sufficient without mentioning the follower. And Allah knows best."

The second. If someone says: how did al-Khidr attribute the story of extracting the boys' treasure to Allah, exalted is He, while in the matter of breaking the boat he said, "So I wanted to damage it" (18:79), attributing the damage to himself?

It is answered: He attributed the wanting in the wall to Allah, exalted is He, because it concerned a new matter, over a long time, a hidden matter among the unseen. So it was fitting to single out this place for mention of Allah, exalted is He. Even if al-Khidr willed it, what Allah informed him was that Allah would will it.

It was also said: since all of that was good, he attributed it to Allah, exalted is He, and he attributed the damage to the boat to himself, out of respect for good manners, because the word was "damage" (ʿayb). So he observed courtesy by attributing the wanting in it only to himself. This is like Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when he said, "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me" (26:80) [[See vol. 13, p. 110.]]. He attributed the act to Allah, exalted is He, both before and after, and he attributed the illness to himself, since it signifies deficiency and affliction. So among the expressions attributed to Allah, exalted is He, only the praiseworthy ones are used, not the blameworthy. This is as He said, "In Your hand is the good" (3:26) [[See vol. 4, p. 55.]], and He confined it to this, so evil was not attributed to Him, though in His hand is good and evil, harm and benefit, for He is over all things powerful, and He is All-Aware of all things.

There is no objection to what he (peace be upon him) related from his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, that He will say on the Day of Resurrection: "O son of Adam, I was ill and you did not visit Me; I asked you for food and you did not feed Me; I asked you for drink and you did not give Me to drink." That is a condescension in address and a gentleness in reproach, whose purpose is to make known the excellence of the Possessor of Majesty and the measures of reward for these deeds. This meaning has already passed.

And Allah, exalted is He, knows best. It is for Allah, exalted is He, to name Himself as He wills, and we name Him only with what He has permitted us of beautiful attributes and noble actions. He is exalted above deficiencies and calamities, exalted to a great degree.

About the young man He said, "So We wanted" (18:80). It is as if He attributed the killing to Himself and the replacement to Allah, exalted is He.

"Maturity" (ashudd) means the completeness of physical form and intellect. The discussion of it has already passed in *al-Anʿam* [[See vol. 7, p. 134 onward.]], and praise be to Allah.

The third. Our shaykh, the Imam Abu al-ʿAbbas, said: Some people from the Batiniyya heretics (zanadiqa) went on a path that entails the abandonment of these legal rulings. They said: "These general legal rulings are applied only to prophets and to the common people. As for the saints (awliya') and the people of special knowledge, they do not need those texts. Rather, what falls into their hearts is added to them, and they are judged by what dominates their thoughts."

They said: "That is because their hearts are purified of turbidity and empty of foreign things, so the divine sciences and the Lordly realities are disclosed to them. They come to know the secrets of existence and know the rulings of particulars, so they dispense with the universal rulings of the sacred law, just as happened to al-Khidr, for he was content with the knowledge that was revealed to him, instead of the understandings that Musa had."

And it has come in what they report: "Consult your heart, even if the jurists have issued fatwas to you."

Our shaykh (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "This statement is heresy (zandaqa) and unbelief. Its speaker is to be killed and is not to be asked to repent, because it denies what is known from the sacred law. Allah, exalted is He, has established His custom and executed His wisdom that His rulings are known only through His messengers, His envoys between Him and His creation. They are those who convey His message and His word, and who make clear His laws and rulings. He chose them for this and singled them out with it, as He said: 'Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing' (22:75). And He said: 'Allah knows best where to place His message' (6:124) [[This is the recitation of Nafiʿ, which the commentator used to recite. See vol. 7, p. 79.]]. And He said: 'Mankind was one community, then Allah sent prophets as bearers of good news and as warners' (2:213) [[See vol. 3, p. 30.]]. And other verses besides these."

In sum, definite knowledge and necessary certainty have been reached, and the consensus of the earlier and later generations, that there is no way to know the rulings of Allah, exalted is He, which return to His command and prohibition, and none of them is known except through the messengers. Whoever says that there is another way by which His command and prohibition are known, apart from the messengers, so that one can dispense with the messengers, is an unbeliever to be killed, not asked to repent, and with whom there is no need for questions or answers. Moreover, this statement affirms prophets after our Prophet (peace be upon him), whom Allah made the Seal of His prophets and messengers, so there is no prophet after him and no messenger.

The explanation of this: whoever says that he takes from his heart, and that what falls into it [is] [[From (ج) (ك) (ى).]] the ruling of Allah, exalted is He, and that he acts according to its requirement, and that he needs no Book and no Sunna along with it, has thereby claimed for himself the special status of prophethood. This is similar to what [the Messenger of Allah [[From (ج) (ك) (ى).]]] (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed the Holy Spirit breathed into my heart..." and the hadith continues.

The fourth. The majority of people hold that al-Khidr has died (peace be upon him).

A group said: he is alive, because he drank from the Spring of Life, and he remains on the earth, and he performs the Hajj to the House.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "Al-Naqqash has elaborated greatly on this meaning and mentioned in his book many things from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) and others, but none of them stands on a leg (i.e., none is sound)."

"If al-Khidr (peace be upon him) were alive and performing the Hajj, he would have been manifest in the religion of Islam. Allah, who knows the details of things, is the Lord, and there is no lord besides Him."

From what decides that al-Khidr (peace be upon him) is dead now is his saying (peace be upon him): "Do you see this night of yours? No one who is upon the face of the earth today will remain." [[The hadith is as it stands in the originals; its authentication follows below.]]

I say: al-Bukhari adopted this view, and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi chose it. The correct view is the second, that he is alive, as we will mention.

This hadith was also transmitted by Muslim in his Sahih from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in the night prayer of ʿIsha one night, at the end of his life. When he finished the greeting, he stood and said: 'Do you see this night of yours? At the end of a hundred years from it, no one who is upon the face of the earth will remain.'" Ibn ʿUmar said: "The people erred (wahala) regarding the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning those narrations that people discuss, about a hundred years. Rather, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one who is upon the face of the earth today will remain.' He meant by that that this generation would come to an end." [[Wahala ila al-shay' means he erred and his thoughts went in a direction contrary to the correct one. The meaning is that the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) erred and their thoughts went in a direction contrary to the correct one in interpreting the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ). So some of them said: "The Hour will come at the end of a hundred years." Ibn ʿUmar clarified the Prophet's meaning, saying: "He meant that this generation would come to an end." It may also be pronounced wahila, like taʿiba.]]

And he also narrated it from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say a month before he died: 'You ask me about the Hour, and its knowledge is only with Allah. I swear by Allah that there is no living soul upon the earth that a hundred years will pass over.'" In another version, Salim said: "We discussed that it [the Hour] is created on that day." In another: "No living soul today, a hundred years will pass over it while it is alive on that day." ʿAbd al-Rahman, the man in charge of the water-supply (sahib al-siqaya), explained it, saying: "It is the reduction of the lifespan." Something similar to this hadith is also narrated from Abu Said al-Khudri.

Our scholars said: the essential content of this hadith is that he (peace be upon him) informed, a month before his death, that everyone among the children of Adam then existing would not have a lifespan exceeding a hundred years, because of his saying (peace be upon him): "No living soul..." This wording does not include the angels or the jinn, since it is not established that they are of this kind, nor does it include non-rational animals, because of his saying: "Of those who are upon the face of the earth, no one." This is applied in its original usage to those who have intellect. So it is determined that the intended meaning is the children of Adam.

Ibn ʿUmar himself clarified this meaning, saying: "He meant by that that this generation would come to an end."

There is no proof for those who cite this hadith to refute the view of those who say that al-Khidr is alive, by the generality of his statement:

(مَا مِنْ نَفْسٍ مَنْفُوسَةٍ) Because a general expression, though it emphasizes comprehensiveness ('umum), is not explicit in covering everything. Rather, it is open to specification (takhsis).

Just as it does not include ʿIsa (peace be upon him), who did not die and was not killed, and is alive by the text and meaning of the Qur'an, it also does not include the Dajjal, even though he is alive, based on the hadith of al-Jassasa [[al-Jassasa: the beast of the earth that emerges at the end of time, and was named al-Jassasa because it spies on news for the Dajjal.]]. Likewise, it does not include al-Khidr (peace be upon him), who is not visible to people and does not mix with them such that he comes to mind when people address one another. Such a general expression does not encompass a figure like this.

It has been said:
The Companions of the Cave are alive and will perform the Hajj with ʿIsa (peace and blessings be upon him), as has already been mentioned.

Likewise, Musa's young companion (fata), according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, as we have mentioned.

Abu Ishaq al-Thaʿlabi mentioned in his book (al-ʿAraʾis):
The correct view is that al-Khidr [[In J and K: "and al-Khidr according to all the views."]] is a prophet who lives a long life, veiled from sight. Muhammad ibn al-Mutawakkil narrated from [Dhamrah ibn Rabiʿah] from ʿAbd Allah ibn [Shawdhab [[The addition and correction are from (ʿIqd al-Jumanʾ) of al-ʿAyni, quoting al-Thaʿlabi.
In J, K and Ya: Muhammad ibn al-Mutawakkil narrated from Dhamrah from ʿAbd Allah ibn Sawwar.]]] who said:
Al-Khidr (peace be upon him) is of the descendants of Persia, and Ilyas is of the Children of Israel. The two meet each year at the Hajj season.

And from ʿAmr ibn Dinar, who said:
Al-Khidr and Ilyas will continue to be alive on the earth as long as the Qur'an is on the earth. When it is lifted, they will both die.

Our shaykh, the Imam Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Muʿti ibn Mahmud ibn ʿAbd al-Muʿti al-Lakhmi, mentioned in his commentary on al-Qushayri's Risala many accounts from a group of righteous men and women that they saw al-Khidr (peace be upon him) and met him. Taken together, these reports produce a strong presumption of his being alive, along with what al-Naqqash, al-Thaʿlabi and others have mentioned.

It has come in Sahih Muslim:
(The Dajjal will reach some of the salt flats (sibakh) that lie next to Madinah, and on that day a man who is the best of people, or one of the best of people, will go out to him) — the hadith... At its end, Abu Ishaq said:
That is, it is said that this man is al-Khidr.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned in his book (al-Hawatif) [the unseen callers]:
With a chain that traces it back [In K: "that stops at"; in J: "that stops at"] to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he met al-Khidr, who taught him this supplication, and he mentioned that in it there is great reward, forgiveness and mercy for whoever says it after every prayer. It is:
O You whom hearing one thing does not distract from another, O You whom questions do not confuse, O You who are not wearied by the insistence of those who insist, make me taste the coolness of Your pardon and the sweetness of Your forgiveness.

He also mentioned, regarding this very supplication, something similar to what was reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning his hearing it from al-Khidr, transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

He also mentioned the meeting of Ilyas with the Prophet (peace be upon him).

If Ilyas's survival until the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) is permissible, then al-Khidr's survival is permissible. It is also mentioned that the two meet at the House (the Kaʿbah) every year, and that when they part they say:
(Whatever Allah wills, whatever Allah wills. None turns away evil except Allah. Whatever blessing there is, it is from Allah. Whatever Allah wills, whatever Allah wills. I put my trust in Allah. Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian.)

As for the report about Ilyas, it will come in (al-Saffat) [see vol. 15, p. 115], if Allah wills.

Abu ʿUmar Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned in his book (al-Tamhid), from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:
When the Prophet (ﷺ) died and was covered with a cloth, a hatif (unseen caller) called out from the direction of the house. They heard his voice but did not see his person:
Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings, peace be upon you, people of the house. ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Al ʿImran: 185] — and so on. Indeed, in Allah there is a successor from every one who perishes, a replacement for every thing lost, and consolation for every calamity. So place your trust in Allah, and hope in Him alone, for the afflicted one is he who is deprived of reward.

They used to think that this was al-Khidr (peace be upon him).

That is, the Companions of the Prophet (peace be upon him).

The alif and lam in His saying (ʿala al-ard, "upon the earth") is for a specific reference (ʿahd), not for the whole category (jins), and it refers to the land of the Arabs, as evidenced by their dealings in it and their frequent coming and going in it, rather than the land of Yajuj and Majuj, and the far regions of India and Sind, whose names do not strike the ear and whose knowledge is not known.

And there is no answer concerning the Dajjal.

Al-Suhayli said:
The name of al-Khidr has been disputed in widely differing ways. From Ibn Munabbih, he said:
Ilya ibn Malkan ibn Faligh ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

It has also been said:
He is the son of ʿAmil ibn Samaqhin ibn Arya ibn ʿAlqama ibn ʿIsu ibn Ishaq, and that his father was a king, and that his mother was the daughter of Persia, named Alma, and that she gave birth to him in a cave, and that a sheep was found there that nursed him every day from the flock of a man from the village. The man took him and raised him. When he grew up, his father, the king, sought a scribe and gathered people of knowledge and nobility to write the scrolls that had been revealed to Ibrahim and Shith. Among those who came forward as scribes was his son al-Khidr, though he did not recognize him. When he admired his handwriting and his knowledge, and inquired into his circumstances, he came to know that he was his son [In J: "he came to know his name"]. So he took him into his own care [In K: "into himself"] and put him in charge of the affairs of the people. Then al-Khidr fled from the king for reasons whose account would be long, until he found the Spring of Life and drank from it. So he is alive until the Dajjal comes out, and he is the man whom the Dajjal will kill, cut into pieces, and then Allah will bring him back to life.

It has also been said:
He did not live to see the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), but this is not sound.

Al-Bukhari and a group of the people of hadith, among them our shaykh Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
He died before the end of the hundred years, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): (At the end of a hundred years, no one who is upon this earth now will remain upon it.) That is, whoever was alive when this statement was made.

I say: We have already mentioned this hadith and the discussion around it, and we have demonstrated al-Khidr's life up to now, and Allah knows best.

The Fifth Matter: It has been said that when al-Khidr went to part from Musa, Musa said to him: "Advise me." He said: "Be cheerful but do not be a constant laugher, leave off contentiousness, do not walk for no need, do not reproach sinners for their sins, and weep over your own sin, O son of ʿImran."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 79–82 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾. From this verse, those who say that the miskin (the destitute) is in a better condition than the faqir (the poor) derive their evidence. This meaning has already been discussed in full in Surah Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 168 onwards.]]. It has also been said that they were merchants, but because they were travelling in the depths of a sea, in a state of peril (qilla [[In manuscripts j, k and y: that is, on the verge of destruction or in fear. In the first printed edition it is qilla, which is not correct.]]) and in a state of weakness to repel a calamity, they were described as miskin, since they were in a condition that caused pity for them. This is like when you say of a wealthy man who has fallen into a dread or a calamity: "Miskin!" Ka'b and others said: it belonged to ten brothers who were miskin; they had inherited it from their father, five of them were disabled and five worked on the sea. It was also said: they were seven, each of whom had a disability different from the others. Al-Naqqash mentioned their names. As for those who worked, one of them was leprous, the second was one-eyed, the third was lame, the fourth had a hernia (adar), and the fifth had a fever that never left him all his life, and he was the youngest of them. The five who could not work were: blind, deaf, mute, paralysed, and insane. The sea in which they worked lay between Persia and Byzantium, as mentioned by al-Tha'labi. A group read: "limassakin" with a doubled sin, and regarding this it was said: they were the sailors of the boat, because the mass­ak is the one who holds the rudder of the boat, and all the servants are suitable for holding it, so all of them were called massakin. Another group said: by the massakin he meant the tanners of hides (dabaghat al-musuk), and the musuk are hides, whose singular is mask. The more evident reading is "masakin" with a single sin, the plural of miskin, and its meaning is: the boat belonged to weak people, for whom compassion should be felt. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so I desired to damage it﴾. That is, to make it defective. One says: "I made the thing defective (ʿibtu al-shay'a), so it became defective (ʿāb), when it became faulty; it is then maʿīb and ʿāʾib." His saying: (and behind them was a king who seized every boat by force). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr read: (ṣaḥīḥa, sound), and Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan also read (ṣāliḥa, good). The original meaning of (warā') is "behind," and some exegetes said: he was behind them, and their return was past him. But most hold that the meaning of (warā') here is "in front of," supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr: "and there was in front of them a king who seized every sound boat by force." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "warāahum" according to me retains its proper sense, because these expressions are used with regard to time: the event that comes first and exists is "in front," and what comes after it is "behind," which is what is left behind. This is contrary to what appears at first glance. Examine these expressions in their places where they occur and you will find them consistent. So the meaning of this verse is: these people, their work and their effort, will be followed in time by the seizure of this king. Whoever reads "amamahum" means in place, i.e., as if they were travelling to a town. The saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "The prayer is in front of you" [[The hadith concerns combining Maghrib and ʿIsha at Muzdalifa.]] means in place; otherwise their being at that time was in front of the prayer in time. Consider this statement, for it relieves the confusion of these expressions. In Tabari's book, Qatada's reading is "wa-kana warahum malik," and Qatada said: "amamahum" (in front of them). Do you not see that He says: "from behind them is Jahannam" [45:10], while it lies before them? This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic speech that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to complain of, as Zajjaj said. I say: this imam's choice was anticipated in this by Ibn ʿArafa. Al-Harawi said: Ibn ʿArafa said: someone will say, how did He say "min warā'ihi" when it is "amamahu"? Abu ʿUbayd and Abu ʿAli Qutrub claimed that this is one of the words with contrary meanings (adhdad), and that warā' means qudam (in front). This is not well grounded, because amam is the opposite of warā'; this usage is only appropriate with regard to places and times, as when you say to a man who promised something in Rajab for Ramadan and then said: "and behind you is Sha'ban," it would be permissible though it is in front of him, because it follows him up to the time of his promise. Al-Qushayri also pointed to this view and said: this is said only of times, and one does not say to a man "amamaka" that it is "warāka." Al-Farra' said: others permitted it. The people did not know of the king's affair, so Allah informed al-Khidr so that he damaged the boat, as mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Al-Mawardi said: the grammarians differed about the use of warā' in place of amam in three views. First: it is permissible to use it in every case and in every place, and it is among the contrary-meaning words; Allah says: ﴿from behind them is Jahannam﴾ [45:10], meaning in front of them. The poet said: [[It is Sawwar ibn al-Mudrib.]]
"Do the sons of Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people, Tamim, and the wilderness are behind me?"
meaning in front of me. Second: warā' is used in place of amam only with respect to times and periods, because a person may pass them, so they become behind him, and it is not used otherwise. Third: it is permissible with bodies that have no front, such as two facing stones, each of which is behind the other, and it is not permissible with other things. This is the view of ʿAli ibn ʿIsa. The name of this king has been disputed: it was said Hudad ibn Budad; it was said al-Jalandi, which is what al-Suhayli said. Al-Bukhari mentioned the name of the king who seized every boat by force, saying: he is [Hudad ibn Budad, and the boy who was killed] named Jaysur; this is how we have vowelled it in the (Jami') from the narration of Yazid al-Marwazi, while in other narrations it is Hayswar with a ḥa', and in my margin of the book there is a third narration: Haysun. He used to seize every good boat by force, therefore al-Khidr found fault with it and damaged it. In this there is jurisprudence of acting upon public interest when its benefit is clearly established, and the permissibility of preserving the whole of property by damaging a part of it, which has already been discussed. In Sahih Muslim is the wisdom of damaging the boat, namely his saying: "When the one who commandeers it comes and finds it damaged, he will pass it by; they then repaired it with a plank," and so on. From this is derived an exhortation to patience in hardships, for how many benefits are contained within that disliked matter. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾ [2:216].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers﴾ [18:80]. It came in sound hadith: "He was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever," and the apparent meaning supports that he was not yet mature, though it may be a report about him while he was mature, as has already been mentioned. [This meaning [[From j, k and y.]]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so we feared that he would overburden them﴾ [18:80]. It has been said: this is from the words of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and it is what the context of the speech indicates; this is the view of many exegetes, meaning: we feared that he would overburden them ﴿with rebellion and disbelief﴾ [18:80]. Allah had permitted him to exercise independent judgement regarding the killing of souls in this respect. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, exalted is He, and it is by this that al-Khidr expressed himself. Tabari said: its meaning is "so We knew," and Ibn ʿAbbas likewise said: that is, "so We knew." This is like how knowledge is referred to by fear in His saying: ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah﴾ [2:229]. It is reported that Ubayy read: "so your Lord knew." It was also said: fear here means dislike, as one says: "I separated them, fearing that they would fight," meaning, disliking that. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the more evident interpretation in my view, though the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor, meaning according to the assumption of the created beings and the addressees: had they known his state, fear of the overburdening of the parents would have arisen in them. Ibn Mas'ud read: "so your Lord feared," and this is clear as a metaphor. This is similar to what occurs in the Qur'an regarding Allah, exalted is He, of "perhaps," "it may be," and "that"; all of this, with its expectation, apprehension and fear, is only in accordance with your reckoning, O addressees. And ﴿overburden them﴾ means to impose upon them and burden them; the meaning is that his love might cast them into following him, so that they would go astray and adopt his religion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so We desired that their Lord should replace them﴾. The majority read with a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the dal; ʿAsim read with a sukun on the ba' and a light dal, meaning: that Allah should grant them a child.

(better than him in purity) that is, in religion and righteousness. It is said: badala and abdala, like mahhala and amhala, and nazzala and anzala.

(and nearer in kinship) Ibn ʿAbbas read "ruhuman" with a ḍamma. The poet said:
"How can there be oppression against a girl, when gentleness and kinship (ruhum) are in her?"
The rest read it with a sukun. From this is the saying of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj:
"O you who sent down kinship (ruhm) upon Idris, and sent down the curse upon Iblis."
There is variation from Abu ʿAmr. "Ruhman" is coordinated with "zakatan," meaning mercy; one says: "rahimahu rahmatan wa ruhman," and its feminine marker is for the feminine, while its masculine is ruhm. It has also been said that ruhm here means rahim (womb); Ibn ʿAbbas read it: "wa-awsala ruhman," meaning rahiman (near in womb). He also read "azka minhu." It is reported from Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj that they were replaced with a girl. Al-Kalbi said: a prophet among the prophets married her, and she bore him a prophet, through whom Allah guided a nation among the nations. Qatada said: she bore twelve prophets. It is also reported from Ibn Jurayj that the mother of the boy, on the day he was killed, was pregnant with a Muslim boy, while the one killed was a disbeliever. From Ibn ʿAbbas: she bore a girl who bore a prophet; in another narration: Allah replaced him for them with a girl who bore seventy prophets. Ja'far ibn Muhammad said this on the authority of his father. Our scholars said: this is far-fetched, and the multitude of prophets is only known among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not among them. From this verse is derived the easing of calamities by the loss of children, even if they are pieces of the liver; and whoever submits to the decree, his outcome will reveal the white hand. Qatada said: his parents rejoiced at his birth and grieved over him when he was killed, and had he lived, their ruin would have been in him. So it is obligatory upon everyone to be content with Allah's decree, for Allah's decree for the believer in what he dislikes is better for him than His decree for him in what he loves.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two boys﴾. These two boys were young, as indicated by describing them as orphans. Their names were Asram and Sarim [[In j, k and y: Asyram.]]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "There is no orphanhood after puberty." This is the apparent meaning. It may also be that the name of orphanhood remains upon them after puberty, if they were orphans, in the sense of compassion for them. It has already been noted [[See vol. 2, p. 14.]] that orphanhood among people is from the loss of the father, and among other animals from the loss of the mother. His saying, "in the town," indicates that a village is called a town (madina), and from this is the hadith: "I have been commanded to go to a town that devours the villages" [[The town is the city of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; its devouring the villages means what is opened by the hands of its people from the cities, and they take from their spoils.]], and in the hadith of the emigration: "To whom do you belong?" The man said: "From the people of the town," meaning Mecca.

The Qur'anic verse: "And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them both" (18:82).
