Al-Jawhari said: the she-camel shukarat (شَكَرَتِ), yashkuru shukran, so she is shakira; and ashkara al-darʻ (the udder) meant it was filled with milk.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Dhul-Qarnayn saw them, and the height of one of them was like half of a man of average build among us. They had claws in the places of nails, molars and fangs like beasts of prey, and jaws like those of camels. They had hair on them that covered them. Each one of them had two large ears; he wraps himself in one and spreads the other as a bed. Each one of them knows his term; he does not die until there come out of his loins a thousand men, if it is a male, or from her womb a thousand women, if it is a female.

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of Yajuj and Majuj who came out to raid. Dhul-Qarnayn came and struck the barrier, and they remained on this side. Al-Suddi said: the barrier was built over twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Qatada also said this.

I say: if this is so, then the Prophet (ﷺ) described the Turks as he described Yajuj and Majuj. He, peace be upon him, said: "The Hour will not come until the Muslims fight the Turks, a people whose faces are like hammered shields, who wear hair and walk in hair." In another narration: "who wear hair as sandals." Muslim and Abu Dawud and others recorded it.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) knew their number, their multitude, and the sharpness of their might, he, peace be upon him, said: "Leave the Turks as long as they leave you." At this time, peoples of them have come out that none can count except Allah, and none can turn them back from the Muslims except Allah, until it is as if they were Yajuj and Majuj, or their vanguard.

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Bakra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People of my nation will settle in a low land they call Basra, by a river called Dijla, over which there is a bridge; its people will be many, and it will be among the cities of the emigrants." Ibn Yahya said, Abu Ma'mar said: "and it will be among the cities of the Muslims." "Then when it is the end of time, the sons of Qantura will come, broad-faced and small-eyed, until they descend on the bank of the river. Its people will split into three groups: one group will take the tails of cows and the desert, and they will perish; one group will take for themselves and disbelieve; and one group will place their offspring behind their backs and fight them, and they are the martyrs."

Al-ghA'it is the low-lying land; al-Basra is soft stones, and Basra was named after it. The sons of Qantura are the Turks. It is said that Qantura was the name of a slave-girl who belonged to Ibrahim (peace and blessings be upon him), who bore him children, and from their descendants came the Turks.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute (kharj, خَرْجاً)﴾, is a question asked out of good manners. Kharj means payment (ja'l). It was read as kharaj (خَرَاجًا). Al-kharj is more specific than al-kharaj. It is said: "Pay the kharj of your head and the kharaj of your city." Al-Azhari said: al-kharaj applies to a tax, applies to the property of fay' (booty taken without battle), applies to the jizya (poll tax), and applies to produce. Al-kharaj is the name of what is paid from the obligatory dues on wealth. Al-kharj is the verbal noun. The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿on condition that you set up a barrier (saddan, سَدًّا) between us and them﴾, that is, a barrier of stacked stones (radman, رَدْمًا). The radm is what is placed one part upon another until it joins. A garment is mudarram, meaning patched, as al-Harawi said. It is said: radamtu al-thulma, ardimuha with a kasra, radman, meaning I closed it. Al-radm is also the noun, which is the same as al-sadd. It was said: al-radm is more emphatic than al-sadd, since al-sadd is anything with which one closes, while al-radm is placing one thing upon another, of stones or earth or the like, until a strong screen stands from that. From this comes radama his garment when he patched it with thick patches, one upon another. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

"Have the poets left any patched place (mutaraddam)?"

[The verse continues:]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 92–98 (part 2 of 3):

Am hal 'arafta al-dar ba'da tawahhum [[a line of poetry]]: that is, from a speech that is composed of one part upon another.

"Sadda" is also read with a fatha on the sin. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the damma form is the noun (ism) and the fatha form is the verbal noun (masdar). Al-Kisa'i said: the fatha and the damma are two dialects with one meaning. 'Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: whatever is part of Allah's creation, in which no one has shared by any action, is with a damma, and whatever is the work of humans is with a fatha. The adherents of this view must read "saddan" (in 18:94, "sadda" with the sin pointed) with a fatha, while before it "bayna al-saddayn" is read with a damma. This is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i. Abu Hatim, citing Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah, related the reverse of what Abu 'Ubayda said. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see is sudd with a damma, and what is not seen is sadd with a fatha.

The second issue: this verse is evidence for the establishment of prisons and for confining people of corruption in them, preventing them from acting as they wish. They are not left in their condition; rather, they are beaten, imprisoned, or made to pay (yunakkalun), and then released, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did.

[[In MS k: yunakkalun.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾. The meaning is: Dhu al-Qarnayn said to them, "What Allah the Exalted has extended to me of power and sovereignty is better than your tribute (kharj) and your wealth. But help me with physical strength, that is, with men and labour from you, with bodies, and with the tools with which I will build the barrier (ridm), which is the sadd." This is an affirmation from Allah the Exalted of Dhu al-Qarnayn in this dialogue. For if the people had gathered a tribute for him, no one would have helped him; if they left the construction to him, and their help was with their own persons, it would be more beautiful for him and quicker in completing this work, and perhaps what they offered him would exceed the tribute.

Ibn Kathir alone read: "ma makkananiy" with two nuns (manna). The rest read: "ma makkanni fihi rabbi" (as in the standard reading).

[[In MS j and k: bi-l-aydi (with the hands).]]

The second issue: this verse is evidence that a ruler is obliged to protect the creation: to preserve their domain, to close their gaps, and to repair their frontiers, from their wealth that is abundant for them and from their rights, which their treasury gathers under his hand and his supervision. Even if the rights consume it and the expenses exhaust it, it would be incumbent upon them to make up that from their own wealth, and it is incumbent upon him to look well after them. This rests on three conditions:

First: that he not monopolise anything for himself over them.
Second: that he begin with the people in need and help them.
Third: that he distribute the gifts among them equally according to their ranks.

If, after this, the treasury is depleted and remains empty, and events bring about a matter, they must spend themselves before their wealth. If that does not suffice, their wealth is taken from them in a measured way and disposed of with careful management. This is Dhu al-Qarnayn: when they offered him wealth so that he would hold back from them what they feared from the aggression of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, he said: "I do not need it; I need you." So, ﴿help me with strength﴾, that is, serve me with your own selves; the wealth is with me and the men are with you. He saw that wealth would not avail them, for if he took it as a wage, that would diminish what he needed, and it would return upon them as a burden. So voluntary service with bodies was preferable. The rule is: no one's wealth is lawful to take except out of a necessity that arises; then that wealth is taken openly, not secretly, and spent justly, not by monopolising it, and by the consensus of the community, not by autocratic decision. And Allah the Exalted is the One who grants success to what is correct.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is, give me blocks of iron and hand them to me. He ordered them to transport the tool. All of this is only a request for a gift that is not meant as a gift, but rather a request for handing over, because he had already tied it to his statement that he would not take tribute from them. So there remained only a request for handing over and labour of bodies. "Zubar al-hadid" means pieces of iron. The root of the word is gathering, and from it comes "zubrat al-asad" (the lion's mane), because the hair gathers on its shoulder. And "zabartu al-kitab" means I wrote the book and gathered its letters.

Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "ridman ā-tūnī" (ridm, then "ātūnī") from "al-ityan," which is coming, meaning: bring me the blocks of iron. When the preposition is dropped, the verb takes the accusative, as in the line of the poet:

[[This is 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib al-Zubaydi, and the full line is:
"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded,
for I have left you possessing wealth and property."]]

"Amartuka al-khayr..." — the preposition is omitted, so the verb takes the accusative.

The majority read "zubar" with a fatha on the ba'. Al-Hasan read it with a damma. All of these are plural forms of "zubrah," which is a great piece of it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until, when he had levelled (sawa)﴾, meaning the building, and it was omitted because of the strength of the statement that indicates it.

(Bayna al-sadafayn): Abu 'Ubayda said: they are the two sides of the mountain, and they were called that because they meet (tasadufihima), that is, because they encounter each other. This was also said by al-Zuhri and Ibn 'Abbas. It is as if each one turns away from the other, from ṣudūf (turning away). The poet said:

"Both sadafs are pierced by its light,
blazing like the lamp of darkness."

And a high building is called "sadaf," as a comparison to the side of a mountain. In a hadith: when he passed by a leaning sadaf, he walked quickly. Abu 'Ubayd said: "sadaf" and "hadaf" are any great, high building. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "al-sadafan" are the two mountains facing each other (mutanawihan, meeting face to face). One does not say "sadaf" for a single one; it is said "sadafan" for two, because one of them confronts the other.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-sadafayn" with a fatha on the sad, with its shadda, and a fatha on the dal. This is the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda, because it is the most common of the dialects. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "al-sudufayn" with a damma on the sad and the dal. 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "al-sudfayn" with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal, like "al-jurf" and "al-jarf"; this is a lightening. Ibn al-Majishun read with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal. Qatadah read "bayna al-sadfayn" with a fatha on the sad and a sukun on the dal. All of these have one meaning, and they are the two mountains that face each other.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "Blow"﴾ until the end of the verse, meaning: upon the blocks of iron, with bellows. He used to order a layer of blocks and stones to be placed, then wood and charcoal would be lit beneath them with bellows until they were heated, and iron, when fire is kindled on it, becomes like fire. This is His saying: ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾. Then molten copper, or lead, or iron, according to the difference in the region, would be brought and poured upon that stacked layer. When it joined together and hardened and the parts adhered to one another, they began placing another layer, until the work was completed and it became a solid mountain. Qatadah said: it was like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe.

It is related that a man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have seen the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj." He said: "How did you see it?" He said: "I saw it like striped cloth, a yellow stripe, a red stripe and a black stripe." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have seen it."

The meaning of ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾ is: like fire. The meaning of ﴿Bring me, that I may pour upon it molten copper﴾ is: give me copper that I may pour upon it, with inversion of order. And whoever read "i'tūnī" (come to me), the meaning for him is: come, I will pour copper upon it. "Qitr" according to most exegetes is molten copper, and its root is from "qatr" (dripping), because when it is melted it drips as water drips. Another group said: "qitr" is molten iron. And a group, among them Ibn al-Anbari, said: it is molten lead. It is derived from "qatara yaqtur qatran" (to drip). From this comes ﴿And We caused a fount of qitr to flow for him﴾.

[[See vol. 14, p. 268.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾, that is: Ya'juj and Ma'juj were unable to climb over it and ascend it, because it is smooth and level with the mountain, and the mountain is high and unattainable. The height of the barrier is two hundred and fifty cubits. It is reported that its length between the two ends of the mountains is a hundred farsakhs, and its width is fifty farsakhs; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

﴿Nor were they able to pierce it﴾ because of the breadth of its width and its strength. It is reported in the Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this," and he formed (a circle) with his hand: ninety (in another narration) and he made a ring with his thumb and the finger next to it. He mentioned the hadith. Yahya ibn Sallam mentioned from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya'juj and Ma'juj dig through the barrier every day, until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one over them says: 'Go back, for you will dig through it tomorrow.' Then Allah restores it as strong as it was, until, when their term is fulfilled and Allah wills to send them against the people, they dig until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one over them says: 'Go back, for you will dig through it tomorrow, if Allah wills.' They return to it, and it is in the state in which they left it, so they dig through it and come out upon the people." The hadith [is as mentioned], and it has been mentioned before.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they were not able﴾ with the lightening of the ta' according to the reading of the majority. It was said: it is a dialect with the meaning of "istata'u" (they were able). It was also said: rather, "istata'u" itself is common in Arabic speech, so some of them omitted the ta' from it and said "ista'u," and some omitted the ta' from it and said "ista'a yasti'u," with the meaning of "istata'a yastati'u," and this is a well-known dialect. Hamza alone read "fa-ma isṭṭa'u" with a shadda on the ta', as if he intended "istata'u," then assimilated the ta' into the ta', and so doubled it. This is a weak reading; Abu 'Ali said: it is not permissible. [[Al-Nahhas said: no one can rely on it, because the sin is quiescent and the assimilated ta' is quiescent. Sibawayh said: this is impossible.]] Al-A'mash read "fa-ma istata'u an yazharuhu wa-ma istata'u lahu naqban" with the ta' in both places.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾. The speaker is Dhu al-Qarnayn, and by "this" he pointed to the barrier, and to the strength to build it, and to the benefit of it in averting the harm of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "hadhihi rahmatun min rabbi" (this is a mercy from my Lord).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the time of their emergence.

(Ja'alahu dakkan): that is, made level with the earth. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder (dakkan dakkan)﴾ [al-Fajr: 21]. Ibn 'Arafah said: that is, it was made level, with no hillock in it. And from this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He made it a dakk (level)﴾. Al-Yazidi said: that is, levelled. It is said: a she-camel "dakka'" when her hump has gone. Al-Qutabi said: that is, he made it crushed and pressed flat against the earth. Al-Kalbi said: pieces, broken in pieces, and he said:

Is it not that the one who came (to it) pounded a cave so that it collapsed? Al-Azhari said: it is said "dakktuhu," meaning "daqqaqtuhu" (I crushed it).

As for the one who read "dakkā'" (with a long vowel), he intended "He made the mountain into a level ground, dakkā'," and that is the raised ground that does not reach the height of a mountain; its plural is dakkāwāt.

Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "dakkā'" with the long vowel (madd), by way of comparison with the she-camel dakkā' (dakkā', the one without a hump). In the speech there is an elision whose sense is: "He made it like a dakkā'," and this elision must be assumed, because the barrier (sadd) is masculine, so it is not described as dakkā'.

As for the one who read "dakkan," it is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of dakka, yadukku, when it means to demolish and grind down. It is possible that "ja'ala" (made) here means "khalaqa" (created). "Dakkā'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The same accusative applies also in the reading of the one who used the long vowel; it admits both possibilities.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 92–98 (part 1 of 3):

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾ until, when he reached between the two barriers, ﴿he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾. The two barriers are two mountains on the side of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Ata al-Khurasani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Between the two barriers" means the two mountains of Armenia and Azerbaijan. ﴿Beside them﴾ means behind them.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yufqihuna (يُفْقِهُونَ) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the qaf, from afqaha (to make clear), meaning they could not make others understand speech. The rest read it with a fatha on the ya' and the qaf (yafqahuna, يَفْقَهُونَ), meaning they could not understand. Both readings are sound: they neither understand others nor are understood by others.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: O Dhul-Qarnayn!﴾ That is, a righteous community of mankind said to him: ﴿Indeed, Gog and Magog are corrupters in the earth.﴾

Al-Akhfash said: whoever hamzes Ya'juj and makes the two alifs part of the root, says Ya'juj is on the pattern of yaf'ul and Ma'juj on the pattern of maf'ul, as if it derives from ajij al-nar (the crackling of fire). He said: whoever does not hamz it and treats the two alifs as added letters, says "Yajuj" is from yajajtu and "Majuj" is from majajta, and both are not diptoted (ghayr munsarifayn). Ru'ba said:

"If Yajuj and Majuj together,
and 'Ad 'Ad and they gathered an army of Tubba'..."

al-Jawhari mentioned it. It was also said that they are not diptoted because they are foreign names, like Talut and Jalut, not derived, and their two reasons for not taking tanwin are foreignness and definiteness and feminine form. A group said: it is arabized from ajja and ajjaja, and its two reasons for not taking tanwin are definiteness and feminine form. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that both are Arabic. Whoever hamzes Ya'juj, it is on the pattern of yaf'ul, like yarbu', from your saying ajjat al-nar, meaning it blazed; and from it comes al-ajij, and from it comes milh ujaj (salty water). Whoever does not hamz it, it is possible that he lightened the hamza and changed it into an alif, like ra's. As for Majuj, it is maf'ul from ajja, and the two words are of one root in derivation. Whoever does not hamz, it is possible that he lightened the hamza, and it is possible that it is fa'ul from majja, and the omission of tanwin in both is for feminine form and definiteness, as if it were the name of a tribe.

The scholars differed about their corruption. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: their corruption is their eating of the children of Adam. A group said: their corruption was only anticipated, that is, they would corrupt, so they sought a way to guard against them. A group said: their corruption is oppression, violence, killing, and all the other forms of corruption known among humans. And Allah knows best.

Reports have come about their description, their emergence, and that they are from the offspring of Yafith. Abu Hurayra narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Nuh had three sons: Sam, Ham, and Yafith. Sam fathered the Arabs, Persians, and Romans, and goodness is among them. Yafith fathered Yajuj and Majuj, the Turks and the Slavs, and there is no goodness among them. Ham fathered the Copts, the Berbers, and the Sudanese."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Adam (peace be upon him) had a wet dream, and his semen mixed with the dust, and he was distressed, so they were created from that water. Thus they are connected to us through the father, not through the mother. This is open to question, because the prophets (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them) do not have wet dreams, and they are only from the offspring of Yafith. Muqatil and others said the same.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man of them dies until there are born to his loins a thousand men." He means Yajuj and Majuj. Abu Sa'id also said: "They are twenty-five tribes beyond Yajuj and Majuj. No man of these or of Yajuj and Majuj dies until there comes out of his loins a thousand men." Al-Qushayri mentioned it.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Yajuj and Majuj, and he said, peace be upon him: "Yajuj and Majuj are two peoples, each people four hundred thousand peoples [the addition is from al-Durr al-Manthur], each people whose number none knows except Allah. No man of them dies until there are born to him a thousand male offspring from his loins, all of whom bear arms." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, describe them to us." He said: "They are three kinds. One kind is like al-arz [al-arz: the pine tree], a tree in Syria, whose height is one hundred and twenty cubits. Another kind whose width and length are equal, about a cubit. Another kind which spreads its ear as a bed and covers itself with the other. They do not pass by an elephant, a wild beast, or a pig without eating it, and they eat whoever of them dies. Their vanguard is in Syria and their rearguard is in Khurasan. They drink the rivers of the East and the lake of Tiberias, and Allah prevents them from reaching Mecca, Medina, and Bayt al-Maqdis."

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "And one kind of them is a span tall, with claws and fangs like those of beasts of prey, the cooing of doves, the mating of animals, the howling of wolves; and hair that protects them from heat and cold; and large ears, one of which is woolly, in which they lie down for winter, and the other is a skin in which they spend summer. They dig the barrier until they almost break through it, but Allah restores it as it was, until they say: 'We shall break through it tomorrow, if Allah wills.' Then they break through it and come out, and people fortify themselves in fortresses. They shoot arrows toward the sky, and the arrow returns to them smeared with blood. Then Allah destroys them with the nagaf in their necks." Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it. (Nagaf, with a fatha on the na' and a sukun on the ghayn, is a worm that is found in the noses of camels and sheep; its singular is nagafa.)

'Ali also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Yajuj is a people having four hundred commanders, and likewise Majuj. No one of them dies until he sees a thousand horsemen from his offspring."

I say: it has come as a marfu' hadith from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, which Ibn Majah recorded in al-Sunan. He said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yajuj and Majuj dig every day, until when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one who is over them says: 'Return, and you will dig it tomorrow.' Then Allah restores it stronger than it was. When their term is complete and Allah wills to send them against people, they dig until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, he says: 'Return, and you will dig it tomorrow, if Allah wills,' and they add the exception. They return to it, and it is in the state they left it, so they dig it out, and they come out against people and drink up the water. People fortify themselves against them in their fortresses. They shoot their arrows toward the sky, and the blood returns upon them [this is from the narrator's words, which I remember (note in Ibn Majah)]. They say: 'We have conquered the people of the earth and exalted over the people of heaven.' Then Allah sends upon them nagaf in their necks, and kills them with it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the beasts of the earth will grow fat and be satisfied with their flesh."

Al-Jawhari said: the she-camel shukarat (شَكَرَتِ), yashkuru shukran, so she is shakira; and ashkara al-darʻ (the udder) meant it was filled with milk.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Dhul-Qarnayn saw them, and the height of one of them was like half of a man of average build among us. They had claws in the places of nails, molars and fangs like beasts of prey, and jaws like those of camels. They had hair on them that covered them. Each one of them had two large ears; he wraps himself in one and spreads the other as a bed. Each one of them knows his term; he does not die until there come out of his loins a thousand men, if it is a male, or from her womb a thousand women, if it is a female.

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of Yajuj and Majuj who came out to raid. Dhul-Qarnayn came and struck the barrier, and they remained on this side. Al-Suddi said: the barrier was built over twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Qatada also said this.

I say: if this is so, then the Prophet (ﷺ) described the Turks as he described Yajuj and Majuj. He, peace be upon him, said: "The Hour will not come until the Muslims fight the Turks, a people whose faces are like hammered shields, who wear hair and walk in hair." In another narration: "who wear hair as sandals." Muslim and Abu Dawud and others recorded it.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) knew their number, their multitude, and the sharpness of their might, he, peace be upon him, said: "Leave the Turks as long as they leave you." At this time, peoples of them have come out that none can count except Allah, and none can turn them back from the Muslims except Allah, until it is as if they were Yajuj and Majuj, or their vanguard.

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Bakra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People of my nation will settle in a low land they call Basra, by a river called Dijla, over which there is a bridge; its people will be many, and it will be among the cities of the emigrants." Ibn Yahya said, Abu Ma'mar said: "and it will be among the cities of the Muslims." "Then when it is the end of time, the sons of Qantura will come, broad-faced and small-eyed, until they descend on the bank of the river. Its people will split into three groups: one group will take the tails of cows and the desert, and they will perish; one group will take for themselves and disbelieve; and one group will place their offspring behind their backs and fight them, and they are the martyrs."

Al-ghA'it is the low-lying land; al-Basra is soft stones, and Basra was named after it. The sons of Qantura are the Turks. It is said that Qantura was the name of a slave-girl who belonged to Ibrahim (peace and blessings be upon him), who bore him children, and from their descendants came the Turks.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute (kharj, خَرْجاً)﴾, is a question asked out of good manners. Kharj means payment (ja'l). It was read as kharaj (خَرَاجًا). Al-kharj is more specific than al-kharaj. It is said: "Pay the kharj of your head and the kharaj of your city." Al-Azhari said: al-kharaj applies to a tax, applies to the property of fay' (booty taken without battle), applies to the jizya (poll tax), and applies to produce. Al-kharaj is the name of what is paid from the obligatory dues on wealth. Al-kharj is the verbal noun. The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿on condition that you set up a barrier (saddan, سَدًّا) between us and them﴾, that is, a barrier of stacked stones (radman, رَدْمًا). The radm is what is placed one part upon another until it joins. A garment is mudarram, meaning patched, as al-Harawi said. It is said: radamtu al-thulma, ardimuha with a kasra, radman, meaning I closed it. Al-radm is also the noun, which is the same as al-sadd. It was said: al-radm is more emphatic than al-sadd, since al-sadd is anything with which one closes, while al-radm is placing one thing upon another, of stones or earth or the like, until a strong screen stands from that. From this comes radama his garment when he patched it with thick patches, one upon another. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

"Have the poets left any patched place (mutaraddam)?"

[The verse continues:]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 92–98 (part 2 of 3):

Am hal 'arafta al-dar ba'da tawahhum [[a line of poetry]]: that is, from a speech that is composed of one part upon another.

"Sadda" is also read with a fatha on the sin. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the damma form is the noun (ism) and the fatha form is the verbal noun (masdar). Al-Kisa'i said: the fatha and the damma are two dialects with one meaning. 'Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: whatever is part of Allah's creation, in which no one has shared by any action, is with a damma, and whatever is the work of humans is with a fatha. The adherents of this view must read "saddan" (in 18:94, "sadda" with the sin pointed) with a fatha, while before it "bayna al-saddayn" is read with a damma. This is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i. Abu Hatim, citing Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah, related the reverse of what Abu 'Ubayda said. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see is sudd with a damma, and what is not seen is sadd with a fatha.

The second issue: this verse is evidence for the establishment of prisons and for confining people of corruption in them, preventing them from acting as they wish. They are not left in their condition; rather, they are beaten, imprisoned, or made to pay (yunakkalun), and then released, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did.

[[In MS k: yunakkalun.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾. The meaning is: Dhu al-Qarnayn said to them, "What Allah the Exalted has extended to me of power and sovereignty is better than your tribute (kharj) and your wealth. But help me with physical strength, that is, with men and labour from you, with bodies, and with the tools with which I will build the barrier (ridm), which is the sadd." This is an affirmation from Allah the Exalted of Dhu al-Qarnayn in this dialogue. For if the people had gathered a tribute for him, no one would have helped him; if they left the construction to him, and their help was with their own persons, it would be more beautiful for him and quicker in completing this work, and perhaps what they offered him would exceed the tribute.

Ibn Kathir alone read: "ma makkananiy" with two nuns (manna). The rest read: "ma makkanni fihi rabbi" (as in the standard reading).

[[In MS j and k: bi-l-aydi (with the hands).]]

The second issue: this verse is evidence that a ruler is obliged to protect the creation: to preserve their domain, to close their gaps, and to repair their frontiers, from their wealth that is abundant for them and from their rights, which their treasury gathers under his hand and his supervision. Even if the rights consume it and the expenses exhaust it, it would be incumbent upon them to make up that from their own wealth, and it is incumbent upon him to look well after them. This rests on three conditions:

First: that he not monopolise anything for himself over them.
Second: that he begin with the people in need and help them.
Third: that he distribute the gifts among them equally according to their ranks.

If, after this, the treasury is depleted and remains empty, and events bring about a matter, they must spend themselves before their wealth. If that does not suffice, their wealth is taken from them in a measured way and disposed of with careful management. This is Dhu al-Qarnayn: when they offered him wealth so that he would hold back from them what they feared from the aggression of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, he said: "I do not need it; I need you." So, ﴿help me with strength﴾, that is, serve me with your own selves; the wealth is with me and the men are with you. He saw that wealth would not avail them, for if he took it as a wage, that would diminish what he needed, and it would return upon them as a burden. So voluntary service with bodies was preferable. The rule is: no one's wealth is lawful to take except out of a necessity that arises; then that wealth is taken openly, not secretly, and spent justly, not by monopolising it, and by the consensus of the community, not by autocratic decision. And Allah the Exalted is the One who grants success to what is correct.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is, give me blocks of iron and hand them to me. He ordered them to transport the tool. All of this is only a request for a gift that is not meant as a gift, but rather a request for handing over, because he had already tied it to his statement that he would not take tribute from them. So there remained only a request for handing over and labour of bodies. "Zubar al-hadid" means pieces of iron. The root of the word is gathering, and from it comes "zubrat al-asad" (the lion's mane), because the hair gathers on its shoulder. And "zabartu al-kitab" means I wrote the book and gathered its letters.

Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "ridman ā-tūnī" (ridm, then "ātūnī") from "al-ityan," which is coming, meaning: bring me the blocks of iron. When the preposition is dropped, the verb takes the accusative, as in the line of the poet:

[[This is 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib al-Zubaydi, and the full line is:
"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded,
for I have left you possessing wealth and property."]]

"Amartuka al-khayr..." — the preposition is omitted, so the verb takes the accusative.

The majority read "zubar" with a fatha on the ba'. Al-Hasan read it with a damma. All of these are plural forms of "zubrah," which is a great piece of it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until, when he had levelled (sawa)﴾, meaning the building, and it was omitted because of the strength of the statement that indicates it.

(Bayna al-sadafayn): Abu 'Ubayda said: they are the two sides of the mountain, and they were called that because they meet (tasadufihima), that is, because they encounter each other. This was also said by al-Zuhri and Ibn 'Abbas. It is as if each one turns away from the other, from ṣudūf (turning away). The poet said:

"Both sadafs are pierced by its light,
blazing like the lamp of darkness."

And a high building is called "sadaf," as a comparison to the side of a mountain. In a hadith: when he passed by a leaning sadaf, he walked quickly. Abu 'Ubayd said: "sadaf" and "hadaf" are any great, high building. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "al-sadafan" are the two mountains facing each other (mutanawihan, meeting face to face). One does not say "sadaf" for a single one; it is said "sadafan" for two, because one of them confronts the other.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-sadafayn" with a fatha on the sad, with its shadda, and a fatha on the dal. This is the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda, because it is the most common of the dialects. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "al-sudufayn" with a damma on the sad and the dal. 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "al-sudfayn" with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal, like "al-jurf" and "al-jarf"; this is a lightening. Ibn al-Majishun read with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal. Qatadah read "bayna al-sadfayn" with a fatha on the sad and a sukun on the dal. All of these have one meaning, and they are the two mountains that face each other.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "Blow"﴾ until the end of the verse, meaning: upon the blocks of iron, with bellows. He used to order a layer of blocks and stones to be placed, then wood and charcoal would be lit beneath them with bellows until they were heated, and iron, when fire is kindled on it, becomes like fire. This is His saying: ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾. Then molten copper, or lead, or iron, according to the difference in the region, would be brought and poured upon that stacked layer. When it joined together and hardened and the parts adhered to one another, they began placing another layer, until the work was completed and it became a solid mountain. Qatadah said: it was like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe.

It is related that a man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have seen the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj." He said: "How did you see it?" He said: "I saw it like striped cloth, a yellow stripe, a red stripe and a black stripe." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have seen it."

The meaning of ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾ is: like fire. The meaning of ﴿Bring me, that I may pour upon it molten copper﴾ is: give me copper that I may pour upon it, with inversion of order. And whoever read "i'tūnī" (come to me), the meaning for him is: come, I will pour copper upon it. "Qitr" according to most exegetes is molten copper, and its root is from "qatr" (dripping), because when it is melted it drips as water drips. Another group said: "qitr" is molten iron. And a group, among them Ibn al-Anbari, said: it is molten lead. It is derived from "qatara yaqtur qatran" (to drip). From this comes ﴿And We caused a fount of qitr to flow for him﴾.

[[See vol. 14, p. 268.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾, that is: Ya'juj and Ma'juj were unable to climb over it and ascend it, because it is smooth and level with the mountain, and the mountain is high and unattainable. The height of the barrier is two hundred and fifty cubits. It is reported that its length between the two ends of the mountains is a hundred farsakhs, and its width is fifty farsakhs; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

﴿Nor were they able to pierce it﴾ because of the breadth of its width and its strength. It is reported in the Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this," and he formed (a circle) with his hand: ninety (in another narration) and he made a ring with his thumb and the finger next to it. He mentioned the hadith. Yahya ibn Sallam mentioned from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya'juj and Ma'juj dig through the barrier every day, until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one over them says: 'Go back, for you will dig through it tomorrow.' Then Allah restores it as strong as it was, until, when their term is fulfilled and Allah wills to send them against the people, they dig until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one over them says: 'Go back, for you will dig through it tomorrow, if Allah wills.' They return to it, and it is in the state in which they left it, so they dig through it and come out upon the people." The hadith [is as mentioned], and it has been mentioned before.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they were not able﴾ with the lightening of the ta' according to the reading of the majority. It was said: it is a dialect with the meaning of "istata'u" (they were able). It was also said: rather, "istata'u" itself is common in Arabic speech, so some of them omitted the ta' from it and said "ista'u," and some omitted the ta' from it and said "ista'a yasti'u," with the meaning of "istata'a yastati'u," and this is a well-known dialect. Hamza alone read "fa-ma isṭṭa'u" with a shadda on the ta', as if he intended "istata'u," then assimilated the ta' into the ta', and so doubled it. This is a weak reading; Abu 'Ali said: it is not permissible. [[Al-Nahhas said: no one can rely on it, because the sin is quiescent and the assimilated ta' is quiescent. Sibawayh said: this is impossible.]] Al-A'mash read "fa-ma istata'u an yazharuhu wa-ma istata'u lahu naqban" with the ta' in both places.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾. The speaker is Dhu al-Qarnayn, and by "this" he pointed to the barrier, and to the strength to build it, and to the benefit of it in averting the harm of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "hadhihi rahmatun min rabbi" (this is a mercy from my Lord).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the time of their emergence.

(Ja'alahu dakkan): that is, made level with the earth. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder (dakkan dakkan)﴾ [al-Fajr: 21]. Ibn 'Arafah said: that is, it was made level, with no hillock in it. And from this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He made it a dakk (level)﴾. Al-Yazidi said: that is, levelled. It is said: a she-camel "dakka'" when her hump has gone. Al-Qutabi said: that is, he made it crushed and pressed flat against the earth. Al-Kalbi said: pieces, broken in pieces, and he said:

Is it not that the one who came (to it) pounded a cave so that it collapsed? Al-Azhari said: it is said "dakktuhu," meaning "daqqaqtuhu" (I crushed it).

As for the one who read "dakkā'" (with a long vowel), he intended "He made the mountain into a level ground, dakkā'," and that is the raised ground that does not reach the height of a mountain; its plural is dakkāwāt.

Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "dakkā'" with the long vowel (madd), by way of comparison with the she-camel dakkā' (dakkā', the one without a hump). In the speech there is an elision whose sense is: "He made it like a dakkā'," and this elision must be assumed, because the barrier (sadd) is masculine, so it is not described as dakkā'.

As for the one who read "dakkan," it is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of dakka, yadukku, when it means to demolish and grind down. It is possible that "ja'ala" (made) here means "khalaqa" (created). "Dakkā'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The same accusative applies also in the reading of the one who used the long vowel; it admits both possibilities.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 92–98 (part 1 of 3):

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾ until, when he reached between the two barriers, ﴿he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾. The two barriers are two mountains on the side of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Ata al-Khurasani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Between the two barriers" means the two mountains of Armenia and Azerbaijan. ﴿Beside them﴾ means behind them.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yufqihuna (يُفْقِهُونَ) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the qaf, from afqaha (to make clear), meaning they could not make others understand speech. The rest read it with a fatha on the ya' and the qaf (yafqahuna, يَفْقَهُونَ), meaning they could not understand. Both readings are sound: they neither understand others nor are understood by others.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: O Dhul-Qarnayn!﴾ That is, a righteous community of mankind said to him: ﴿Indeed, Gog and Magog are corrupters in the earth.﴾

Al-Akhfash said: whoever hamzes Ya'juj and makes the two alifs part of the root, says Ya'juj is on the pattern of yaf'ul and Ma'juj on the pattern of maf'ul, as if it derives from ajij al-nar (the crackling of fire). He said: whoever does not hamz it and treats the two alifs as added letters, says "Yajuj" is from yajajtu and "Majuj" is from majajta, and both are not diptoted (ghayr munsarifayn). Ru'ba said:

"If Yajuj and Majuj together,
and 'Ad 'Ad and they gathered an army of Tubba'..."

al-Jawhari mentioned it. It was also said that they are not diptoted because they are foreign names, like Talut and Jalut, not derived, and their two reasons for not taking tanwin are foreignness and definiteness and feminine form. A group said: it is arabized from ajja and ajjaja, and its two reasons for not taking tanwin are definiteness and feminine form. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that both are Arabic. Whoever hamzes Ya'juj, it is on the pattern of yaf'ul, like yarbu', from your saying ajjat al-nar, meaning it blazed; and from it comes al-ajij, and from it comes milh ujaj (salty water). Whoever does not hamz it, it is possible that he lightened the hamza and changed it into an alif, like ra's. As for Majuj, it is maf'ul from ajja, and the two words are of one root in derivation. Whoever does not hamz, it is possible that he lightened the hamza, and it is possible that it is fa'ul from majja, and the omission of tanwin in both is for feminine form and definiteness, as if it were the name of a tribe.

The scholars differed about their corruption. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: their corruption is their eating of the children of Adam. A group said: their corruption was only anticipated, that is, they would corrupt, so they sought a way to guard against them. A group said: their corruption is oppression, violence, killing, and all the other forms of corruption known among humans. And Allah knows best.

Reports have come about their description, their emergence, and that they are from the offspring of Yafith. Abu Hurayra narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Nuh had three sons: Sam, Ham, and Yafith. Sam fathered the Arabs, Persians, and Romans, and goodness is among them. Yafith fathered Yajuj and Majuj, the Turks and the Slavs, and there is no goodness among them. Ham fathered the Copts, the Berbers, and the Sudanese."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Adam (peace be upon him) had a wet dream, and his semen mixed with the dust, and he was distressed, so they were created from that water. Thus they are connected to us through the father, not through the mother. This is open to question, because the prophets (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them) do not have wet dreams, and they are only from the offspring of Yafith. Muqatil and others said the same.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man of them dies until there are born to his loins a thousand men." He means Yajuj and Majuj. Abu Sa'id also said: "They are twenty-five tribes beyond Yajuj and Majuj. No man of these or of Yajuj and Majuj dies until there comes out of his loins a thousand men." Al-Qushayri mentioned it.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Yajuj and Majuj, and he said, peace be upon him: "Yajuj and Majuj are two peoples, each people four hundred thousand peoples [the addition is from al-Durr al-Manthur], each people whose number none knows except Allah. No man of them dies until there are born to him a thousand male offspring from his loins, all of whom bear arms." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, describe them to us." He said: "They are three kinds. One kind is like al-arz [al-arz: the pine tree], a tree in Syria, whose height is one hundred and twenty cubits. Another kind whose width and length are equal, about a cubit. Another kind which spreads its ear as a bed and covers itself with the other. They do not pass by an elephant, a wild beast, or a pig without eating it, and they eat whoever of them dies. Their vanguard is in Syria and their rearguard is in Khurasan. They drink the rivers of the East and the lake of Tiberias, and Allah prevents them from reaching Mecca, Medina, and Bayt al-Maqdis."

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "And one kind of them is a span tall, with claws and fangs like those of beasts of prey, the cooing of doves, the mating of animals, the howling of wolves; and hair that protects them from heat and cold; and large ears, one of which is woolly, in which they lie down for winter, and the other is a skin in which they spend summer. They dig the barrier until they almost break through it, but Allah restores it as it was, until they say: 'We shall break through it tomorrow, if Allah wills.' Then they break through it and come out, and people fortify themselves in fortresses. They shoot arrows toward the sky, and the arrow returns to them smeared with blood. Then Allah destroys them with the nagaf in their necks." Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it. (Nagaf, with a fatha on the na' and a sukun on the ghayn, is a worm that is found in the noses of camels and sheep; its singular is nagafa.)

'Ali also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Yajuj is a people having four hundred commanders, and likewise Majuj. No one of them dies until he sees a thousand horsemen from his offspring."

I say: it has come as a marfu' hadith from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, which Ibn Majah recorded in al-Sunan. He said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yajuj and Majuj dig every day, until when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one who is over them says: 'Return, and you will dig it tomorrow.' Then Allah restores it stronger than it was. When their term is complete and Allah wills to send them against people, they dig until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, he says: 'Return, and you will dig it tomorrow, if Allah wills,' and they add the exception. They return to it, and it is in the state they left it, so they dig it out, and they come out against people and drink up the water. People fortify themselves against them in their fortresses. They shoot their arrows toward the sky, and the blood returns upon them [this is from the narrator's words, which I remember (note in Ibn Majah)]. They say: 'We have conquered the people of the earth and exalted over the people of heaven.' Then Allah sends upon them nagaf in their necks, and kills them with it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the beasts of the earth will grow fat and be satisfied with their flesh."

Al-Jawhari said: the she-camel shukarat (شَكَرَتِ), yashkuru shukran, so she is shakira; and ashkara al-darʻ (the udder) meant it was filled with milk.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Dhul-Qarnayn saw them, and the height of one of them was like half of a man of average build among us. They had claws in the places of nails, molars and fangs like beasts of prey, and jaws like those of camels. They had hair on them that covered them. Each one of them had two large ears; he wraps himself in one and spreads the other as a bed. Each one of them knows his term; he does not die until there come out of his loins a thousand men, if it is a male, or from her womb a thousand women, if it is a female.

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of Yajuj and Majuj who came out to raid. Dhul-Qarnayn came and struck the barrier, and they remained on this side. Al-Suddi said: the barrier was built over twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Qatada also said this.

I say: if this is so, then the Prophet (ﷺ) described the Turks as he described Yajuj and Majuj. He, peace be upon him, said: "The Hour will not come until the Muslims fight the Turks, a people whose faces are like hammered shields, who wear hair and walk in hair." In another narration: "who wear hair as sandals." Muslim and Abu Dawud and others recorded it.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) knew their number, their multitude, and the sharpness of their might, he, peace be upon him, said: "Leave the Turks as long as they leave you." At this time, peoples of them have come out that none can count except Allah, and none can turn them back from the Muslims except Allah, until it is as if they were Yajuj and Majuj, or their vanguard.

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Bakra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People of my nation will settle in a low land they call Basra, by a river called Dijla, over which there is a bridge; its people will be many, and it will be among the cities of the emigrants." Ibn Yahya said, Abu Ma'mar said: "and it will be among the cities of the Muslims." "Then when it is the end of time, the sons of Qantura will come, broad-faced and small-eyed, until they descend on the bank of the river. Its people will split into three groups: one group will take the tails of cows and the desert, and they will perish; one group will take for themselves and disbelieve; and one group will place their offspring behind their backs and fight them, and they are the martyrs."

Al-ghA'it is the low-lying land; al-Basra is soft stones, and Basra was named after it. The sons of Qantura are the Turks. It is said that Qantura was the name of a slave-girl who belonged to Ibrahim (peace and blessings be upon him), who bore him children, and from their descendants came the Turks.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute (kharj, خَرْجاً)﴾, is a question asked out of good manners. Kharj means payment (ja'l). It was read as kharaj (خَرَاجًا). Al-kharj is more specific than al-kharaj. It is said: "Pay the kharj of your head and the kharaj of your city." Al-Azhari said: al-kharaj applies to a tax, applies to the property of fay' (booty taken without battle), applies to the jizya (poll tax), and applies to produce. Al-kharaj is the name of what is paid from the obligatory dues on wealth. Al-kharj is the verbal noun. The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿on condition that you set up a barrier (saddan, سَدًّا) between us and them﴾, that is, a barrier of stacked stones (radman, رَدْمًا). The radm is what is placed one part upon another until it joins. A garment is mudarram, meaning patched, as al-Harawi said. It is said: radamtu al-thulma, ardimuha with a kasra, radman, meaning I closed it. Al-radm is also the noun, which is the same as al-sadd. It was said: al-radm is more emphatic than al-sadd, since al-sadd is anything with which one closes, while al-radm is placing one thing upon another, of stones or earth or the like, until a strong screen stands from that. From this comes radama his garment when he patched it with thick patches, one upon another. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

"Have the poets left any patched place (mutaraddam)?"

[The verse continues:]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verses 92–98 (part 2 of 3):

Am hal 'arafta al-dar ba'da tawahhum [[a line of poetry]]: that is, from a speech that is composed of one part upon another.

"Sadda" is also read with a fatha on the sin. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the damma form is the noun (ism) and the fatha form is the verbal noun (masdar). Al-Kisa'i said: the fatha and the damma are two dialects with one meaning. 'Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: whatever is part of Allah's creation, in which no one has shared by any action, is with a damma, and whatever is the work of humans is with a fatha. The adherents of this view must read "saddan" (in 18:94, "sadda" with the sin pointed) with a fatha, while before it "bayna al-saddayn" is read with a damma. This is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i. Abu Hatim, citing Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah, related the reverse of what Abu 'Ubayda said. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see is sudd with a damma, and what is not seen is sadd with a fatha.

The second issue: this verse is evidence for the establishment of prisons and for confining people of corruption in them, preventing them from acting as they wish. They are not left in their condition; rather, they are beaten, imprisoned, or made to pay (yunakkalun), and then released, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did.

[[In MS k: yunakkalun.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾. The meaning is: Dhu al-Qarnayn said to them, "What Allah the Exalted has extended to me of power and sovereignty is better than your tribute (kharj) and your wealth. But help me with physical strength, that is, with men and labour from you, with bodies, and with the tools with which I will build the barrier (ridm), which is the sadd." This is an affirmation from Allah the Exalted of Dhu al-Qarnayn in this dialogue. For if the people had gathered a tribute for him, no one would have helped him; if they left the construction to him, and their help was with their own persons, it would be more beautiful for him and quicker in completing this work, and perhaps what they offered him would exceed the tribute.

Ibn Kathir alone read: "ma makkananiy" with two nuns (manna). The rest read: "ma makkanni fihi rabbi" (as in the standard reading).

[[In MS j and k: bi-l-aydi (with the hands).]]

The second issue: this verse is evidence that a ruler is obliged to protect the creation: to preserve their domain, to close their gaps, and to repair their frontiers, from their wealth that is abundant for them and from their rights, which their treasury gathers under his hand and his supervision. Even if the rights consume it and the expenses exhaust it, it would be incumbent upon them to make up that from their own wealth, and it is incumbent upon him to look well after them. This rests on three conditions:

First: that he not monopolise anything for himself over them.
Second: that he begin with the people in need and help them.
Third: that he distribute the gifts among them equally according to their ranks.

If, after this, the treasury is depleted and remains empty, and events bring about a matter, they must spend themselves before their wealth. If that does not suffice, their wealth is taken from them in a measured way and disposed of with careful management. This is Dhu al-Qarnayn: when they offered him wealth so that he would hold back from them what they feared from the aggression of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, he said: "I do not need it; I need you." So, ﴿help me with strength﴾, that is, serve me with your own selves; the wealth is with me and the men are with you. He saw that wealth would not avail them, for if he took it as a wage, that would diminish what he needed, and it would return upon them as a burden. So voluntary service with bodies was preferable. The rule is: no one's wealth is lawful to take except out of a necessity that arises; then that wealth is taken openly, not secretly, and spent justly, not by monopolising it, and by the consensus of the community, not by autocratic decision. And Allah the Exalted is the One who grants success to what is correct.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is, give me blocks of iron and hand them to me. He ordered them to transport the tool. All of this is only a request for a gift that is not meant as a gift, but rather a request for handing over, because he had already tied it to his statement that he would not take tribute from them. So there remained only a request for handing over and labour of bodies. "Zubar al-hadid" means pieces of iron. The root of the word is gathering, and from it comes "zubrat al-asad" (the lion's mane), because the hair gathers on its shoulder. And "zabartu al-kitab" means I wrote the book and gathered its letters.

Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "ridman ā-tūnī" (ridm, then "ātūnī") from "al-ityan," which is coming, meaning: bring me the blocks of iron. When the preposition is dropped, the verb takes the accusative, as in the line of the poet:

[[This is 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib al-Zubaydi, and the full line is:
"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded,
for I have left you possessing wealth and property."]]

"Amartuka al-khayr..." — the preposition is omitted, so the verb takes the accusative.

The majority read "zubar" with a fatha on the ba'. Al-Hasan read it with a damma. All of these are plural forms of "zubrah," which is a great piece of it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until, when he had levelled (sawa)﴾, meaning the building, and it was omitted because of the strength of the statement that indicates it.

(Bayna al-sadafayn): Abu 'Ubayda said: they are the two sides of the mountain, and they were called that because they meet (tasadufihima), that is, because they encounter each other. This was also said by al-Zuhri and Ibn 'Abbas. It is as if each one turns away from the other, from ṣudūf (turning away). The poet said:

"Both sadafs are pierced by its light,
blazing like the lamp of darkness."

And a high building is called "sadaf," as a comparison to the side of a mountain. In a hadith: when he passed by a leaning sadaf, he walked quickly. Abu 'Ubayd said: "sadaf" and "hadaf" are any great, high building. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "al-sadafan" are the two mountains facing each other (mutanawihan, meeting face to face). One does not say "sadaf" for a single one; it is said "sadafan" for two, because one of them confronts the other.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-sadafayn" with a fatha on the sad, with its shadda, and a fatha on the dal. This is the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda, because it is the most common of the dialects. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "al-sudufayn" with a damma on the sad and the dal. 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "al-sudfayn" with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal, like "al-jurf" and "al-jarf"; this is a lightening. Ibn al-Majishun read with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal. Qatadah read "bayna al-sadfayn" with a fatha on the sad and a sukun on the dal. All of these have one meaning, and they are the two mountains that face each other.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "Blow"﴾ until the end of the verse, meaning: upon the blocks of iron, with bellows. He used to order a layer of blocks and stones to be placed, then wood and charcoal would be lit beneath them with bellows until they were heated, and iron, when fire is kindled on it, becomes like fire. This is His saying: ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾. Then molten copper, or lead, or iron, according to the difference in the region, would be brought and poured upon that stacked layer. When it joined together and hardened and the parts adhered to one another, they began placing another layer, until the work was completed and it became a solid mountain. Qatadah said: it was like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe.

It is related that a man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have seen the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj." He said: "How did you see it?" He said: "I saw it like striped cloth, a yellow stripe, a red stripe and a black stripe." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have seen it."

The meaning of ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾ is: like fire. The meaning of ﴿Bring me, that I may pour upon it molten copper﴾ is: give me copper that I may pour upon it, with inversion of order. And whoever read "i'tūnī" (come to me), the meaning for him is: come, I will pour copper upon it. "Qitr" according to most exegetes is molten copper, and its root is from "qatr" (dripping), because when it is melted it drips as water drips. Another group said: "qitr" is molten iron. And a group, among them Ibn al-Anbari, said: it is molten lead. It is derived from "qatara yaqtur qatran" (to drip). From this comes ﴿And We caused a fount of qitr to flow for him﴾.

[[See vol. 14, p. 268.]]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾, that is: Ya'juj and Ma'juj were unable to climb over it and ascend it, because it is smooth and level with the mountain, and the mountain is high and unattainable. The height of the barrier is two hundred and fifty cubits. It is reported that its length between the two ends of the mountains is a hundred farsakhs, and its width is fifty farsakhs; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

﴿Nor were they able to pierce it﴾ because of the breadth of its width and its strength. It is reported in the Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this," and he formed (a circle) with his hand: ninety (in another narration) and he made a ring with his thumb and the finger next to it. He mentioned the hadith. Yahya ibn Sallam mentioned from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya'juj and Ma'juj dig through the barrier every day, until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one over them says: 'Go back, for you will dig through it tomorrow.' Then Allah restores it as strong as it was, until, when their term is fulfilled and Allah wills to send them against the people, they dig until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one over them says: 'Go back, for you will dig through it tomorrow, if Allah wills.' They return to it, and it is in the state in which they left it, so they dig through it and come out upon the people." The hadith [is as mentioned], and it has been mentioned before.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they were not able﴾ with the lightening of the ta' according to the reading of the majority. It was said: it is a dialect with the meaning of "istata'u" (they were able). It was also said: rather, "istata'u" itself is common in Arabic speech, so some of them omitted the ta' from it and said "ista'u," and some omitted the ta' from it and said "ista'a yasti'u," with the meaning of "istata'a yastati'u," and this is a well-known dialect. Hamza alone read "fa-ma isṭṭa'u" with a shadda on the ta', as if he intended "istata'u," then assimilated the ta' into the ta', and so doubled it. This is a weak reading; Abu 'Ali said: it is not permissible. [[Al-Nahhas said: no one can rely on it, because the sin is quiescent and the assimilated ta' is quiescent. Sibawayh said: this is impossible.]] Al-A'mash read "fa-ma istata'u an yazharuhu wa-ma istata'u lahu naqban" with the ta' in both places.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾. The speaker is Dhu al-Qarnayn, and by "this" he pointed to the barrier, and to the strength to build it, and to the benefit of it in averting the harm of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "hadhihi rahmatun min rabbi" (this is a mercy from my Lord).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the time of their emergence.

(Ja'alahu dakkan): that is, made level with the earth. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder (dakkan dakkan)﴾ [al-Fajr: 21]. Ibn 'Arafah said: that is, it was made level, with no hillock in it. And from this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He made it a dakk (level)﴾. Al-Yazidi said: that is, levelled. It is said: a she-camel "dakka'" when her hump has gone. Al-Qutabi said: that is, he made it crushed and pressed flat against the earth. Al-Kalbi said: pieces, broken in pieces, and he said:

Is it not that the one who came (to it) pounded a cave so that it collapsed? Al-Azhari said: it is said "dakktuhu," meaning "daqqaqtuhu" (I crushed it).

As for the one who read "dakkā'" (with a long vowel), he intended "He made the mountain into a level ground, dakkā'," and that is the raised ground that does not reach the height of a mountain; its plural is dakkāwāt.

Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "dakkā'" with the long vowel (madd), by way of comparison with the she-camel dakkā' (dakkā', the one without a hump). In the speech there is an elision whose sense is: "He made it like a dakkā'," and this elision must be assumed, because the barrier (sadd) is masculine, so it is not described as dakkā'.

As for the one who read "dakkan," it is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of dakka, yadukku, when it means to demolish and grind down. It is possible that "ja'ala" (made) here means "khalaqa" (created). "Dakkā'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The same accusative applies also in the reading of the one who used the long vowel; it admits both possibilities.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 18, verse 92–98 (part 1 of 3):

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾ until, when he reached between the two barriers, ﴿he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾. The two barriers are two mountains on the side of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Ata al-Khurasani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Between the two barriers" means the two mountains of Armenia and Azerbaijan. ﴿Beside them﴾ means behind them.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yufqihuna (يُفْقِهُونَ) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the qaf, from afqaha (to make clear), meaning they could not make others understand speech. The rest read it with a fatha on the ya' and the qaf (yafqahuna, يَفْقَهُونَ), meaning they could not understand. Both readings are sound: they neither understand others nor are understood by others.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: O Dhul-Qarnayn!﴾ That is, a righteous community of mankind said to him: ﴿Indeed, Gog and Magog are corrupters in the earth.﴾

Al-Akhfash said: whoever hamzes Ya'juj and makes the two alifs part of the root, says Ya'juj is on the pattern of yaf'ul and Ma'juj on the pattern of maf'ul, as if it derives from ajij al-nar (the crackling of fire). He said: whoever does not hamz it and treats the two alifs as added letters, says "Yajuj" is from yajajtu and "Majuj" is from majajta, and both are not diptoted (ghayr munsarifayn). Ru'ba said:

"If Yajuj and Majuj together,
and 'Ad 'Ad and they gathered an army of Tubba'..."

al-Jawhari mentioned it. It was also said that they are not diptoted because they are foreign names, like Talut and Jalut, not derived, and their two reasons for not taking tanwin are foreignness and definiteness and feminine form. A group said: it is arabized from ajja and ajjaja, and its two reasons for not taking tanwin are definiteness and feminine form. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that both are Arabic. Whoever hamzes Ya'juj, it is on the pattern of yaf'ul, like yarbu', from your saying ajjat al-nar, meaning it blazed; and from it comes al-ajij, and from it comes milh ujaj (salty water). Whoever does not hamz it, it is possible that he lightened the hamza and changed it into an alif, like ra's. As for Majuj, it is maf'ul from ajja, and the two words are of one root in derivation. Whoever does not hamz, it is possible that he lightened the hamza, and it is possible that it is fa'ul from majja, and the omission of tanwin in both is for feminine form and definiteness, as if it were the name of a tribe.

The scholars differed about their corruption. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: their corruption is their eating of the children of Adam. A group said: their corruption was only anticipated, that is, they would corrupt, so they sought a way to guard against them. A group said: their corruption is oppression, violence, killing, and all the other forms of corruption known among humans. And Allah knows best.

Reports have come about their description, their emergence, and that they are from the offspring of Yafith. Abu Hurayra narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Nuh had three sons: Sam, Ham, and Yafith. Sam fathered the Arabs, Persians, and Romans, and goodness is among them. Yafith fathered Yajuj and Majuj, the Turks and the Slavs, and there is no goodness among them. Ham fathered the Copts, the Berbers, and the Sudanese."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Adam (peace be upon him) had a wet dream, and his semen mixed with the dust, and he was distressed, so they were created from that water. Thus they are connected to us through the father, not through the mother. This is open to question, because the prophets (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them) do not have wet dreams, and they are only from the offspring of Yafith. Muqatil and others said the same.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No man of them dies until there are born to his loins a thousand men." He means Yajuj and Majuj. Abu Sa'id also said: "They are twenty-five tribes beyond Yajuj and Majuj. No man of these or of Yajuj and Majuj dies until there comes out of his loins a thousand men." Al-Qushayri mentioned it.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Yajuj and Majuj, and he said, peace be upon him: "Yajuj and Majuj are two peoples, each people four hundred thousand peoples [the addition is from al-Durr al-Manthur], each people whose number none knows except Allah. No man of them dies until there are born to him a thousand male offspring from his loins, all of whom bear arms." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, describe them to us." He said: "They are three kinds. One kind is like al-arz [al-arz: the pine tree], a tree in Syria, whose height is one hundred and twenty cubits. Another kind whose width and length are equal, about a cubit. Another kind which spreads its ear as a bed and covers itself with the other. They do not pass by an elephant, a wild beast, or a pig without eating it, and they eat whoever of them dies. Their vanguard is in Syria and their rearguard is in Khurasan. They drink the rivers of the East and the lake of Tiberias, and Allah prevents them from reaching Mecca, Medina, and Bayt al-Maqdis."

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "And one kind of them is a span tall, with claws and fangs like those of beasts of prey, the cooing of doves, the mating of animals, the howling of wolves; and hair that protects them from heat and cold; and large ears, one of which is woolly, in which they lie down for winter, and the other is a skin in which they spend summer. They dig the barrier until they almost break through it, but Allah restores it as it was, until they say: 'We shall break through it tomorrow, if Allah wills.' Then they break through it and come out, and people fortify themselves in fortresses. They shoot arrows toward the sky, and the arrow returns to them smeared with blood. Then Allah destroys them with the nagaf in their necks." Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it. (Nagaf, with a fatha on the na' and a sukun on the ghayn, is a worm that is found in the noses of camels and sheep; its singular is nagafa.)

'Ali also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Yajuj is a people having four hundred commanders, and likewise Majuj. No one of them dies until he sees a thousand horsemen from his offspring."

I say: it has come as a marfu' hadith from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, which Ibn Majah recorded in al-Sunan. He said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yajuj and Majuj dig every day, until when they almost see the rays of the sun, the one who is over them says: 'Return, and you will dig it tomorrow.' Then Allah restores it stronger than it was. When their term is complete and Allah wills to send them against people, they dig until, when they almost see the rays of the sun, he says: 'Return, and you will dig it tomorrow, if Allah wills,' and they add the exception. They return to it, and it is in the state they left it, so they dig it out, and they come out against people and drink up the water. People fortify themselves against them in their fortresses. They shoot their arrows toward the sky, and the blood returns upon them [this is from the narrator's words, which I remember (note in Ibn Majah)]. They say: 'We have conquered the people of the earth and exalted over the people of heaven.' Then Allah sends upon them nagaf in their necks, and kills them with it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the beasts of the earth will grow fat and be satisfied with their flesh."

Al-Jawhari said: the she-camel shukarat (شَكَرَتِ), yashkuru shukran, so she is shakira; and ashkara al-darʻ (the udder) meant it was filled with milk.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Dhul-Qarnayn saw them, and the height of one of them was like half of a man of average build among us. They had claws in the places of nails, molars and fangs like beasts of prey, and jaws like those of camels. They had hair on them that covered them. Each one of them had two large ears; he wraps himself in one and spreads the other as a bed. Each one of them knows his term; he does not die until there come out of his loins a thousand men, if it is a male, or from her womb a thousand women, if it is a female.

Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of Yajuj and Majuj who came out to raid. Dhul-Qarnayn came and struck the barrier, and they remained on this side. Al-Suddi said: the barrier was built over twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Qatada also said this.

I say: if this is so, then the Prophet (ﷺ) described the Turks as he described Yajuj and Majuj. He, peace be upon him, said: "The Hour will not come until the Muslims fight the Turks, a people whose faces are like hammered shields, who wear hair and walk in hair." In another narration: "who wear hair as sandals." Muslim and Abu Dawud and others recorded it.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) knew their number, their multitude, and the sharpness of their might, he, peace be upon him, said: "Leave the Turks as long as they leave you." At this time, peoples of them have come out that none can count except Allah, and none can turn them back from the Muslims except Allah, until it is as if they were Yajuj and Majuj, or their vanguard.

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Bakra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People of my nation will settle in a low land they call Basra, by a river called Dijla, over which there is a bridge; its people will be many, and it will be among the cities of the emigrants." Ibn Yahya said, Abu Ma'mar said: "and it will be among the cities of the Muslims." "Then when it is the end of time, the sons of Qantura will come, broad-faced and small-eyed, until they descend on the bank of the river. Its people will split into three groups: one group will take the tails of cows and the desert, and they will perish; one group will take for themselves and disbelieve; and one group will place their offspring behind their backs and fight them, and they are the martyrs."

Al-ghA'it is the low-lying land; al-Basra is soft stones, and Basra was named after it. The sons of Qantura are the Turks.
